items.text: Mishnah: Dispute on when to mention rain
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute on when to mention rain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the start date for mentioning rain in prayer. Rabbi Yehoshua argues that since rain is a curse on Sukkot, one should not mention it then, but Rabbi Eliezer clarifies he only means to mention 'Mashiv haruach umorid hageshem' in its proper season, not to ask for rain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the question of when to mention the might of rain in prayer, and presents Rabbi Eliezer's position that it begins on the first day of Sukkot.
Rabbi Yehoshua counters that the mention begins on the last day of Sukkot.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects that since rain is a curse on Sukkot, why mention it at all during the festival.
Rabbi Eliezer clarifies that he only meant to mention 'Mashiv haruach umorid hageshem' in its proper season, not to ask for rain.
Rabbi Yehoshua retorts that if so, one should mention it all year round.

items.text: Mishnah: When to ask for rain and Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Mishnah: When to ask for rain and Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one only asks for rain close to the rainy season. Rabbi Yehuda adds a ruling about the prayer leader on the last day of Sukkot and the first day of Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that one only asks for rain close to the rainy season.
Rabbi Yehuda adds a ruling about when the prayer leader mentions rain on the last day of Sukkot and the first day of Passover.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why is this Mishnah placed here?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why is this Mishnah placed here?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna placed this Mishnah here, suggesting it should have been placed earlier in the tractate. It questions why the Tanna skipped the earlier context and only now teaches 'me'eimatai'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the Tanna is standing to teach 'me'eimatai', and answers that he is standing in the context of the earlier Mishnah about mentioning rain in the Amidah.
The Gemara objects: why not teach this Mishnah there (in the earlier context), and why skip until here?

items.text: Answer: The Tanna comes from Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Answer: The Tanna comes from Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Tanna is continuing from the discussion of Rosh Hashanah, where it was taught that on Sukkot the world is judged regarding water. Therefore, the Tanna now teaches when to mention rain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Tanna is continuing from the discussion of Rosh Hashanah, where it was taught that on Sukkot the world is judged regarding water, so the Tanna now teaches when to mention rain.

items.text: פירוש 'גבורות גשמים'
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why 'gevurot geshamim'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says 'gevurot geshamim' instead of just 'geshamim'. Rabbi Yochanan explains that rain comes with great force, citing verses. Rabba bar Sheila derives this from a verbal analogy between 'cheker' in Job and 'cheker' in Isaiah.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע נקראים 'גבורות גשמים', ורבי יוחנן משיב מפני שיורדים בגבורה, ומביא פסוקים. רבא בר שיילא דורש גזירה שווה 'חקר' מ'חקר' מבריאת העולם, ומקשר לגבורה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the phrase 'gevurot geshamim' (might of rains) instead of simply 'geshamim' (rains).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע המשנה לא אמרה 'מזכירים על הגשמים' אלא 'גבורות גשמים'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that rains are called 'gevurot' because they descend with great force, citing verses from Job and Isaiah.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע המשנה לא אמרה 'מזכירים על הגשמים' אלא 'גבורות גשמים'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the cited verses imply force.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן מוכח שהפסוקים עוסקים בגבורה.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Sheila derives the connection through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) on the word 'cheker' (investigation) between the creation of the world and the rains, citing a verse that describes God as 'girded with might'.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן מוכח שהפסוקים עוסקים בגבורה.

items.text: מקור הזכרת גשמים בתפילה
items.text_en: Source that rain is mentioned in prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraitha that derives from the verse 'to love the Lord your God and to serve Him with all your heart' that service of the heart is prayer, and the following verse discusses rain, establishing the connection.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הדורשת את הפסוק 'ולעבדו בכל לבבכם' – זו תפילה, וסמוך לו 'ונתתי מטר ארצכם', ללמד שמבקשים גשמים בתפילה.

sub.desc_en: The baraitha derives from the verse 'to love the Lord your God and to serve Him with all your heart' that service of the heart is prayer, and the following verse discusses rain, establishing the connection.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הדורשת 'ולעבדו בכל לבבכם' זו תפילה, וסמוך לו 'ונתתי מטר ארצכם', ללמד שמבקשים גשמים בתפילה.

items.text: שלושת המפתחות שביד הקב"ה
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: Three keys not given to an agent
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that three keys are in God's hand alone: the key of rain, the key of childbirth, and the key of resurrection. The key of rain is derived from Deuteronomy, and the key of childbirth from Genesis.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן אומר ששלושה מפתחות לא נמסרו לשליח: מפתח גשמים, חיה (לידה) ותחיית המתים. הגמרא מביאה פסוקים לגשמים ולידה, ומתחילה פסוק לתחיית המתים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan declares that three keys—rain, childbirth, and resurrection—are held exclusively by God and not entrusted to any agent.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן פותח ואומר ששלושה מפתחות ביד הקב"ה שלא נמסרו לשליח: גשמים, חיה ותחיית המתים.

sub.text_en: Supporting scriptural proof for the key of rain
sub.desc_en: The key of rain is proven from Deuteronomy 28:12, where God opens His good treasure to give rain.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מביא ראיה מהפסוקים למפתח הגשמים (דברים כח, יב) ולמפתח החיה (בראשית ל, כב).

sub.text_en: Supporting scriptural proof for the key of childbirth
sub.desc_en: The key of childbirth is derived from Genesis 30:22, where God remembers Rachel and opens her womb.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מביא ראיה מהפסוקים למפתח הגשמים (דברים כח, יב) ולמפתח החיה (בראשית ל, כב).

items.text: The three keys and the status of rain
items.text_en: The three keys and the status of rain
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the three keys (rain, childbirth, resurrection) and notes that in the West they add a key for sustenance. Rabbi Yochanan does not count it because rain is sustenance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses for the keys of childbirth and resurrection.
The Western sages add a key for sustenance, citing a verse.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan does not count the key of sustenance.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that rain is itself sustenance, so no separate key is needed.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's source: lulav or water-libation?
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's source: lulav or water-libation?
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether Rabbi Eliezer learns the time for mentioning rain from the lulav (daytime) or from the water-libation (nighttime). Rabbi Avahu resolves that he learned it from the lulav, though some say he had a tradition or a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: from which source did Rabbi Eliezer derive the time for mentioning rain — from the lulav (daytime) or from the water-libation (nighttime)?
The Gemara explores both possibilities: if from the lulav, the mention is by day; if from the water-libation, it is by night, as the libation can be performed at night.
Rabbi Avahu resolves that Rabbi Eliezer learned it from the lulav, though some say he had a tradition or a baraita.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabbi Yehoshua on the time of mention
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabbi Yehoshua on the time of mention
items.desc_en: A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says from the time of taking the lulav, Rabbi Yehoshua says from the time of putting it down. Rabbi Eliezer argues that the four species require water, so mention begins with them. Rabbi Yehoshua objects that rain on Sukkot is a curse, but Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes between asking and mentioning, comparing it to resurrection. Rabbi adds that one stops mentioning when one stops asking.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says mention begins from the time of taking the lulav, Rabbi Yehoshua says from the time of putting it down.
Rabbi Eliezer argues that the four species require water, so mention begins with them.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects that rain on Sukkot is a curse.
Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes between asking and mentioning, comparing it to resurrection.
Rabbi adds that one stops mentioning when one stops asking.

items.text: Other opinions: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Other opinions: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says mention on the second day of Sukkot, Rabbi Akiva on the sixth. Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua says the last prayer leader on the last day of Sukkot mentions, the first does not; on the first day of Passover, the first mentions, the last does not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira states that one mentions rain on the second day of Sukkot.
Rabbi Akiva states that one mentions rain on the sixth day of Sukkot.

Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua rules that on the last day of Sukkot the last prayer leader mentions rain and the first does not; on the first day of Passover the first mentions and the last does not.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Eliezer's analogy
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Eliezer's analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer's argument seems strong, but Rabbi Yehoshua could respond: resurrection is always timely, but rain after Nissan is a curse, as per the Mishnah. Thus the analogy fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yehoshua could reject Rabbi Eliezer's argument, since it appears strong.

sub.text: Gemara's answer on behalf of Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer on behalf of Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehoshua could respond: resurrection is always timely, so the analogy with rain is flawed.
The Gemara objects that rain after Nissan is a curse, as per the Mishnah, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's reason: the water-libation hint
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's reason: the water-libation hint
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's view: the word 'ונסכיהם' on the second day hints at water (mem-yud-mem = 40+10+40 = 90 = mayim). He specifically picks the second day because the hint is there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's reason for beginning the mention of rain on the second day of Sukkot.

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira cites the verses from the second, sixth, and seventh days of Sukkot, noting that the letters mem-yud-mem in the second day's verse hint at water (מַיִם), providing a Torah hint for the water libation.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira specifically picks the second day because the hint for water is found in the verse of the second day, so the mention of rain begins then.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's reason: two libations on the sixth day
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's reason: two libations on the sixth day
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva says mention on the sixth day because the verse 'וּנְסָכֶיהָ' implies two libations (water and wine). The Gemara questions why it couldn't be both wine, and answers that he agrees with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira that water is hinted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva states that one mentions rain on the sixth day of Sukkot, citing the verse 'וּנְסָכֶיהָ' (its libations) which implies two libations—water and wine.
The Gemara objects: perhaps both libations are wine, not water.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who taught that water is hinted in the verses.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's position on the water libation
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's position on the water libation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rabbi Akiva does not hold like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira regarding the water libation, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Nathan derives both water and wine libations from the verse 'בקודש הסך נסך שכר לה''.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, why does he not rule like him regarding the water libation?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva holds the extra libation verse refers to the sixth day, not the seventh.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Nathan derives both water and wine libations from the verse 'בקודש הסך נסך שכר לה''.
The Gemara objects: perhaps both libations refer to wine, and the double expression is merely stylistic.
The Gemara resolves that the unusual phrasing 'הסך נסך' indicates one libation of water and one of wine.

items.text: זיהוי בעל המשנה 'ניסוך המים כל שבעה'
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah: water libation all seven days
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions who holds that the water libation is performed all seven days of Sukkot, considering the views of Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira. It first suggests Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, but then raises a difficulty from the timing of the water libation in the Torah.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מי התנא של משנה זו, ודוחה את האפשרויות: רבי יהושע (יום אחד), רבי עקיבא (יומיים), רבי יהודה בן בתירא (שישה ימים). לבסוף מסבירה שרבי יהודה בן בתירא סובר כרבי יהודה במשנה אחרת, אך נדחה כי גם השמיני קשה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah that teaches the water libation (ניסוך המים) is performed all seven days of Sukkot, noting that Rabbi Yehoshua would say one day, Rabbi Akiva two days, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira six days.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: המשנה האומרת שניסוך המים כל שבעה, מי הוא התנא? ומפרטת שאף אחד מהתנאים המוזכרים אינו מתאים בדיוק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it is Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who holds like Rabbi Yehuda of the Mishnah, who says the water libation is performed with a log (לוג) all eight days, excluding the first and including the eighth.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: לעולם רבי יהודה בן בתירא היא, וסבירא ליה כרבי יהודה במשנה שאומר שניסוך המים כל שמונה, ומוציא ראשון ומכניס שמיני.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why exclude the first day? Because the water libation is hinted in the Torah only from the second day; similarly, the eighth day is excluded because the hint is only until the seventh day.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מה שונה ראשון שאינו ניסוך, הרי רמיזת מים בשני; ושמיני נמי, הרי רמיזת מים בשביעי? ומשתמטת.

items.text: קביעת המשנה כרבי יהושע והלכה למשה מסיני
items.text_en: Water libation as a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the mishnah is Rabbi Yehoshua's view, and the water libation all seven days is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai, citing a tradition from Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Nechunya.
items.desc: הגמרא קובעת שהמשנה היא כרבי יהושע, וניסוך המים כל שבעה היא הלכה למשה מסיני, כפי שאמר רבי יוחנן בשם רבי נחוניא. מובאת רשימת שלוש הלכות: עשר נטיעות, ערבה, וניסוך המים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by identifying the mishnah as Rabbi Yehoshua's view and stating that the water libation for all seven days is a received halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai.
sub.desc: הגמרא קובעת שהמשנה היא כרבי יהושע, וניסוך המים כל שבעה הוא הלכה למשה מסיני.

sub.text: רבי אמי בשם רבי יוחנן בשם רבי נחוניא
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Nechunya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami transmits a tradition in the name of Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Nechunya that ten saplings, the willow branch, and the water libation are all halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai.
sub.desc: מביא מסורת כי עשר נטיעות, ערבה וניסוך המים הם הלכה למשה מסיני.

items.text: ברייתא על הזכרת גשמים ומחלוקת רבי יהודה ורבי יהושע בן בתירא
items.text_en: Conflicting traditions about mentioning rain in prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda cites Rabbi Yehoshua regarding when to mention rain, and another where Rabbi Yehuda cites ben Beteira. It identifies the correct Rabbi Yehoshua and ben Beteira, resolving the contradictions with Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira.
items.desc: רבי יהודה אומר בשם רבי יהושע: באחרון של חג האחרון מזכיר, בראשון של פסח הראשון מזכיר. הגמרא מקשה: איזה רבי יהושע? ומתרצת שמדובר ברבי יהושע בן בתירא, שלפעמים נקרא בשמו ולפעמים בשם אביו.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua that on the last day of Sukkot the prayer leader mentions rain, but on the first day of Passover the first leader mentions rain and the last does not.
sub.desc: הבאת ברייתא: רבי יהודה בשם רבי יהושע קובע מתי מזכירים גשמים בתפילה בחג ובפסח.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Rabbi Yehoshua is meant, noting that the Rabbi Yehoshua of the Mishnah holds that one mentions rain only on the last day of Sukkot.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: לאיזה רבי יהושע התכוון רבי יהודה? אם למשנתנו, הרי הוא אומר שמזכירים מהאחרון, ולא כפי שנאמר בברייתא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it must be Rabbi Yehoshua of the baraita, who holds that one mentions rain from the time of placing the willow branch.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: אולי הכוונה לרבי יהושע דברייתא, אך גם הוא אומר שמזכירים משעת הנחתו, דהיינו מסוף היום השביעי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of ben Beteira that the last leader mentions rain, and asks which ben Beteira is meant, noting that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira holds one mentions rain on the second day of the festival.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה קושיה נוספת: גם בברייתא אחרת רבי יהודה אומר בשם בן בתירא, אך אם הכוונה לרבי יהודה בן בתירא, הרי הוא אומר שמזכירים מהשני בחג.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by identifying the figure as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira, who is sometimes called by his own name and sometimes by his father's name, and the two baraitot reflect different stages: before and after his ordination (סמיכה).
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק מיישב: הכוונה לרבי יהושע בן בתירא, שלפעמים נקרא בשמו ולפעמים בשם אביו, לפי אם נסמך קודם או אחר כך.

items.text: דין הזכרת טל ורוחות
items.text_en: Dew and winds: not obligatory to mention
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that the Sages did not obligate mentioning dew and winds in prayer, but if one wishes, they may. Rabbi Chanina explains the reason: they are not withheld. The Gemara proves that dew is not withheld from the story of Elijah.
items.desc: תניא: בטל וברוחות לא חייבו חכמים להזכיר, ואם בא להזכיר – מזכיר. רבי חנינא מסביר: לפי שאין נעצרים. הגמרא מביאה ראיה מהפסוק באליהו שלא הזכיר טל בעצירת הגשמים.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that the Sages did not obligate mentioning dew and winds in prayer, but if one wishes, they may mention them.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדין טל ורוחות שאין חייבים להזכירם, ואם בא להזכיר – מזכיר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason why dew and winds are not obligatory to mention.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה הטעם שאין חייבים להזכיר טל ורוחות.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina answers that dew and winds are not withheld, so there is no need to pray for them.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדין טל ורוחות שאין חייבים להזכירם, ואם בא להזכיר – מזכיר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proves that dew is not withheld from the story of Elijah, who swore that there would be no dew or rain, but God later promised rain without mentioning dew, implying dew is never withheld.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה הטעם שאין חייבים להזכיר טל ורוחות.

items.text: דיון על טל וברכתו
items.text_en: Clarifying Elijah's statement about dew
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Elijah swore that dew would not come if dew is never withheld. It explains that Elijah meant even the dew of blessing would not come, and why he didn't just restore the dew of blessing.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע אליהו נשבע שלא יהיה טל, והרי טל אינו נעצר. מתרצת שאפילו טל ברכה לא ירד, ואין צורך להחזירו כי אין היכר בין טל ברכה לטל רגיל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Elijah swore that dew would not come, given that dew is never withheld.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הטל אינו נעצר, מדוע נשבע אליהו שלא יהיה טל?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Elijah meant even the dew of blessing would not come, and that he could not restore only the dew of blessing because it would not be noticeable.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הטל אינו נעצר, מדוע נשבע אליהו שלא יהיה טל?

items.text: הוכחה שרוחות אינן נעצרות
items.text_en: Proof that winds are not withheld
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from a verse that winds are never withheld, interpreting the verse as a comparison: just as the world cannot exist without winds, so it cannot exist without Israel.
items.desc: רבי יהושע בן לוי מביא ראיה מהפסוק 'כי כארבע רוחות השמים פרשתי אתכם' שכשם שאי אפשר לעולם בלא רוחות, כך אי אפשר בלא ישראל, ומכאן שרוחות תמידיות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that winds are never withheld?
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד שרוחות אינן נעצרות, ומציעה פירוש אפשרי לפסוק ודוחה אותו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites a verse to prove that winds are never withheld, interpreting it as a comparison: just as the world cannot exist without winds, so it cannot exist without Israel.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד שרוחות אינן נעצרות, ומציעה פירוש אפשרי לפסוק ודוחה אותו.

items.text: Halakha for mentioning wind and rain in prayer
items.text_en: Halakha for mentioning wind and rain in prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules: in the summer, if one said 'Who causes the wind to blow' he is not required to repeat the prayer, but if he said 'Who brings down the rain' he must repeat. In the rainy season, the opposite applies, and even saying 'Who makes the wind pass and the dew vanish' does not require repetition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules that in the summer, if one said 'Who causes the wind to blow' he is not required to repeat the prayer, but if he said 'Who brings down the rain' he must repeat.

Rabbi Chanina rules that in the rainy season, if one did not say 'Who causes the wind to blow' he is not required to repeat, but if he did not say 'Who brings down the rain' he must repeat, and even saying 'Who makes the wind pass and the dew vanish' does not require repetition.

items.text: Tanna's ruling on mentioning clouds and winds
items.text_en: Tanna's ruling on mentioning clouds and winds
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the Sages did not obligate mentioning clouds and winds in prayer, but if one wishes to mention them, he may, because they are never withheld.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna rules that the Sages did not obligate mentioning clouds and winds in prayer, but if one wishes to mention them, he may, because they are never withheld.

items.text: קושיה מברייתא על עצירת רוחות ועננים
items.text_en: Contradiction about clouds and winds being withheld
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita of Rav Yosef that interprets 'He will withhold the heavens' as withholding clouds and winds. It resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between sharp clouds and gentle clouds, and between common winds and uncommon winds, with a further clarification about winds for winnowing.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא של רב יוסף שמפרשת 'ועצר את השמים' כעצירת עננים ורוחות. מתרצת: עננים – הא בחרפי (מוקדמים) הא באפלי (מאוחרים); רוחות – הא ברוח מצויה הא ברוח שאינה מצויה, ורוח שאינה מצויה אפשר לנפות בנפוותא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita of Rav Yosef interprets 'וְעָצַר אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם' (He will withhold the heavens) as withholding clouds and winds, implying they can be withheld.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא של רב יוסף שפסוק 'ועצר את השמים' כולל עצירת עננים ורוחות, בניגוד לקביעה שאינם נעצרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction about clouds by distinguishing between חָרְפֵי (sharp clouds) and אַפְלֵי (gentle clouds).
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: אין קושיה, שעננים מוקדמים (חרפי) אינם נעצרים, אך מאוחרים (אפלי) נעצרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction about winds by distinguishing between רוּחַ מְצוּיָה (common wind) and רוּחַ שֶׁאֵינָהּ מְצוּיָה (uncommon wind).
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: רוח מצויה אינה נעצרת, אך רוח שאינה מצויה נעצרת; ואף שצריך לדיש, אפשר בנפות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that an uncommon wind is useful for winnowing (בֵי דָרֵי), and answers that one can manage with a winnowing fan (נָפְווֹתָא).
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: רוח מצויה אינה נעצרת, אך רוח שאינה מצויה נעצרת; ואף שצריך לדיש, אפשר בנפות.

items.text: עננים ורוחות לאחר גשם
items.text_en: Clouds and winds after rain
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that clouds and winds are secondary to rain. Ulla or Rav Yehuda explains this means after rain. The Gemara questions whether this is beneficial, citing a verse about dust and ashes, and resolves by distinguishing between a gentle wind and a strong wind, or between one that raises dust and one that does not.
items.desc: ברייתא אומרת שעננים ורוחות שניות למטר. עולא ורב יהודה מפרשים שמדובר לאחר גשם. מקשים מהפסוק 'יתן ה' את מטר ארצך אבק ועפר' שמדבר ברוח רעה לאחר גשם. מתרצים: הא דאתי ניחא, הא דאתי רזיא; או הא דמעלה אבק, הא דלא מעלה אבק.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that clouds and winds are secondary to rain.
sub.desc: ברייתא קובעת שעננים ורוחות חשובים כמשניים למטר.

sub.desc_en: Ulla or Rav Yehuda explains that the baraita refers to clouds and winds after rain.
sub.desc: ברייתא קובעת שעננים ורוחות חשובים כמשניים למטר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether this is beneficial, citing a verse about dust and ashes and Ulla's or Rav Yehuda's statement that the wind after rain is destructive.
sub.desc: ברייתא קובעת שעננים ורוחות חשובים כמשניים למטר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a gentle wind and a strong wind, or between one that raises dust and one that does not.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: הרוח הטובה היא הבאה בנחת, והרעה היא החזקה; או תירוץ אחר: הרוח שאינה מעלה אבק טובה, והמעלה אבק רעה.

items.text: Benefits of wind, cloud, sun, and snow after rain
items.text_en: Benefits of wind, cloud, sun, and snow after rain
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that wind after rain is like rain, cloud after rain is like rain, and sun after rain is like two rains. Rava adds that snow on mountains is equivalent to five rains on land, and distinguishes between different types of rain for trees and fruit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that wind after rain is like rain, cloud after rain is like rain, and sun after rain is like two rains, excluding night dew and sun between ice patches.
Rava adds that snow on mountains is equivalent to five rains on land, citing the verse 'For to the snow He says, Be on the earth, and to the shower of rain, and to the showers of His mighty rain.'
Rava further distinguishes that snow benefits mountains, hard rain benefits trees, and gentle rain benefits fruit.

items.text: Aggadic teachings about Torah scholars
items.text_en: Aggadic teachings about Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rava compares a Torah scholar to a mulberry shoot that once it sprouts, it sprouts. Rava also says that a Torah scholar who gets angry is inflamed by Torah itself, and Rav Ashi says a scholar must be hard as iron. Rabbi Abba and Ravina add further nuances.

sub.desc_en: The gemara explains the word 'עורפילא' (a mulberry shoot) and cites Rava's teaching that a Torah scholar is like a mulberry shoot: once it sprouts, it sprouts.
Rava adds that a Torah scholar who gets angry is inflamed by Torah itself, citing the verse 'Is not My word like fire?'
Rav Ashi teaches that a Torah scholar who is not hard as iron is not a Torah scholar, citing the verse 'like a hammer that shatters a rock.'
Rabbi Abba tells Rav Ashi that they derive the hardness of a Torah scholar from a different verse: 'a land whose stones are iron,' read as 'whose builders are iron.'
Ravina concludes that even so, a person must learn with gentleness, citing the verse 'remove anger from your heart.'

items.text: Three who asked improperly: Eliezer, Saul, and Jephthah
items.text_en: Three who asked improperly: Eliezer, Saul, and Jephthah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan lists three who asked improperly: Eliezer, Saul, and Jephthah. Two were answered properly (Eliezer and Saul), but Jephthah was answered improperly. The Gemara elaborates on each case and connects Jephthah's vow to the prophet's rebuke.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan lists three who asked improperly: Eliezer, Saul, and Jephthah.
The Gemara explains that Eliezer asked improperly by leaving the sign open to any girl, but was answered properly when Rivka appeared.
The Gemara explains that Saul asked improperly by offering his daughter to any killer, but was answered properly when David killed Goliath.
The Gemara explains that Jephthah asked improperly by vowing to sacrifice whatever came out of his house, and was answered improperly when his daughter came out.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the prophet's rebuke
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the prophet's rebuke
sub.desc_en: The Gemara connects Jephthah's improper vow to the prophet's rebuke in Jeremiah, asking why there is no remedy in Gilead.
The Gemara interprets the verse: 'which I did not command' refers to Mesha's son, 'did not speak' refers to Jephthah, and 'did not arise in My heart' refers to Isaac.

items.text: Knesset Yisrael also asked improperly
items.text_en: Knesset Yisrael also asked improperly
items.desc_en: Rabbi Berechya adds that Knesset Yisrael (the congregation of Israel) also asked improperly twice. God answered properly each time, promising to be like dew and to engrave them on His palms.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Berechya opens by stating that Knesset Yisrael also asked improperly, citing the verse about seeking God like rain.
God responds properly, promising to be like dew (טל) which is always available, unlike rain which is intermittent.
Knesset Yisrael asks a second time improperly, requesting to be like a seal on God's heart and arm, and God responds properly by promising to engrave them on His palms.

items.text: Halakhic debate: asking for rain and mentioning rain
items.text_en: Halakhic debate: asking for rain and mentioning rain
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's rule that one does not ask for rain. It considers whether asking and mentioning are the same. Rava says the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who says one asks from the time of placing the etrog. Abaye objects that even Rabbi Eliezer might distinguish between asking and mentioning. An alternative version is introduced.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the Mishnah's rule forbids asking for rain, and it assumes that asking (שאלה) and mentioning (הזכרה) are the same, then asks which Tanna holds this view.
Rava answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds that one asks for rain from the time of placing the etrog (i.e., after Sukkot).
Abaye objects that even if one attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Eliezer, he might distinguish between asking (שאלה) and mentioning (הזכרה) as separate matters.
The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the discussion, beginning with 'לֵימָא' (let us say).

items.text: Rava's resolution of the Mishnah's dispute
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of the Mishnah's dispute
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the Mishnah can be attributed to Rabbi Yehoshua, but even if it follows Rabbi Eliezer, asking and mentioning are separate matters.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the Mishnah's dispute by stating that even if it follows Rabbi Eliezer, asking (שאלה) and mentioning (הזכרה) are separate matters.

items.text: Contradiction between Mishnah and Baraita
items.text_en: Contradiction between Mishnah and Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says one asks for rain until Passover, while Rabbi Meir says until Nisan, creating a contradiction with the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says one asks for rain until Passover, and Rabbi Meir says until Nisan.
The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah and the Baraita regarding the deadline for asking for rain.

items.text: Rav Chisda's distinction between asking and mentioning
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction between asking and mentioning
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between asking for rain and mentioning rain: one may ask until the end of the season, but mentioning stops on the first festival day.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between asking for rain (which continues until the end of the season) and mentioning rain (which stops on the first festival day).

items.text: Ulla's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Ulla's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Ulla objects to Rav Chisda's distinction using a kal vachomer argument, and instead explains that there are two Tannaim who disagree within Rabbi Yehuda's position.

sub.desc_en: Ulla objects to Rav Chisda's distinction between asking and mentioning, using a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if in a place where one does not ask one still mentions, then in a place where one asks, certainly one should mention.
Ulla resolves the contradiction by asserting that there are two Tannaim who disagree within Rabbi Yehuda's position, rather than relying on Rav Chisda's distinction.

items.text: Rav Yosef's interpretation and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's interpretation and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that 'until Passover' means until the first shaliach tzibbur descends on the first festival day. Abaye questions whether asking occurs on a festival, and Rav Yosef responds with the meturgeman practice, but Abaye rejects this, concluding like Ulla.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that 'until Passover' means until the first shaliach tzibbur (prayer leader) descends on the first festival day of Passover.
Abaye questions whether asking for rain (שאלה) occurs on a festival day at all.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's response and Abaye's rejection
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's response and Abaye's rejection
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef responds that the meturgeman (translator) asks, but Abaye rejects this because the meturgeman only asks what the congregation needs, concluding like Ulla that the matter is a clarification.

items.text: Rabbah's interpretation and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Rabbah's interpretation and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that 'until Passover' means until the time of the Passover sacrifice, drawing an analogy between the beginning and end of the season. Abaye questions the logic for the end, and again concludes like Ulla.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains that 'until Passover' means until the time of the Passover sacrifice, drawing an analogy between the beginning and end of the season: just as at the start one mentions rain even without asking, so too at the end.
Abaye challenges Rabbah: at the start, mentioning rain is a form of requesting, but at the end, what request is there?
The gemara concludes that Rabbah's explanation is merely a clarification, but the true resolution follows Ulla's approach.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports that Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Zeira objects citing a different ruling by Rabbi Yochanan regarding Rabban Gamliel. The Gemara resolves the contradictions by distinguishing between different contexts: for us (Babylonians) and for them (Israelites), and between times when the Temple stands and when it does not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports that Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabbi Yehuda regarding the time for asking for rain.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection to Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection to Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects, citing a Mishnah where Rabban Gamliel gives a different date and Rabbi Elazar reports that Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabban Gamliel.
Rabbi Asi dismisses the objection as a contradiction between different authorities and initially resolves it by distinguishing between asking and mentioning rain.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the first answer
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the first answer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan himself said that where one asks for rain one also mentions it, and that starting and stopping are linked.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the practice for us (Babylonians) and for them (Israelites), and between times when the Temple stands and when it does not.

items.text: Practical ruling for the Diaspora with two festival days
items.text_en: Practical ruling for the Diaspora with two festival days
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the proper procedure for starting and stopping the mention of rain during the additional festival days in the Diaspora, with Shmuel objecting to Rav's approach and offering his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we in the Diaspora, who observe two festival days, should handle the start and stop of rain mention.
Rav rules that one begins mentioning rain in the Musaf prayer, stops in Mincha, evening, and morning prayers, and resumes in Musaf.
Shmuel objects to Rav's ruling, arguing that making the first day sacred and the second day profane is inconsistent.
Shmuel rules that one begins mentioning rain in Musaf and Mincha, stops in evening and morning prayers, and resumes in Musaf.

items.text: הלכה: התחלת הזכרת גשמים
items.text_en: Ruling on not stopping the rain prayer
items.desc_en: Rava and Rav Sheshet rule that once one begins reciting the rain prayer, one does not stop. Rav later retracts his earlier position, and the halakha is established accordingly.
items.desc: רבא ורב ששת פוסקים שמי שהתחיל להזכיר גשמים בתפילה אינו פוסק. רב חזר בו, והלכה כמותם.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that once one begins mentioning rain in prayer, one does not stop.
sub.desc: רבא ורב ששת קובעים שמי שהתחיל להזכיר גשמים אינו פוסק.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet supports Rava's ruling with the same statement.
sub.desc: רבא ורב ששת קובעים שמי שהתחיל להזכיר גשמים אינו פוסק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav retracted his earlier position, as cited by Rav Chananel, and now agrees that once one starts, one does not stop.
sub.desc: רב חזר בו והורה שמונה עשרים ואחד יום מראש השנה ואז מתחיל ואינו פוסק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the halakha is in accordance with the opinion that once one starts, one does not stop.
sub.desc: רב חזר בו והורה שמונה עשרים ואחד יום מראש השנה ואז מתחיל ואינו פוסק.

items.text: משנה: עד מתי שואלים גשמים
items.text_en: Mishnah: Until when do we ask for rain?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says until Passover passes, Rabbi Meir says until Nisan ends, citing the verse 'moreh and malkosh'.
items.desc: רבי יהודה אומר עד שיעבור הפסח, ורבי מאיר אומר עד שיצא ניסן, על פי הפסוק 'ויורד לכם גשם מורה ומלקוש בראשון'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the question: until when do we ask for rain? and presents the first opinion of Rabbi Yehuda (Rabbi Yehuda) that it is until Passover passes.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בשאלה עד מתי שואלים גשמים, ומביאה שתי דעות: רבי יהודה עד הפסח, ורבי מאיר עד סוף ניסן, על פי הפסוק מיספר יואל.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir (Rabbi Meir) gives the second opinion: until Nisan ends, citing the verse 'moreh and malkosh' as support.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בשאלה עד מתי שואלים גשמים, ומביאה שתי דעות: רבי יהודה עד הפסח, ורבי מאיר עד סוף ניסן, על פי הפסוק מיספר יואל.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'moreh' in Nisan
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'moreh' in Nisan
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak how 'moreh' can be in Nisan when the Mishnah states it is in Marcheshvan. Rabbi Yitzchak cites Rabbi Yochanan's explanation that the verse was fulfilled in Joel's time when rain fell on 1 Nisan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak how the term 'moreh' (early rain) can appear in Nisan when the Mishnah states it falls in Marcheshvan.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's answer citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's answer citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak answers that Rabbi Yochanan explained the verse was fulfilled in the days of Joel ben Petuel, when the first rain fell on 1 Nisan after Adar passed without rain.

items.text: Story of the miracle in Joel's time
items.text_en: Story of the miracle in Joel's time
items.desc_en: The prophet told Israel to sow despite the drought; they obeyed, and a miracle occurred revealing hidden food. They sowed and rain fell on 5 Nisan, leading to the omer offering from grain that grew in only 11 days. The verses about sowing in tears and reaping in joy are explained, with Rabbi Yehuda and Rav Chisda offering interpretations.

sub.desc_en: The prophet commands Israel to sow despite the drought; they object, but a miracle reveals hidden food.
They sow, rain falls on 5 Nisan, and the omer offering comes from grain that grew in only 11 days.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse about going and weeping carrying the seed.
Rabbi Yehuda explains that the ox weeps while plowing but joyfully returns eating clods, alluding to the verse.
The Gemara asks the meaning of 'bearing his sheaves' in the verse.
Rav Chisda (or a baraita) explains that a reed is a handbreadth and a stalk is two handbreadths, describing the miraculous growth.

items.text: פירוש הפסוק על רעב של שבע שנים
items.text_en: Explanation of the seven-year famine
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak what was eaten during the seven-year famine. Rabbi Yitzchak cites Rabbi Yochanan's detailed account of what was consumed each year, culminating in eating their own arms, fulfilling the verse.
items.desc: רב נחמן שואל מה אכלו בשבע שנות רעב, ורבי יצחק משיב בשם רבי יוחנן: שנה ראשונה אכלו מה שבבתים, שניה בשדות, שלישית בשר בהמה טהורה, רביעית טמאה, חמישית שקצים ורמשים, שישית בשר בניהם ובנותיהם, שביעית בשר זרועותיהם.

sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's question to Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak what people ate during the seven-year famine.
sub.desc: רב נחמן שואל את רבי יצחק מה אכלו בשבע שנות הרעב המוזכרות בפסוק.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan's detailed account
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak cites Rabbi Yochanan's account of what was consumed each year, culminating in eating their own arms, fulfilling the verse 'איש בשר זרועו יאכלו' (each man will eat the flesh of his own arm).
sub.desc: רבי יצחק משיב בשם רבי יוחנן ומפרט את שבעת השלבים של הרעב, מהמזון שבבתים ועד אכילת בשר זרועותיהם.

items.text: פירוש הפסוק 'בקרבך קדוש ולא אבוא בעיר'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Kadosh in your midst'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak about the verse 'Kadosh in your midst, and I will not come into the city.' Rabbi Yitzchak cites Rabbi Yochanan that God will not enter the heavenly Jerusalem until He enters the earthly one. The existence of a heavenly Jerusalem is proven from Psalms.
items.desc: רב נחמן שואל על הפסוק, ורבי יצחק משיב בשם רבי יוחנן: הקב"ה אומר שלא יבוא לירושלים של מעלה עד שיבוא לירושלים של מטה. הגמרא מביאה ראיה שיש ירושלים של מעלה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak about the verse 'קדוש בקרבך' (Holy in your midst) and whether God's not entering the city is because of that holiness.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מקשה על הפסוק: וכי בגלל שהקדוש ברוך הוא בקרבך לא יבוא לעיר?

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's answer citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak answers in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the Holy One, blessed be He, will not enter the heavenly Jerusalem until He enters the earthly Jerusalem.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מקשה על הפסוק: וכי בגלל שהקדוש ברוך הוא בקרבך לא יבוא לעיר?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there is a heavenly Jerusalem at all.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת אם יש ירושלים של מעלה, ומביאה ראיה מפסוק שיש ירושלים בנויה כעיר שחוברה לה יחדיו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers affirmatively, citing the verse 'ירושלים הבנויה כעיר שחוברה לה יחדיו' (Jerusalem built as a city that is joined together) as proof of a heavenly Jerusalem.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת אם יש ירושלים של מעלה, ומביאה ראיה מפסוק שיש ירושלים בנויה כעיר שחוברה לה יחדיו.

items.text: פירוש הפסוק 'ובאחת יבערו ויכסלו מוסר הבלים עץ הוא'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'one thing that burns'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak about the verse 'in one thing they are foolish.' Rabbi Yitzchak cites Rabbi Yochanan that idolatry is the one thing that burns the wicked in Gehinnom, as derived from a verbal analogy.
items.desc: רב נחמן שואל על הפסוק, ורבי יצחק משיב בשם רבי יוחנן: האחת שמבערת רשעים בגיהנם היא עבודה זרה, על פי גזרה שווה 'הבל'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak about the meaning of the verse 'ובאחת יבערו ויכסלו מוסר הבלים עץ הוא' (in one thing they are foolish, the instruction of vanities is wood).
Rabbi Yitzchak responds that Rabbi Yochanan (רבי יוחנן) explained: 'One thing' refers to the one thing that burns the wicked in Gehinnom — and that is idolatry (עבודה זרה).

Rabbi Yitzchak supports the identification by citing a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): the verse uses 'הבלים' (vanities) here, and the same root 'הבל' appears in the verse about idolatry 'הבל המה מעשה תעתועים' (they are vanity, works of mockery).

items.text: פירוש הפסוק 'כי שתים רעות עשה עמי'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'two evils'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak about the verse 'two evils My people have done,' questioning why only two are mentioned when there are many. The text cuts off, but Rabbi Yitzchak cites Rabbi Yochanan's answer.
items.desc: רב נחמן שואל מדוע נאמרו רק שתים רעות, והרי יש עשרים וארבע עבירות. רבי יצחק משיב בשם רבי יוחנן: האחת שהיא שקולה כנגד כולן היא עבודה זרה.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's question to Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's question to Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak why the verse 'כי שתים רעות עשה עמי' (for two evils My people have done) mentions only two evils, when there are twenty-four sins.

items.text: חטא עבודה זרה כחטא כפול
items.text_en: Gemara's exposition on the verse about idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that idolatry is considered equivalent to two transgressions, citing verses from Jeremiah. A baraita contrasts the Kutim and Kedarim, who remained loyal to their gods, with Israel who exchanged their glory for something worthless.
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק מירמיהו, ומסבירה שעם ישראל חטא בעבודה זרה, דבר הנחשב כשתי רעות. הברייתא מבהירה שגויים אינם מחליפים את אלוהיהם אף שיודעים שהם סותרים זה את זה, בניגוד לעם ישראל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what sin is equivalent to two, and answers that it is idolatry, citing verses from Jeremiah.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את הפסוק מירמיהו וקובעת שעבודה זרה נחשבת כשתי רעות, ומביאה הוכחה מהפסוק שעם ישראל המיר את כבודו בדבר שאינו מועיל.

sub.desc_en: A baraita contrasts the Kutim and Kedarim, who remained loyal to their gods, with Israel who exchanged their glory for something worthless.
sub.desc: הברייתא מבהירה שגויים אינם מחליפים את אלוהיהם אף שיודעים שהם סותרים זה את זה, בניגוד לעם ישראל שהמיר את כבודו.

items.text: זקנתו המוקדמת של שמואל
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's question about Samuel's old age and the divine response
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak how Samuel could be described as old when he died at 52. Rabbi Yitzchak cites Rabbi Yochanan that old age jumped upon him because God could not let Samuel die young due to his merit, nor let Saul die, and David's kingship was imminent. Thus, God caused Samuel to age prematurely.
items.desc: רב נחמן מקשה על הפסוק 'ויהי כאשר זקן שמואל', שכן שמואל מת בגיל 52. רבי יצחק משיב בשם רבי יוחנן שזקנה קפצה עליו, משום ששמואל ביקש שלא יבוטל מעשה ידיו (מלכות שאול), והקב"ה הקדים לו זקנה כדי ששאול יישב בגבעה בזכות תפילת שמואל.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak how Samuel could be described as old when he died at only fifty-two years old.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that old age sprang upon Samuel, and explains Samuel's prayer that his handiwork not be annulled as was the case with Moses and Aaron.

sub.text: Holy One Blessed be He (narrated by Gemara)
sub.text_en: Holy One Blessed be He (narrated by Gemara)
sub.desc_en: God considers the dilemma: He cannot let Saul die because Samuel prevents it, nor let Samuel die young lest people murmur, nor delay David's kingship, since one kingdom does not overlap with another.

sub.text: Holy One Blessed be He (narrated by Gemara)
sub.text_en: Holy One Blessed be He (narrated by Gemara)
sub.desc_en: God resolves the dilemma by springing old age upon Samuel, and the verse about Saul dwelling in Gibeah is explained as resulting from Samuel's prayer.

items.text: דחיית אדם מפני אדם
items.text_en: Proof that one person can be pushed aside for another
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one person can be pushed aside for another, and answers affirmatively, citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan on a verse from Hosea indicating that God's words can cause displacement.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת אם ניתן לדחות אדם מפני אדם, ועונה בשם רבי יוחנן שכן, כפי שנאמר 'הרגתים באימרי פי' – הקב"ה גוזר והנביאים מתים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one person can be pushed aside for another.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם ניתן לדחות אדם מפני אדם?

sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers affirmatively, citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan on a verse from Hosea indicating that God's words can cause displacement.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם ניתן לדחות אדם מפני אדם?

items.text: אין משיחין בסעודה
items.text_en: The prohibition of speaking during a meal
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak to say something during their meal. Rabbi Yitzchak cites Rabbi Yochanan that one should not converse during a meal, lest the windpipe precede the esophagus and cause danger.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן אומר שאין לשוחח בשעת סעודה, שמא יקדים קנה לוושט ויבוא לידי סכנה.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yitzchak were sitting at a meal, and Rav Nachman asked Rabbi Yitzchak to say something.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מבקש מרבי יצחק לומר דבר תורה בסעודה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak responds by citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one should not converse during a meal, lest the windpipe (קנה) precede the esophagus (ושט) and cause danger.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מבקש מרבי יצחק לומר דבר תורה בסעודה.

items.text: יעקב אבינו לא מת
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Jacob did not die
items.desc_en: After the meal, Rabbi Yitzchak cites Rabbi Yochanan that Jacob our father did not die. Rav Nachman objects, noting the mourners, embalmers, and buriers. Rabbi Yitzchak explains he derives it from a verse that likens Jacob to his descendants: just as his descendants are alive, so is he.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן אומר שיעקב אבינו לא מת, על סמך דרשת הפסוק 'ואתה אל תירא עבדי יעקב' – המקיש אותו לזרעו, מה זרעו בחיים אף הוא בחיים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak, after the meal, cites Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Jacob our father did not die.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן פותח ואומר שיעקב אבינו לא מת.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects, pointing to the historical reality of mourners, embalmers, and buriers for Jacob.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן פותח ואומר שיעקב אבינו לא מת.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains he derives the statement from a verse that likens Jacob to his descendants: just as his descendants are alive, so is he.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן פותח ואומר שיעקב אבינו לא מת.

items.text: אמירת 'רחב' גורמת לקרי
items.text_en: The danger of saying 'Rachav' twice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that anyone who says 'Rachav' twice immediately has a seminal emission. Rav Nachman says he says it and is unconcerned. Rabbi Yitzchak clarifies that the statement applies to one who knows her and is familiar with her.
items.desc: רבי יצחק אומר שכל האומר 'רחב רחב' מיד נקרי, ורב נחמן משיב שאינו חושש, ורבי יצחק מבהיר שדבריו אמורים דווקא ביודעה ומכירה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that anyone who says 'Rachav' twice immediately has a seminal emission.
Rav Nachman objects that he himself says 'Rachav' twice and is unconcerned.
Rabbi Yitzchak clarifies that his statement applies only to one who knows Rachav and is familiar with her.

items.text: משל האילן והברכה
items.text_en: The blessing parable of the tree
items.desc_en: As they part, Rav Nachman asks for a blessing. Rabbi Yitzchak tells a parable of a man who finds a tree with sweet fruit, pleasant shade, and a water source. When leaving, he blesses the tree that all its future plantings be like it. The section ends mid-parable.
items.desc: רבי יצחק מסרב לברך את רב נחמן ישירות, וממשל במשל אדם שמצא אילן עם פירות מתוקים, צל נאה ומים, ומברך אותו שכל נטיעותיו יהיו כמוהו – רמז לכך שרב נחמן אינו זקוק לברכתו.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: as Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yitzchak part, Rav Nachman asks for a blessing, and Rabbi Yitzchak responds with a parable of a man in the desert who finds a tree with sweet fruit, pleasant shade, and a water source, and enjoys them.

Rabbi Yitzchak continues the parable: when the man prepares to leave, he considers what to bless the tree with, noting its fruit is already sweet, its shade already pleasant, and the water already flowing, so he blesses that all future plantings from it be like it.

items.text: ברכת 'יהיו כמוך'
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about blessing
items.desc_en: A story about blessing someone whose children should be like them, leading to a discussion of the term 'moreh'.
items.desc: הקטע הפותח עוסק בברכה לאדם שכבר יש לו הכל: תורה, עושר ובנים. הברכה הראויה היא שצאצאיו יהיו כמוהו.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts a story where one person blesses another that his descendants should be like him, and the recipient asks what blessing to give in return, concluding with the wish that his offspring be like him.
sub.desc: פתיחה המציגה את נוסח הברכה הראויה למי שכבר יש לו תורה, עושר ובנים: שצאצאיו יהיו כמוהו.

items.text: פירוש 'יורה' ו'מלקוש'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'moreh' and 'malkosh'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents multiple interpretations of 'moreh' as teaching, saturating, or gentle rain, and 'malkosh' as a blessing, with scriptural proof.
items.desc: ברייתא ראשונה דנה במשמעות 'יורה': מורה לבריות, מרוה את הארץ, יורד בנחת. ברייתא שנייה דנה באפשרות ש'יורה' ו'מלקוש' הם גשמי ברכה, ומביאה ראיה מספר יואל ש'יורה' הוא גשם של ברכה.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma interprets 'moreh' as teaching people to plaster roofs, store produce, and do all their needs.
A second interpretation explains 'moreh' as saturating the earth to the depths, citing the verse 'תְּלָמֶיהָ רַוֵּה'.
A third interpretation explains 'moreh' as rain that falls gently, not violently.
The Gemara objects: perhaps 'moreh' means destructive rain that dislodges fruits and washes away seeds and trees.
The Gemara resolves: the verse pairs 'moreh' with 'malkosh', and since 'malkosh' is a blessing, so too 'moreh' is a blessing.
The Gemara objects: perhaps 'malkosh' means destructive rain that collapses houses, breaks trees, and brings up thorns.
The Gemara resolves: since 'moreh' is a blessing, 'malkosh' is also a blessing.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וּבְנֵי צִיּוֹן גִּילוּ...' to prove that 'moreh' itself is a blessing.

items.text: זמני יורה ומלקוש
items.text_en: Timing of 'moreh' and 'malkosh'
items.desc_en: A baraita states that 'moreh' is in Marcheshvan and 'malkosh' in Nisan, with a scriptural proof from 'be'itto'.
items.desc: ברייתא קובעת שיורה במרחשוון ומלקוש בניסן, ודוחה אפשרויות אחרות (תשרי/אייר) על סמך הפסוק 'בעתו'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that 'moreh' is in Marcheshvan and 'malkosh' in Nisan, with a scriptural proof from 'be'itto'.

items.text: פירוש 'מלקוש'
items.text_en: Etymological interpretations of 'malkosh'
items.desc_en: Rav Nehilai bar Idi citing Shmuel, the school of Rabbi Yishmael, and a baraita offer different etymologies for 'malkosh' relating to Israel's hardness or filling grain with straw.
items.desc: שלושה פירושים למילה 'מלקוש': דבר שמל קשיותן של ישראל (שמואל), דבר שממלא תבואה בקשיה (בית רבי ישמעאל), דבר שיורד על המלילות ועל הקשין (ברייתא).

sub.text: רב נחילאי בר אידי משמיה דשמואל
sub.text_en: Rav Nehilai bar Idi citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nehilai bar Idi citing Shmuel interprets 'malkosh' as something that cuts (מל) the hardness (קשיות) of Israel.
sub.desc: מביא פירוש ראשון ל'מלקוש': דבר שמל קשיותן של ישראל.

sub.text: רב נחילאי בר אידי משמיה דשמואל
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that 'malkosh' fills the grain with straw (קש).
sub.desc: מביא פירוש ראשון ל'מלקוש': דבר שמל קשיותן של ישראל.

sub.text: רב נחילאי בר אידי משמיה דשמואל
sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'malkosh' falls on the ears of grain (מלילות) and on the straw (קשין).
sub.desc: מביא פירוש ראשון ל'מלקוש': דבר שמל קשיותן של ישראל.

items.text: זמן יורה: מרחשוון או כסלו?
items.text_en: Debate on the month of 'moreh'
items.desc_en: A baraita questions whether 'moreh' is in Marcheshvan or Kislev, concluding from 'be'itto' that it is in its proper time, and notes that rain after Nisan is not a blessing.
items.desc: ברייתא נוספת דנה באפשרות שיורה בכסלו, ומסיקה שגם יורה וגם מלקוש צריכים להיות בעיתם, ואם יורדים גשמים אחרי ניסן זה סימן רע.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that 'moreh' (the early rain) falls in Marcheshvan and 'malkosh' (the late rain) in Nisan, then questions whether 'moreh' might instead be in Kislev.
The gemara answers by citing the verse 'be'itto' (in its proper time), concluding that 'moreh' is in its proper time (Marcheshvan) and that rain after Nisan is not a blessing.

items.text: מחלוקת רבי מאיר ורבי יוסי בזמני רביעה
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei on rain timing
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Meir's view that 'moreh' is in Marcheshvan and 'malkosh' in Nisan, while the Sages (identified as Rabbi Yosei) say 'moreh' is in Kislev. Rabbi Yosei's opinion is supported by a baraita on the first rain and fasting.
items.desc: ברייתא מביאה מחלוקת: רבי מאיר אומר יורה במרחשוון ומלקוש בניסן, וחכמים (רבי יוסי) אומרים יורה בכסלו. מובאים זמני רביעה ראשונה לפי רבי מאיר, רבי יהודה ורבי יוסי, ורבי יוסי קובע שאין היחידים מתענין עד ראש חודש כסלו.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Meir's view that 'moreh' (the early rain) falls in Marcheshvan and 'malkosh' (the late rain) in Nisan.
sub.desc: ברייתא מביאה את שיטת רבי מאיר שיורה במרחשוון ומלקוש בניסן.

sub.desc_en: The Sages (identified later as Rabbi Yosei) argue that 'moreh' falls in Kislev.
sub.desc: ברייתא מביאה את שיטת רבי מאיר שיורה במרחשוון ומלקוש בניסן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who these 'Sages' are.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מיהם החכמים שסוברים שיורה בכסלו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda identifies the anonymous Sages as Rabbi Yosei.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מיהם החכמים שסוברים שיורה בכסלו.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited detailing the opinions of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei on the dates of the first rain and fasting, supporting Rabbi Yosei's view that the first rain is in Kislev.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מיהם החכמים שסוברים שיורה בכסלו.

items.text: הלכה כרבי יוסי, ופירוט זמני שאלה ותענית
items.text_en: Halachic rulings and further discussion
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules like Rabbi Yosei, and Amemar teaches this in another context regarding asking for rain. The Gemara then discusses the three rain periods and their purposes, with Rabbi Zeira explaining the second period is for vows.
items.desc: רב חסדא פוסק הלכה כרבי יוסי. מובאת מסורת בשם אמימר ורבן גמליאל לגבי מועד שאלת גשמים. ברייתא של רבן שמעון בן גמליאל קובעת שגשמים שירדו שבעה ימים רצופים נמנים כרביעה ראשונה ושנייה או שנייה ושלישית. רבי זירא מסביר שהרביעה השנייה חשובה לעניין נדרים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosei regarding the dates of the first rain period.
sub.desc: רב חסדא פוסק שהלכה כרבי יוסי לגבי זמני הרביעה.

sub.desc_en: Amemar teaches Rav Chisda's ruling in a different formulation: regarding the date to begin asking for rain, Rav Chisda rules like Rabban Gamliel.
sub.desc: רב חסדא פוסק שהלכה כרבי יוסי לגבי זמני הרביעה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to whom does the baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, which counts seven consecutive days of rain as three rain periods, align? It answers: like Rabbi Yosei.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: לאיזה חכם מכוונת הברייתא של רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, ועונה שהיא כרבי יוסי.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda reiterates that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosei.
sub.desc: רב חסדא פוסק שוב שהלכה כרבי יוסי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the first rain period is for asking for rain, the third for fasting, but what is the purpose of the second rain period?
sub.desc: רב חסדא פוסק שוב שהלכה כרבי יוסי.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira answers that the second rain period is for vows (נדרים), as taught in a Mishnah.
sub.desc: רב חסדא פוסק שוב שהלכה כרבי יוסי.

items.text: פתיחה: נדר עד הגשמים
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows 'until the rains' is bound until the second rainfall (רביעה שניה) falls.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שהנודר 'עד הגשמים' – נדרו תקף מהגשם הראשון ועד השני.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who vows 'until the rains' is bound until the second rainfall (רביעה שניה) falls.

items.text: משמעות ה'רביעה השנייה' במסכתות שונות
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of 'second rainfall'
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid explains that the second rainfall refers to olives, citing a Mishnah about gleaning. The Gemara then defines 'נמושות' and discusses other halakhic uses of the second rainfall, such as for walking on paths and burning seventh-year produce.
items.desc: רב זביד מקשר את ה'רביעה השנייה' להלכות זיתים (לקט, שכחה, פאה). רב פפא ורב נחמן בר יצחק מביאים דינים נוספים התלויים בזמן זה: הליכה בשבילי רשות ובעור פירות שביעית. הגמרא מסבירה את הטעם לבעור פירות שביעית על פי הפסוק.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid answers that the second rainfall refers to olives, citing a Mishnah about gleaning rights.
sub.desc: רב זביד מביא ברייתא הקושרת את ה'רביעה השנייה' לזמן שבו מותר לכל אדם ללקט זיתים (לקט, שכחה ופאה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of 'נמושות' and provides two definitions: Rabbi Yochanan says 'old men who walk on the mountain' and Reish Lakish says 'gleaners after gleaners'.
sub.desc: הגמרא דנה בפירוש המונח 'נמושות' ומביאה שתי דעות: רבי יוחנן וריש לקיש.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the second rainfall is the measure for when it is permitted to walk on paths, citing a teaching that everyone may walk on paths until the second rainfall.
sub.desc: רב פפא מביא דין נוסף התלוי ברביעה השנייה: מותר ללכת בשבילי רשות עד אז.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the second rainfall is the deadline for burning seventh-year produce, citing a Mishnah about when one may benefit from and burn seventh-year straw.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק מביא דין נוסף: עד מתי מותר ליהנות מתבן וקש של שביעית – עד רביעה שנייה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides the scriptural basis for the seventh-year law: as long as wild animals eat in the field, you may feed your domesticated animal at home; when the field is bare, you must remove the produce from your home.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה את הטעם לבעור פירות שביעית: כל זמן שחיה אוכלת בשדה – האכל לבהמתך בבית; כלה לחיה מן השדה – כלה לבהמתך מן הבית.

items.text: פירוש 'רביעה' ושיעוריה
items.text_en: Etymology and measure of 'רביעה'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that 'רביעה' means something that saturates the ground, and defines the first rainfall as enough to penetrate a handbreadth, and the second as enough to seal the mouth of a barrel. Rav Chisda adds that such rains are not subject to the curse of withholding.
items.desc: רבי אבהו מפרש ש'רביעה' מלשון 'רובע את הקרקע', ומביא דברי רב יהודה שהגשם הוא בעל האדמה. הוא גם נותן שיעורים לרביעה ראשונה (טפח) ושנייה (כדי לגוף פי חבית). רב חסדא מוסיף שגשמים במידה זו מונעים את קללת 'ועצר'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu asks what the etymology of the term 'רביעה' (rainfall) is, and answers that it means something that saturates the ground.
Rav Yehuda supports this with a verse, saying rain is the 'husband' of the land, as it saturates and causes growth.
Rabbi Avahu defines the first rainfall as enough to penetrate a handbreadth into the ground, and the second as enough to seal the mouth of a barrel.
Rav Chisda rules that rains sufficient to seal a barrel's mouth are not subject to the curse of withholding (וְעָצַר).

items.text: גשמים לפני 'ועצר' – הבדל בין ערבית לשחרית
items.text_en: Rains before 'ועצר' and morning clouds
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says rains before 'ועצר' are not subject to the curse. Abaye clarifies this applies only to the evening 'ועצר', not the morning one, citing a verse about morning clouds. Rav Pappa questions this with a folk saying, and resolves it by distinguishing between clouds tied to a stalk and those tied to clouds.
items.desc: רב חסדא אומר שגשם שירד לפני קריאת 'ועצר' (בשחרית) אינו נחשב לקללה. אביי מחלק: אם ירד לפני 'ועצר' של ערבית – אינו נחשב, אך אם ירד לפני 'ועצר' של שחרית – יש בו משום 'ועצר', כי ענני בוקר אינם מבשרי גשם טוב. רב פפא מקשה ממנהג העולם, ומתרץ שהדבר תלוי בסוג העננים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that rains which fell before the 'ועצר' (the curse of withholding) are not subject to the curse.
Abaye qualifies Rav Chisda's statement, limiting it to rains before the evening 'ועצר', but not the morning one, citing a verse about morning clouds.
Rav Pappa objects by citing a folk saying that implies morning rains are beneficial, contradicting Abaye's negative view of morning clouds.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between clouds tied to a stalk (עֵיבָא, which bring beneficial rain) and clouds tied to clouds (עֲנָנֵי, which are unreliable).

items.text: דיון על גשמי טבת
items.text_en: Good and bad rains in Tevet
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says a widow-like Tevet is good, with two explanations. Rav Chisda says a barren Tevet is good. The contradiction is resolved: if rain came from the beginning, it is good; if not, it is bad.
items.desc: רב יהודה אומר שטוב לשנת טבת להיות 'אלמנה' (ללא גשם), ורב חסדא אומר שטוב שתהיה 'מנוולת' (מגושמת). הגמרא מיישבת: תלוי אם ירד גשם לפני טבת או לא.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that a widow-like (rainless) Tevet is good for the year, with two explanations offered.
The Gemara objects by citing Rav Chisda, who says a barren (rainless) Tevet is good, contradicting Rav Yehuda's statement.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if rain came from the beginning (of Tevet), a widow-like Tevet is good; if not, a barren Tevet is good.

items.text: גשמים על מקצת מדינה
items.text_en: Partial rain and the curse
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says rain on part of a country is not subject to the curse. This is challenged by a verse about rain on one city and not another, which Rav Yehuda says is a curse. The resolution: abundant rain is a curse, but rain as needed is not. Rav Ashi supports this from the verse.
items.desc: רב חסדא אומר שגשם שיורד על חלק מהארץ אינו נחשב ל'ועצר'. הגמרא מקשה מפסוק בעמוס שרב יהודה פירשו כקללה. מתרצים: הפסוק מדבר על גשם מוגזם, ואילו רב חסדא מדבר על גשם במידה הראויה. רב אשי מדקדק מלשון הפסוק.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that rain falling on only part of a country is not subject to the curse of withholding (וְעָצַר).
The Gemara objects by citing a verse where rain on one city and not another is described as a curse, and Rav Yehuda in Rav's name confirms both are for a curse.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: abundant rain (טוּבָא) on part of the land is a curse, but rain as needed (כִּדְמִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ) is not.
Rav Ashi supports the resolution by noting that the verse uses the term 'תִּמָּטֵר' (shall be rained upon), implying a place of rain, i.e., abundant rain, not normal rain.

items.text: ברכת הגשמים
items.text_en: Blessing for rain and its formula
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states when to bless for rain. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav gives the blessing, and Rabbi Yochanan adds a longer version. Rava and Rav Pappa discuss the correct wording, concluding with 'אל ההודאות'.
items.desc: רבי אבהו קובע מתי מברכים על הגשמים: משיצא חתן לקראת כלה (כשהמים ניתזים). רב יהודה בשם רב מביא נוסח ברכה, ורבי יוחנן מוסיף לה סיום. הגמרא דנה בנוסח 'רוב ההודאות' ומציעה 'אל ההודאות'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu asks when one should recite the blessing for rain, and answers: from the time a groom goes out to meet the bride (i.e., when the rain is so abundant that puddles form and a groom would need to go out to meet his bride).
sub.desc: רבי אבהו קובע את הזמן לברכת הגשמים: משיצא חתן לקראת כלה, כלומר כשהמים ניתזים מן הקרקע.

sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav gives the blessing formula: 'We give thanks to You, Lord our God, for every drop that You have brought down for us.'
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו נוסח הברכה שמברכים על הגשמים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan adds a longer conclusion to the blessing, including the phrase 'Blessed is the One who is abundant in thanksgivings' (רוֹב הַהוֹדָאוֹת).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו נוסח הברכה שמברכים על הגשמים.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: why does the blessing say 'abundant in thanksgivings' (רוֹב) rather than 'all thanksgivings' (כׇּל)?
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב מביא את נוסח הברכה הפותח במילים 'מודים אנחנו לך ה' אלוהינו על כל טיפה וטיפה שהורדת לנו'.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the objection by suggesting the correct wording should be 'אֵל הַהוֹדָאוֹת' (God of thanksgivings) instead of 'רוֹב הַהוֹדָאוֹת'.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב מביא את נוסח הברכה הפותח במילים 'מודים אנחנו לך ה' אלוהינו על כל טיפה וטיפה שהורדת לנו'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa concludes the discussion, presumably affirming Rava's correction (the text breaks off here).
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב מביא את נוסח הברכה הפותח במילים 'מודים אנחנו לך ה' אלוהינו על כל טיפה וטיפה שהורדת לנו'.

items.text: פתיחה: ברכות הגשם
items.text_en: Opening statement about blessings for rain
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that we recite both 'אל ההודאות' and 'רוב ההודאות' in the blessings for rain.
items.desc: הגמרא מציעה לומר בתפילה על הגשמים את הברכות 'אל ההודאות' ו'רוב ההודאות'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that we recite both 'אל ההודאות' and 'רוב ההודאות' in the blessings for rain.

items.text: Rain greater than resurrection of the dead
items.text_en: Rain greater than resurrection of the dead
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu argues that the day of rain is greater than the resurrection of the dead, because resurrection is only for the righteous, while rain benefits both righteous and wicked. This contradicts Rav Yosef, who says rain is equal to resurrection and thus placed in the resurrection blessing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu declares that the day of rain is greater than the resurrection of the dead, because resurrection is only for the righteous, while rain benefits both righteous and wicked.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Avahu's statement disagrees with Rav Yosef, who said that rain is equal to resurrection and therefore was placed in the resurrection blessing.

items.text: Rain compared to the giving of the Torah
items.text_en: Rain compared to the giving of the Torah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says the day of rain is as great as the day the Torah was given, citing the verse 'יַעֲרֹף כַּמָּטָר לִקְחִי'. Rava adds that rain is even greater, since the verse implies the smaller (rain) is hung on the larger (Torah).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says that the day of rain is as great as the day the Torah was given, citing the verse 'יַעֲרֹף כַּמָּטָר לִקְחִי' where 'לֶקַח' refers to Torah.
Rava argues that rain is greater than the day the Torah was given, reasoning from the verse that the smaller (rain) is hung upon the greater (Torah).

items.text: Contradiction between 'dew' and 'rain' for Torah
items.text_en: Contradiction between 'dew' and 'rain' for Torah
items.desc_en: Rava resolves a contradiction: one verse compares Torah to rain, another to dew. If the student is worthy, Torah is like dew; if not, it is like rain that kills.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction between the verse 'יַעֲרֹף כַּמָּטָר לִקְחִי' and the verse 'תִּזַּל כַּטַּל אִמְרָתִי'.
Rava resolves: if the Torah scholar is worthy, his words are like dew; if not, break him like rain.

items.text: Torah as elixir of life or death
items.text_en: Torah as elixir of life or death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Bena'ah teaches: one who studies Torah for its own sake finds it an elixir of life; one who studies not for its own sake finds it a potion of death, as 'עֲרִיפָה' implies killing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Bena'ah teaches that one who studies Torah for its own sake (לִשְׁמָהּ) finds it a elixir of life, citing verses about the tree of life and healing.
Rabbi Bena'ah adds that one who studies Torah not for its own sake finds it a poison of death, interpreting 'יַעֲרֹף' as killing, from the calf whose neck is broken.

items.text: משל האדם כעץ השדה
items.text_en: The student as a tree of the field
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira to teach; Rabbi Zeira declines due to weakness but offers aggadah. Rabbi Yochanan explains the verse 'כִּי הָאָדָם עֵץ הַשָּׂדֶה': if the student is worthy, one may benefit from him; if not, one may cut him down.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן דורש את הפסוק 'כי האדם עץ השדה': תלמיד חכם הגון – 'ממנו תאכל ואותו לא תכרות', ואם לאו – 'אותו תשחית וכרת'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira to teach him.
Rabbi Zeira declines due to physical weakness.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira to teach an aggadic teaching instead.
Rabbi Zeira cites Rabbi Yochanan's question on the verse 'כי האדם עץ השדה'.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction: a worthy student is like a tree one may benefit from, an unworthy one may be cut down.

items.text: משלים ללימוד תורה: ברזל, אש, עץ, מים
items.text_en: Torah study sharpens through interaction
items.desc_en: A series of teachings: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina compares Torah scholars to iron sharpening iron; Rabbah bar bar Chanah compares Torah to fire that does not burn alone; Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina warns of sword and folly for those who study alone; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak compares Torah to a tree where small kindles large, and Rabbi Chanina says he learned more from students than teachers.
items.desc: סדרת משלים: ברזל בברזל – תלמידי חכמים מחדדים זה את זה; אש – תורה אינה מתקיימת ביחיד; חרב על הבדים – הלומדים לבד מתטפשים וחוטאים; עץ קטן מדליק גדול – תלמידים מחדדים את רבותיהם.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina compares Torah scholars to iron sharpening iron, teaching that they sharpen each other in halacha.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah compares Torah to fire that does not burn alone, implying Torah does not endure in isolation.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina warns that Torah scholars studying alone bring a sword upon themselves and become foolish and sinful, citing verses.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak compares Torah to a tree where small kindles large, and Rabbi Chanina states he learned more from students than from teachers.

items.text: Torah compared to water, wine, milk, and humility
items.text_en: Torah compared to water, wine, milk, and humility
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa and Rabbi Chanina bar Chama resolve contradictions about Torah study: a worthy student is sought out; an unworthy one must seek. Rabbi Chanina bar Idi says Torah is like water, flowing to low places; Rabbi Oshaya compares Torah to water, wine, and milk, which are kept in humble vessels. The story of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the Caesar's daughter illustrates that wisdom is best placed in a humble vessel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa raises a contradiction between two verses about water and the worthy student.
He resolves: if the student is worthy, Torah comes to him; if not, he must go to it.
Rabbi Chanina bar Chama raises a contradiction between two verses about spreading Torah.
He resolves: if the student is worthy, spread Torah; if not, keep it to yourself.
Rabbi Chanina bar Idi compares Torah to water, which flows to low places, teaching that Torah endures only with a humble person.
Rabbi Oshaya compares Torah to water, wine, and milk, which are kept in humble vessels, teaching that Torah endures only with a humble person.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the Caesar's daughter
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the Caesar's daughter
sub.desc_en: The Caesar's daughter questions why wisdom is placed in an ugly vessel; Rabbi Yehoshua responds by analogy to wine stored in clay vessels, suggesting she store it in gold and silver.

The daughter reports to her father, who tests the idea; wine in gold vessels turns sour; the Caesar summons Rabbi Yehoshua, who explains his parable, and the Caesar objects that there are handsome Torah scholars.

items.text: משל המים, היין והחלב לתורה
items.text_en: Opening analogy: Torah forgotten through distraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a metaphor comparing Torah study to three liquids that become invalid only through distraction; similarly, Torah is forgotten only through distraction.
items.desc: רבי יהושע משיב שאם היו מכוערים היו חכמים יותר, וממשיל את התורה למים, יין וחלב, שאינם נפסלים אלא בהיסח הדעת, כמו שתורה נשכחת רק בהיסח הדעת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a metaphor comparing Torah study to three liquids that become invalid only through distraction; similarly, Torah is forgotten only through distraction.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע משיב שאם היו מכוערים היו חכמים יותר, וממשיל את התורה למים, יין וחלב, שאינם נפסלים אלא בהיסח הדעת, כמו שתורה נשכחת רק בהיסח הדעת.

items.text: Greatness of the day of rain
items.text_en: Greatness of the day of rain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina and Rav Oshaya declare that the day of rain is as great as the day of creation, and that salvation flourishes with rain. Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai adds that rain only falls when Israel's sins are forgiven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina declares that the day of rain is as great as the day of creation, citing a verse that uses the singular 'I created it' to link rain and creation.
Rav Oshaya adds that rain is so great that even salvation flourishes on that day, as the verse says 'let the earth open and salvation flourish'.
Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai teaches that rain only falls when Israel's sins are forgiven, citing a verse from Psalms that links rain to forgiveness.

items.text: Source for forgiveness before rain and drought as punishment
items.text_en: Source for forgiveness before rain and drought as punishment
items.desc_en: Ze'iri tells Ravina that they derive the teaching about forgiveness before rain from one verse, while he derives it from another. Rabbi Tanchum bar Chiya states that drought only comes when Israel is deserving of destruction, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: Ze'iri tells Ravina that they (the Babylonians) derive the teaching about forgiveness before rain from one verse, while he (Ze'iri) derives it from another verse.
Rabbi Tanchum bar Chiya states that drought only comes when Israel is deserving of destruction, citing a verse.

items.text: Drought due to neglect of tithes and evil speech
items.text_en: Drought due to neglect of tithes and evil speech
