items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says drought occurs because of neglect of terumot and ma'asrot, as expounded by the school of Rabbi Yishmael. Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi says it is due to slanderers.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that drought occurs only due to neglect of terumot and ma'asrot, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael's exposition of the verse.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi adds that drought is also caused by slanderers, citing the verse about a north wind and an angry face.

items.text: עצירת גשמים בשל עזי פנים
items.text_en: Drought due to brazenness; consequences of impudence
items.desc_en: Rav Salla quoting Rav Hamnuna says drought is due to brazen-faced people, and that such a person eventually stumbles into sin. Rav Nachman says it is known they have already sinned. Rabba bar Rav Huna says one with brazenness may be called wicked; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it is permitted to hate him.
items.desc: רב סלא בשם רב המנונא אומר שגשמים נעצרים בשל עזי פנים, ומוסיף שעזות פנים מובילה לעבירה. רב נחמן מדייק מהפסוק שמדובר בעבר שכבר נעשה. רבה בר רב הונא ורב נחמן בר יצחק דנים בעזות פנים ובמותר לשנוא את בעליה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Salla citing Rav Hamnuna states that drought is caused only by brazen-faced people, citing a verse.

sub.text: Rav Salla citing Rav Hamnuna (second statement)
sub.text_en: Rav Salla citing Rav Hamnuna (second statement)
sub.desc_en: Rav Salla citing Rav Hamnuna adds that anyone with brazenness will eventually stumble into sin, citing the same verse.
Rav Nachman objects that it is already known that such a person has sinned, based on the verse's past tense.
Rabba bar Rav Huna rules that one with brazenness may be called wicked, citing a verse.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that it is permitted to hate such a person, based on a homiletic reading of a verse.

items.text: עצירת גשמים בשל ביטול תורה
items.text_en: Drought due to neglect of Torah
items.desc_en: Rav Katina says drought is due to neglect of Torah, interpreting a verse about laziness causing God to become poor. Rav Yosef adds another verse indicating that even when the sky is clear for rain, a wind may clear it away due to lack of Torah.
items.desc: רב קטינא אומר שגשמים נעצרים בשל ביטול תורה, ומפרש את הפסוק כמתייחס לעוני של הקב"ה. רב יוסף מביא מקור אחר לאותו רעיון, ובית רבי ישמעאל מוסיף שאפילו כשהשמים בהירים, רוח יכולה לפזר את העננים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Katina states that drought is caused by neglect of Torah, interpreting the verse 'בעצלתים ימך המקרה' (through laziness the roof sinks) to mean that God becomes poor due to Israel's idleness in Torah study.

Rav Yosef adds a supporting verse, interpreting 'אור' (light) as Torah and 'רוח עברה ותטהרם' (a wind passed and cleared them) to mean that even when the sky is clear for rain, a wind may clear it away due to lack of Torah.
The School of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that even when the sky is perfectly clear for rain, a wind may pass and clear it away, reinforcing the idea that drought stems from Torah neglect.

items.text: עצירת גשמים בשל גזל ותקנת תפילה
items.text_en: Drought due to theft; remedy through prayer and strengthening mercy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami says drought is due to the sin of theft, interpreting a verse. The remedy is to increase prayer. He further explains that if the sky becomes hard like iron, it is because of corrupt deeds; the remedy is to strengthen in mercy.
items.desc: רבי אמי אומר שגשמים נעצרים בשל גזל, ומציע כתקנה להרבות בתפילה. הוא ממשיך בדרשה על הפסוק "אם קהה הברזל" ומסביר שאם השמים קהים כברזל, הדבר נובע ממעשי הדור המקולקלים, והתקנה היא להתגבר ברחמים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states that drought is caused by the sin of theft (גזל), citing a verse.
The Gemara asks what the remedy is and answers that one should increase prayer (תפילה), citing a verse.
Rabbi Ami interprets a verse to mean that if the sky becomes hard like iron, it is due to the corrupt deeds of the generation.
The Gemara states the remedy is to strengthen in mercy (רחמים), citing a verse, and adds that it is even better if their deeds were already proper from the start.

items.text: פתיחת דרשת ריש לקיש
items.text_en: Beginning of Resh Lakish's statement
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish begins a statement about a student, but the text is cut off.
items.desc: ריש לקיש מתחיל דרשה על הפסוק, אך הדף נקטע כאן.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish begins a statement about a student, but the text is cut off.
sub.desc: ריש לקיש פותח בדרשה על הפסוק, אך הדבר נקטע כאן.

items.text: First cause of difficult learning: student's own lack of review
items.text_en: First cause of difficult learning: student's own lack of review
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a student's learning is as hard as iron, it is because his mishnah is not well-ordered (reviewed). The remedy is to increase his study sessions, as the verse says 'and he shall increase strength'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that if a student's learning is as hard as iron, it is because his mishnah is not well-ordered (reviewed), citing a verse.
The Gemara asks what the remedy is and answers that the student should increase his study sessions, citing a verse, and adds that it is even better if his mishnah was well-ordered from the start.

items.text: Exemplary practice of Reish Lakish and Rav Adda bar Ahava
items.text_en: Exemplary practice of Reish Lakish and Rav Adda bar Ahava
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the practice of Reish Lakish who reviewed his mishnah forty times before entering before Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Adda bar Ahava who reviewed twenty-four times before entering before Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the exemplary practice of Reish Lakish, who reviewed his mishnah forty times before entering before Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Adda bar Ahava, who reviewed it twenty-four times before entering before Rava.

items.text: קושי בלימוד מחמת רב שאינו מאיר פנים
items.text_en: Second cause of difficult learning: teacher's lack of clarity
items.desc_en: Rava offers an alternative explanation: if a student's learning is hard, it is because his teacher does not show him a friendly face. The remedy is to increase friends, as the verse says 'and he shall increase strength'.
items.desc: רבה מציע הסבר נוסף לקושי בלימוד: רב שאינו מסביר פנים לתלמיד. התיקון הוא שהתלמיד ירבה רעים שיתערבו עבורו אצל הרב.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that if a student's learning is hard as iron, it is because his teacher does not show him a friendly face, citing the verse 'והוא לא פנים קלקל'.

Rava provides the remedy: the student should increase friends, citing the verse 'וחיילים יגבר ויתרון הכשיר חכמה', and adds that this is especially true if his deeds were already favorable before his teacher from the outset.

items.text: עצירת גשמים ותיקונה בתפילה
items.text_en: Drought due to slanderers and the remedy of prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi explains that drought occurs because of slanderers in the generation. The remedy is to go to one who knows how to whisper (pray). If the prayer is not answered, one should go to a pious person to increase prayer. If one becomes haughty after successful prayer, he brings anger to the world.
items.desc: רבי אמי דורש פסוק מקהלת על נחש ולחש, ומקישו לעצירת גשמים בגלל חוסר בלחשי תפילה. התיקון הוא לפנות למי שיודע ללחוש, ואם לא נענה – לפנות לחסיד הדור שירבה בתפילה. מי שמתגאה בהצלחת תפילתו מביא אף לעולם.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi interprets the verse about a snake biting without whispering to mean that drought occurs because of slanderers (לוחשי לחישות) in the generation.
The Gemara answers that the remedy is to go to one who knows how to whisper (pray), and notes that one who can whisper but does not gains no benefit.
The Gemara asks what the remedy is if one whispered (prayed) but was not answered, and answers that one should go to a pious person to increase prayer, citing verses that equate 'פגיעה' with prayer.
The Gemara concludes that if one whispered successfully and becomes haughty, he brings anger (אף) to the world, as per the verse 'מקנה אף על עולה'.

items.text: תלמידי חכמים שאינם נוחים זה לזה
items.text_en: Two Torah scholars who disagree bring anger
items.desc_en: Rava says that two Torah scholars who live in the same city and do not get along in halakha become jealous and bring anger upon themselves, as the verse says 'acquiring anger upon the one who ascends'.
items.desc: רבה דורש את הפסוק 'מקנה אף על עולה' על שני תלמידי חכמים בעיר אחת שאינם נוחים זה לזה בהלכה, והם מעלים אף לעולם.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that two Torah scholars in the same city who disagree in halakha become jealous and bring anger upon themselves, citing the verse 'acquiring anger upon the one who ascends'.

items.text: משל הנחש והחיות על לשון הרע
items.text_en: Allegory of the snake and slanderers
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish interprets the verse about the snake: in the future, all animals will gather and ask the snake what benefit it gets from biting without a whisper, and the snake answers that there is no benefit for the slanderer.
items.desc: ריש לקיש דורש את הפסוק 'אם ישך הנחש בלא לחש' כמשל לעתיד לבוא, בו החיות שואלות את הנחש מה הנאתו, והוא משיב שאין יתרון לבעל הלשון, כלומר למלשין.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish interprets the verse about the snake: in the future, all animals will gather and ask the snake what benefit it gets from biting without a whisper, and the snake answers that there is no benefit for the slanderer.

items.text: תנאי קבלת תפילה: יחיד מול ציבור
items.text_en: Prayer requires placing one's soul in one's hand
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi says that a person's prayer is only heard if he places his soul in his hand, citing a verse. The Gemara raises a contradiction from Samuel's teaching that even when the heart is not right, God is merciful. The resolution: for an individual, prayer requires full devotion; for the community, God is merciful even without it.
items.desc: רבי אמי אומר שתפילת אדם נשמעת רק אם הוא שם נפשו בכפו. הגמרא מקשה משמואל שדרש פסוקים שמראים שגם תפילה חסרת כוונה מתקבלת, ומתרצת: ביחיד התנאי נדרש, בציבור התפילה מתקבלת גם בלא כוונה שלמה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi states that a person's prayer is only heard if he places his soul in his hand, citing the verse 'נִשָּׂא לְבָבֵנוּ אֶל כַּפָּיִם' (we lift our hearts to our hands).

The Gemara objects: Did not Samuel the Amora establish and expound that even when the people's heart was not right with God, as per the verse 'וַיְפַתּוּהוּ בְּפִיהֶם... וְלִבָּם לֹא נָכוֹן עִמּוֹ', nevertheless 'וְהוּא רַחוּם יְכַפֵּר עָוֹן' (He, being merciful, forgives iniquity)?
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: for an individual (יחיד), prayer requires full devotion; for the community (ציבור), God is merciful even without it.

items.text: גשמים בזכות בעלי אמונה ומידת הדין
items.text_en: Rain falls for the faithful, and the reward of righteousness
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi says rain falls only for the faithful. He then praises those who are faithful, citing the example of the weasel and the pit. Rabbi Yochanan says that one who justifies himself below is justified from above. Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi discuss the joy in suffering and the bringing of salvation.
items.desc: רבי אמי קובע שגשמים יורדים רק בזכות בעלי אמונה. לאחר מכן דנים במידת הדין: רבי יוחנן אומר שהמצדיק עצמו מלמטה מצדיקים עליו דין מלמעלה, וריש לקיש ורבי יהושע בן לוי דורשים פסוקים נוספים על כך שהשמח בייסוריו מביא ישועה לעולם.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi states that rain falls only for the faithful, citing the verse 'אמת מארץ תצמח וצדק משמים נשקף' (Truth springs from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven).

Rabbi Ammi praises the faithful, deriving their greatness from the story of the weasel and the pit (חולדה ובור), arguing that if one who trusts in a weasel and pit is rewarded, how much more so one who trusts in God.

Rabbi Yochanan teaches that one who justifies himself below (מצדיק את עצמו מלמטה) is justified from above, citing the same verse 'אמת מארץ תצמח', and Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin in the name of Rav Huna adds a supporting verse 'וכיראתך עברתך' (As Your fear, so Your wrath).

sub.text: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish cites a different verse 'פגעת את שש ועושה צדק' (You meet the joyful and the righteous), and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that one who rejoices in suffering (שמח ביסורין) brings salvation to the world, as the verse concludes 'בהם עולם ונושע' (in them we have sinned, and we are saved).

items.text: משל עצירת שמים לאישה מחבלת
items.text_en: Drought compared to a woman in labor
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says that when the heavens are restrained from rain, it is like a woman who is in labor but cannot give birth. This is from Bar Kappara's teaching that the same word 'restraint' is used for rain and for a woman.
items.desc: ריש לקיש דורש את הפסוק 'ועצר את השמים' וממשיל עצירת גשמים לאישה שמחבלת ואינה יולדת, ומציין שנאמרה עצירה בגשמים ובאישה.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish interprets the verse 'וְעָצַר אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם' (He will restrain the heavens) as comparing a drought to a woman in labor who cannot give birth.
Reish Lakish cites Bar Kappara's teaching that the same word 'עֲצִירָה' (restraint) is used both for rain and for a woman in labor, supporting the analogy.

items.text: Rain and women: shared biblical terminology
items.text_en: Rain and women: shared biblical terminology
items.desc_en: The Gemara draws analogies between women and rain using three shared terms: 'עצירה' (restraint), 'לידה' (birth), and 'פקידה' (visitation). Each term is derived from biblical verses applied to both contexts. The section concludes with a brief explanation of the phrase 'פלג אלהים מלא מים'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the first shared term 'עצירה' (restraint) applied to both women and rain, citing biblical verses.
The Gemara introduces the second shared term 'לידה' (birth) applied to both women and rain, citing biblical verses.
The Gemara introduces the third shared term 'פקידה' (visitation) applied to both women and rain, citing biblical verses.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'פלג אלהים מלא מים' (a channel of God full of water).
A Tanna answers that it refers to a kind of vault in the sky from which rains emerge.

items.text: Interpretation of 'אם לשבט אם לארצו אם לחסד ימציאהו'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'אם לשבט אם לארצו אם לחסד ימציאהו'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani interprets a verse from Job, explaining that different types of rain are designated for different purposes: mountains and hills, fields and vineyards, trees, crops, and cisterns.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani introduces the verse and interprets 'אם לשבט' as rain for mountains and hills, and 'אם לחסד ימציאהו לארצו' as rain for fields and vineyards.
He continues the interpretation: 'אם לשבט' refers to trees, 'אם לארצו' to crops, and 'אם לחסד ימציאהו' to cisterns, pits, and caves.

items.text: Prayer for famine versus plague
items.text_en: Prayer for famine versus plague
items.desc_en: During a famine and plague, Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani advises praying for relief from famine rather than plague, as sustenance is a blessing for life. The Gemara then cites sources that one should not pray for two troubles simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dilemma: during a famine and plague in Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani's time, should one pray for relief from both troubles or only one?
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani advises praying for relief from famine rather than plague, because when God provides plenty it is a blessing for life.
The Gemara cites a verse from Ezra showing that one should not pray for two troubles simultaneously, as the phrase 'על זאת' (about this) implies there was another matter not prayed for.
In the West they cite Rabbi Chaggai from Daniel, where the phrase 'על רזא דנה' (about this secret) implies there was another secret not prayed for.

items.text: Fasting during a decree of persecution
items.text_en: Fasting during a decree of persecution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira proposes accepting a fast even though a decree prohibits it, with the intention to complete it later when the decree is lifted. He supports this from Daniel's example of fasting despite potential danger.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: during a decree of persecution (שמד) forbidding fasting, Rabbi Zeira proposes accepting the fast now and completing it later when the decree is lifted.
The sages ask Rabbi Zeira for the source of his ruling.
Rabbi Zeira cites the verse about Daniel, who set his heart to fast despite danger, showing that intention suffices even when the fast cannot be fully observed immediately.

items.text: Rain on Shabbat eve as a curse
items.text_en: Rain on Shabbat eve as a curse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that even if rain falls like in the days of Elijah, if it comes on Shabbat eves it is a curse. Rabba bar Sheila compares a rainy day to a day of judgment, and Ameimar says that if not for the need of creatures, they would pray to stop it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that even years like those of Elijah, with rain falling on Shabbat eves, are a curse.
Rabba bar Sheila supports the idea by comparing a rainy day to a day of judgment.
Ameimar adds that if not for the need of creatures, they would pray to stop the rain.

items.text: Teachings of Rabbi Yitzchak on rain and blessing
items.text_en: Teachings of Rabbi Yitzchak on rain and blessing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that sun on Shabbat is charity for the poor, that rain is great because even a coin in one's pocket is blessed, and that blessing is only found in something hidden from the eye, as supported by a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that sun on Shabbat is charity for the poor, citing the verse 'וְזָרְחָה לָכֶם יִרְאֵי שְׁמִי שֶׁמֶשׁ צְדָקָה וּמַרְפֵּא'.
Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that the day of rain is great, as even a coin in one's pocket is blessed, citing the verse 'לָתֵת מְטַר אַרְצְךָ בְּעִתּוֹ וּלְבָרֵךְ אֵת כׇּל מַעֲשֵׂה יָדֶךָ'.
Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that blessing is found only in something hidden from the eye, citing the verse 'יְצַו ה׳ אִתְּךָ אֶת הַבְּרָכָה בַּאֲסָמֶיךָ'.
A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael supports Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching, stating that blessing is found only in something the eye does not control, citing the same verse.

items.text: Blessing on measuring grain
items.text_en: Blessing on measuring grain
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches the proper procedure for blessing before measuring one's grain: a prayer before starting, a blessing upon beginning, and the prohibition of blessing after measuring, as blessing is not found in measured, weighed, or counted items.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the procedure for blessing before measuring grain: a prayer before starting, a blessing upon beginning, and the prohibition of blessing after measuring, since blessing is not found in measured, weighed, or counted items.

items.text: Greatness of rain: gathering exiles, armies, and charity
items.text_en: Greatness of rain: gathering exiles, armies, and charity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that rain is as great as the ingathering of exiles, that even armies cease because of rain, and that rain is withheld only due to those who pledge charity publicly but do not give. The section begins a new teaching but is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by stating that the day of rain is as great as the day of the ingathering of exiles, citing a verse.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that rain is so great that even armies cease because of it, citing a verse.
Rabbi Yochanan states that rain is withheld only because of those who pledge charity publicly but do not give, citing a verse.
Rabbi Yochanan begins a new inquiry about a verse, but the section is cut off.

items.text: Opening midrash on the tithe verse
items.text_en: Opening midrash on the tithe verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a homiletic reading of 'עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר', interpreting it as 'tithe so that you become wealthy'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a homiletic reading of the verse 'עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר', interpreting it as 'tithe so that you become wealthy'.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan tests Reish Lakish's son
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan tests Reish Lakish's son
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Reish Lakish's son to recite his verse, and the child explains the midrash. When questioned about testing God, the child cites Rabbi Hoshaya's exception from Malachi. Rabbi Yochanan then remarks that if he had reached that verse, he wouldn't have needed the child or Rabbi Hoshaya.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan finds Reish Lakish's son and asks him to recite his verse; the child cites 'עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר' and explains it as 'tithe so that you become wealthy'.
Rabbi Yochanan asks the child for the source of this interpretation, and the child replies 'go and test it'.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that testing God is forbidden, citing the verse 'לֹא תְנַסּוּ אֶת ה׳'.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's son citing Rabbi Hoshaya
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's son citing Rabbi Hoshaya
sub.desc_en: The child answers that Rabbi Hoshaya taught an exception for tithing, citing Malachi 3:10 where God says 'test Me in this'.
Rami bar Chama in the name of Rav explains the phrase 'עַד בְּלִי דָי' as meaning 'until your lips wear out from saying 'enough'.'
Rabbi Yochanan tells the child that if he had reached that verse himself, he would not have needed the child or Rabbi Hoshaya.

items.text: Another encounter and a lesson about testing God
items.text_en: Another encounter and a lesson about testing God
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan finds Reish Lakish's son again, who cites a verse from Proverbs. Rabbi Yochanan wonders if anything in Writings is not hinted at in the Torah. The child responds with a proof from Genesis. Rabbi Yochanan glares at him, and the child's mother takes him away, warning that Rabbi Yochanan might harm him as he did his father.

sub.desc_en: The narrator describes Rabbi Yochanan finding Reish Lakish's son again, who is sitting and reciting a verse from Proverbs about a person's folly perverting their way and their heart raging against God.
Rabbi Yochanan wonders aloud whether anything written in the Writings (Ketuvim) is not already hinted at in the Torah.

The child responds that this verse is indeed hinted at in the Torah, citing the verse from Genesis where the brothers' hearts left them and they trembled, saying 'What is this that God has done to us?'
Rabbi Yochanan glares at the child, and his mother comes and takes him away, warning him that Rabbi Yochanan might harm him as he did his father.

items.text: Rain for an individual, sustenance for the many
items.text_en: Rain for an individual, sustenance for the many
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states a principle: rain comes for an individual, but sustenance (manna) comes for the many, citing verses from Deuteronomy and Exodus.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that rain comes for an individual, citing a verse about God opening the storehouse for rain, while sustenance (manna) comes for the many, citing the verse 'הִנְנִי מַמְטִיר לָכֶם לֶחֶם' (Behold I will rain bread for you).

items.text: Baraita about three providers and an objection
items.text_en: Baraita about three providers and an objection
items.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda lists three good providers (Moses, Aaron, Miriam) and three gifts (well, cloud, manna). The Gemara details their cessation and return. This challenges Rabbi Yochanan's principle, as manna (sustenance) came for Moses (an individual). The Gemara answers that Moses, since he requested for the many, is considered like the many.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three good providers (Moses, Aaron, Miriam) and three gifts (well, cloud, manna) given through their merit.
The baraita details the cessation of the well upon Miriam's death and its return through the merit of Moses and Aaron.
The baraita describes the removal of the clouds of glory upon Aaron's death and the Canaanite king's reaction.
Rabbi Abahu offers a homiletic reading of 'וַיִּרְאוּ' as 'וַיִּירָאוּ', citing Reish Lakish's principle that 'כי' has four meanings.
The baraita concludes that upon Moses' death all three gifts ceased, interpreting the verse 'וָאַכְחִד אֶת שְׁלֹשֶׁת הָרֹעִים' as referring to the gifts' removal in one month.
The Gemara objects that the baraita shows manna (sustenance) came for Moses as an individual, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's principle that sustenance is only for the many.
The Gemara resolves that Moses is exceptional because he requested sustenance for the many, so he is considered like the many.

items.text: Story of Rava's students and Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Story of Rava's students and Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: After Rava's death, his students (Rav Huna bar Manoach, Rav Shmuel bar Idi, Rav Chiyya from Vostanya) go to Rav Pappa. When they disagree with his teachings, they gesture to each other, offending Rav Pappa.

sub.desc_en: The gemara narrates that after Rava's death, his students went to Rav Pappa, and when they disagreed with his teachings by gesturing to each other, Rav Pappa was offended.

items.text: Stories of Rav Shimi bar Ashi and Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Stories of Rav Shimi bar Ashi and Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi was constantly challenging Rav Pappa. One day, Rav Pappa prayed to be saved from Shimi's embarrassment, and Shimi accepted silence, ceasing his challenges.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rav Pappa was shown a verse in a dream, and the next day he dismissed the rabbis with a blessing.
The gemara relates that Rav Shimi bar Ashi, who constantly challenged Rav Pappa, heard Rav Pappa's prayer for deliverance from shame, accepted silence, and ceased his challenges.

items.text: Rain for an individual
items.text_en: Rain for an individual
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish derives from a verse that rain can fall for a single individual, limited to a specific field and even a specific plant. A story about Rav Daniel bar Katina illustrates this, as rain watered only the parts of his garden that needed it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Reish Lakish's position that rain can fall for an individual, citing the verse 'שאלו מה׳ מטר... לאיש עשב בשדה' (Ask rain from God... for each person's grass in the field).
A baraita (תניא) limits the verse: 'לאיש' excludes the public, 'שדה' limits to one field, 'עשב' limits to one plant, showing rain can be restricted to a single individual's specific need.

sub.text: Story about Rav Daniel bar Katina
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Daniel bar Katina
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates the principle: Rav Daniel bar Katina would inspect his garden daily, noting which plots needed water, and rain fell only where needed.

items.text: Signs of rain: פורחות and נהילא
items.text_en: Signs of rain: פורחות and נהילא
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the term 'חזיזים' as 'פורחות', a sign of rain. Rav Yehuda describes 'נהילא' as a sign: if it appears before rain, rain will come; if after, it will stop.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'ה׳ עֹשֶׂה חֲזִיזִים' (the Lord makes lightning) from the verse.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains that the verse teaches that for every righteous person, the Holy One, Blessed be He, makes a special lightning (חזיז) for him alone.
The Gemara asks the specific meaning of the word 'חזיזים' (lightning) in this context.
Rav Yehuda explains that 'חזיזים' refers to 'פורחות' (clouds that spread/flourish), a sign of impending rain.
Rabbi Yochanan confirms that פורחות (spreading clouds) are a sign of rain.
The Gemara asks the precise definition of 'פורחות' (the spreading clouds).
Rav Pappa defines פורחות as a thin cloud beneath a thick cloud, a specific meteorological sign of rain.
Rav Yehuda describes the sign of 'נהילא' (a type of cloud): if it appears before rain, rain will come; if after, it will stop, with mnemonic signs for each case.

items.text: Ulla's experiences in Babylonia
items.text_en: Ulla's experiences in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Ulla visits Babylonia and misinterprets a cloud sign, leading him to disparage Babylonian rains. Later, he sees cheap dates and criticizes Babylonians for not studying Torah, but after being troubled at night, he retracts, acknowledging their Torah study.

sub.text: Narrative: Ulla's first visit to Babylonia
sub.text_en: Narrative: Ulla's first visit to Babylonia
sub.desc_en: Ulla arrives in Babylonia, sees cloud formations (פורחות), and instructs people to clear vessels because rain is coming.
The rain does not come, and Ulla disparages Babylonians and their rains as deceptive.

items.text: Debate: Source of the world's water
items.text_en: Debate: Source of the world's water
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues the world drinks from ocean waters, which are sweetened in clouds. Rabbi Yehoshua argues it drinks from upper waters, with clouds collecting and dispensing rain like a sieve, with drops spaced a hair's breadth apart, showing the greatness of rain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that the entire world drinks from the ocean, citing the verse 'וְאֵד יַעֲלֶה מִן הָאָרֶץ' (a mist rises from the earth), and responds to Rabbi Yehoshua's objection that ocean water is salty by explaining that it is sweetened in the clouds.

Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the world drinks from the upper waters, citing 'לִמְטַר הַשָּׁמַיִם תִּשְׁתֶּה מָּיִם' (you will drink water from the rain of heaven), and explains that the verse about the mist teaches that clouds rise, open like a wineskin, and receive rainwater.

The baraita describes that the clouds are perforated like a sieve, dripping water onto the ground with only a hair's breadth between drops, teaching that the day of rain is as great as the day of creation.
The baraita cites multiple verses to demonstrate the greatness of rain, comparing it to the unfathomable works of creation.

items.text: Reconciling verses with the debate
items.text_en: Reconciling verses with the debate
items.desc_en: The Gemara aligns the verse 'משקה הרים מעליותיו' with Rabbi Yehoshua's view, and explains how Rabbi Eliezer would interpret it. It then asks whose view aligns with Rabbi Chanina's statement about the ocean filling the depths, concluding it follows Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose view aligns with the verse 'משקה הרים מעליותיו' and Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation, concluding it follows Rabbi Yehoshua.
The Gemara explains how Rabbi Eliezer would interpret the verse 'משקה הרים מעליותיו', arguing that since the waters ascend to the heavens, they are called 'from His upper chambers'.
The Gemara asks whose view aligns with Rabbi Chanina's statement about the ocean filling the depths, concluding it follows Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehoshua would interpret the verse differently, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Baraita on the primacy of Eretz Yisrael in creation and rainfall
items.text_en: Baraita on the primacy of Eretz Yisrael in creation and rainfall
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that Eretz Yisrael was created first, is watered directly by God, drinks rainwater, and receives rain first, while the rest of the world is watered through an agent, from runoff, and later. A parable of making cheese illustrates the priority.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that Eretz Yisrael was created first, is watered directly by God, drinks rainwater, and receives rain first, while the rest of the world is watered through an agent, from runoff, and later, illustrated by a parable of making cheese.

items.text: Gemara's question on the sweetening of water in clouds
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the sweetening of water in clouds
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that water is sweetened in the clouds, and answers with a derivation from verses about 'darkness of water' and 'gathering of water', interpreting the latter as 'sweetening'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where does the master derive that waters are sweetened in the clouds?

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites verses 'חשכת מים עבי שחקים' and 'חשׁרת מים עבי שחקים' and interprets them through a wordplay to mean that clouds prepare (מתקנים) the waters.
The Gemara resolves the derivation by combining the two words into 'חכשׁרת' (sweetening), interpreting it as the water being sweetened in the clouds.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's interpretation and the dispute with Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's interpretation and the dispute with Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua interprets the verses about clouds to mean that bright clouds have little water and dark clouds have much water. A baraita about upper waters is aligned with Rabbi Yehoshua, while Rabbi Eliezer interprets the verse differently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehoshua interprets the verses about clouds, and answers that he follows the Western tradition that bright clouds have little water and dark clouds have much water.
The Gemara aligns a baraita about upper waters with Rabbi Yehoshua's view, while Rabbi Eliezer interprets the verse as referring to God's own handiwork.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on the world drinking from Eden's runoff, and the dimensions of Egypt, Kush, the world, Garden, Eden, and Gehinnom
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on the world drinking from Eden's runoff, and the dimensions of Egypt, Kush, the world, Garden, Eden, and Gehinnom
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that the whole world drinks from the runoff of the Garden of Eden. A baraita then gives proportional dimensions: Egypt is 1/60 of Kush, etc., concluding that the world is like a pot lid for Gehinnom, with some saying Gehinnom or Eden have no measure.

sub.desc_en: A baraita gives proportional dimensions: Egypt is 1/60 of Kush, Kush is 1/60 of the world, the world is 1/60 of the Garden, the Garden is 1/60 of Eden, and Eden is 1/60 of Gehinnom, concluding that the world is like a pot lid for Gehinnom, with some saying Gehinnom or Eden have no measure.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya and Rav on Babylon's abundance
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya and Rav on Babylon's abundance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya explains that Babylon's abundant grain is due to its location on many waters. Rav adds that Babylon is rich because it harvests without rain, and Abaye notes a tradition: 'a flood is better than a drought'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya explains that Babylon's abundance of grain is due to its location on abundant waters; Rav adds that Babylon is rich because it harvests without rain; Abaye states a tradition preferring a flood over drought.
Rav adds that Babylon is rich because it harvests without rain.
Abaye notes a tradition that a flood is preferable to a drought.

items.text: Mishnah: When to begin asking for rain
items.text_en: Mishnah: When to begin asking for rain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that we begin asking for rain on the 3rd of Marcheshvan. Rabban Gamliel says on the 7th, 15 days after Sukkot, to allow the last pilgrim to reach the Euphrates.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on the third of Marcheshvan one begins to ask for rain, but Rabban Gamliel says on the seventh, fifteen days after the festival, to allow the last traveler to reach the Euphrates.

items.text: Gemara: Halakhic rulings on the start date for rain prayers in the diaspora
items.text_en: Gemara: Halakhic rulings on the start date for rain prayers in the diaspora
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules like Rabban Gamliel. Chananya says in the diaspora until 60 days after the tekufah. Shmuel rules like Chananya, but a query to Shmuel about when to say 'Vetein tal u'matar' suggests a different date. The Gemara debates whether the 60th day is considered before or after, with Rav and Shmuel disagreeing. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak gives a mnemonic, and Rav Pappa rules like Rav.

sub.desc_en: רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows רבן גמליאל (Rabban Gamliel) regarding the start date for rain prayers.
A ברייתא (baraita) cites חנניה (Chananya) who says that in the diaspora one delays rain prayers until sixty days after the תקופה (autumnal equinox).

sub.text: רב הונא בר חייא אמר שמואל (Rav Huna bar Chiya citing Shmuel)
sub.text_en: רב הונא בר חייא אמר שמואל (Rav Huna bar Chiya citing Shmuel)
sub.desc_en: רב הונא בר חייא (Rav Huna bar Chiya) reports in the name of שמואל (Shmuel) that the הלכה (binding law) follows חנניה (Chananya).
The גמרא (Gemara) objects: But they asked שמואל (Shmuel) himself from when one mentions 'ותן טל ומטר' (and give dew and rain), implying a different date.
שמואל (Shmuel) answered: From when they bring wood into the house of טבות רישבא (Tavut the bird hunter), a sign for sixty days after the תקופה (autumnal equinox).
The גמרא (Gemara) resolves: Perhaps this date and that date are the same measure of time, i.e., both refer to sixty days after the תקופה (autumnal equinox).
A dilemma was raised: Is the sixtieth day itself treated as before the sixtieth day or after it?
Come and hear: רב (Rav) said the sixtieth day is like after sixty, and שמואל (Shmuel) said it is like before sixty.

sub.text: רב נחמן בר יצחק (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak)
sub.text_en: רב נחמן בר יצחק (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak)
sub.desc_en: רב נחמן בר יצחק (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) gives a mnemonic: Those above (higher elevation) need water, those below (lowlands) do not need water, explaining the dispute between רב (Rav) and שמואל (Shmuel).
רב פפא (Rav Pappa) rules that the הלכה (binding law) is that the sixtieth day is considered after sixty, like רב (Rav).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Fasts when rain does not fall
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Fasts when rain does not fall
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the fasts: individuals begin fasting on the 17th of Marcheshvan if no rain, and the court decrees public fasts from Kislev. The Gemara identifies 'individuals' as rabbis, and Rav Huna specifies they fast on Monday, Thursday, Monday. The Gemara clarifies that this applies even to individuals, citing a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if no rain falls by the 17th of Marcheshvan, individuals begin three fasts, and if none by Kislev, the court decrees three public fasts, with lenient restrictions.
The Gemara asks who are the 'individuals' mentioned in the Mishnah, and Rav Huna answers that they are the rabbis.
Rav Huna specifies that the individuals fast on Monday, Thursday, and Monday.
The Gemara questions what Rav Huna teaches, since a baraita already states that the first three fasts are on Monday, Thursday, and Monday.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Huna's statement is necessary lest one think the rule applies only to the community but not to individuals, and a baraita supports this.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing the Mishnah's list of days when fasting is prohibited, including the 'good days' written in Megillat Taanit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's reference to the 'good days' listed in Megillat Taanit, on which fasting is prohibited.

items.text: Definitions of yachid and talmid
items.text_en: Definitions of yachid and talmid
items.desc_en: A baraita defines a yachid as one fit to be a communal leader, and a talmid as one who can answer a halakhic question. A dispute follows: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar say one cannot appoint oneself a yachid but can become a talmid; Rabbi Yosei and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualify this, saying in a matter of praise one cannot, but in a matter of distress one may, and it is to his credit.

sub.desc_en: A baraita defines a 'yachid' as one fit to be a communal leader and a 'talmid' as one who can answer a halakhic question, even from the tractate of the kalla month.
Rabbi Meir rules that not everyone who wishes to make himself a 'yachid' may do so, but one may become a 'talmid'.
Rabbi Yosei says one may do so and is remembered for good, because it is a source of pain, not praise.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar repeats the same ruling as Rabbi Meir.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies: in a matter of praise one cannot, but in a matter of pain one may, and it is to his credit.

items.text: Completing a fast after the reason passes
items.text_en: Completing a fast after the reason passes
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that one who fasted for a trouble that passed or a sick person who recovered must complete the fast. A traveler from a place that does not fast to one that does must fast with them; from a fasting place to a non-fasting place, he must complete his fast.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one who fasted for a trouble that passed or a sick person who recovered must complete the fast, and a traveler from a non-fasting place to a fasting place must fast with them, while one from a fasting place to a non-fasting place must complete his fast.

items.text: One who forgot and ate: not to appear indulgent
items.text_en: One who forgot and ate: not to appear indulgent
items.desc_en: If one forgot and ate or drank on a fast day, he should not appear before the public or indulge himself, citing Jacob's instruction to his sons not to appear sated before Esau and Ishmael.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who forgot and ate or drank should not appear before the public or indulge himself, citing Jacob's instruction to his sons not to show themselves as satiated before Esau and Ishmael to avoid envy.

items.text: Torah study on the road: dispute resolved
items.text_en: Torah study on the road: dispute resolved
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets Joseph's 'al tirgezu baderekh' as a warning not to engage in halakhic discussion lest the road anger you. But Rabbi Il'ai bar Berekhya says two Torah scholars walking without words of Torah deserve to be burned. The Gemara resolves: one is for reviewing (migras) and the other for deep analysis (iyunei).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets Joseph's warning 'אל תרגזו בדרך' (do not quarrel on the way) as a prohibition against engaging in halakhic discussion, lest the road anger them.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Il'ai bar Berekhya, who says two Torah scholars walking without words of Torah deserve to be burned, implying Torah discussion is mandatory on the road.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one position refers to reviewing (מיגרס) previously learned material, while the other refers to deep analysis (עיוני) which can be dangerous on the road.

items.text: Advice for travelers: pace and timing
items.text_en: Advice for travelers: pace and timing
items.desc_en: A baraita advises: do not take large steps (which dims eyesight), and enter the city while it is still light. The latter is supported by Rav Yehuda citing Rav, who says one should always leave and enter with 'ki tov', as per the verse about morning light.

sub.desc_en: A baraita advises against taking large steps, citing Mar's statement that a large step dims one five-hundredth of a person's eyesight.

The baraita's second rule, to enter the city while it is still light, is supported by Rav Yehuda citing Rav, who says one should always leave and enter with 'כי טוב' (when it is good), as per the verse about morning light.

items.text: Eating on the road: limit and reason
items.text_en: Eating on the road: limit and reason
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rabbi Chiyya says a traveler should not eat more than two meals. The reason is disputed: in Babylonia they say due to digestion (ma'yana), in the West due to provisions (mezonei). The Gemara asks what difference there is between them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rabbi Chiyya: a traveler should not eat more than two meals; the Gemara notes that in the West they explain the reason is due to the digestive system (מעיינא), while in Babylonia they say it is due to provisions (מזוני), and the difference between them is explored.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this limit.
In Babylonia they explain the reason is due to digestion (מעיינָא).
In the West (Eretz Yisrael) they explain the reason is due to provisions (מזוני).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations.
The Gemara begins to articulate the practical difference between the two reasons.

items.text: Opening discussion on eating during travel in famine
items.text_en: Opening discussion on eating during travel in famine
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how much one should eat when traveling during a famine, citing Rav Papa's practice of eating one loaf per parasang due to concerns about the digestive tract.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes a traveler who sits on a boat or goes from one inn to another during a famine.
Rav Papa would eat one loaf per parasang, reasoning that it is due to the digestive tract's needs.

items.text: Reward for fasting in famine
items.text_en: Reward for fasting in famine
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches that one who starves himself during famine is saved from an unnatural death, as per the verse 'In famine He redeemed you from death'.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches that one who starves himself during famine is saved from an unnatural death.
The gemara cites the verse 'In famine He redeemed you from death' as support, then clarifies that the verse means reward for starving oneself saves from an unnatural death.

items.text: Marital relations during famine
items.text_en: Marital relations during famine
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish forbids marital relations during famine, citing Joseph's example, while a baraita permits it for those bereft of children.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish forbids marital relations during famine, citing the verse that Joseph's children were born before the famine.
A baraita permits marital relations during famine for those who lack children.

items.text: Communal solidarity in times of distress
items.text_en: Communal solidarity in times of distress
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that one who separates from the community during its distress is punished, and one should rather share in the suffering, as Moses did. It contrasts the fate of the wicked who indulge and the righteous who are taken.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one who separates from the community during its distress is cursed by the ministering angels not to see the community's consolation.
Another baraita warns that one who indulges while the community suffers is condemned by the verse to die without atonement.
The Gemara contrasts the fate of the wicked, who indulge and are punished, with the righteous who are taken from evil.
The Gemara concludes that one should share in the community's suffering, as Moses did by sitting on a stone, and promises that such a person will see the community's consolation.

items.text: Witnesses against a person
items.text_en: Witnesses against a person
items.desc_en: Various opinions are given on who testifies against a person: the stones of his house, the ministering angels, his soul, or his limbs.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises the question of who testifies against a person, and answers that the stones and beams of his house testify, citing the verse 'כִּי אֶבֶן מִקִּיר תִּזְעָק וְכָפִיס מֵעֵץ יַעֲנֶנָּה'.
Beit Rabbi Sheila states that the two ministering angels who accompany a person testify against him, citing the verse 'כִּי מַלְאָכָיו יְצַוֶּה לָּךְ'.
Rabbi Chidka says that a person's own soul testifies against him, citing the verse 'מִשֹּׁכֶבֶת חֵיקֶךָ שְׁמֹר פִּתְחֵי פִיךָ'.
Yesh Omrim (some say) that a person's own limbs testify against him, citing the verse 'אַתֶּם עֵדַי נְאֻם ה׳'.

items.text: Divine justice: reward and punishment
items.text_en: Divine justice: reward and punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds on the verse 'A God of faithfulness and without iniquity', explaining that the righteous are punished in this world for minor sins, and the wicked are rewarded in this world for minor mitzvot. At death, all deeds are reviewed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara expounds on the first part of the verse 'אל אמונה' (God of faithfulness), teaching that the righteous are punished in this world for minor sins just as the wicked are punished in the World to Come.

The Gemara expounds on the second part of the verse 'ואין עול' (and without iniquity), teaching that the wicked are rewarded in this world for minor mitzvot just as the righteous are rewarded in the World to Come.

The Gemara expounds on the final part of the verse 'צדיק וישר הוא' (righteous and upright is He), describing how at death all deeds are reviewed before the person, who acknowledges and signs the record, and even justifies the divine judgment.

items.text: Debate: Is one who fasts a sinner or holy?
items.text_en: Debate: Is one who fasts a sinner or holy?
items.desc_en: Shmuel says one who fasts is called a sinner, citing Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's kal vachomer from the nazirite. Rabbi Elazar calls him holy, also from the nazirite. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one who afflicts himself from wine and one who becomes impure.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that one who fasts is called a sinner.
Shmuel's view aligns with a baraita where Rabbi Elazar HaKappar uses a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from the nazirite who only abstained from wine yet is called a sinner.
Rabbi Elazar objects, citing the same nazirite verse to argue that one who fasts is called holy, not a sinner.
The Gemara asks Shmuel: but the nazirite is also called holy (קדוש) in the verse?
The Gemara answers that the term 'holy' in the nazirite verse refers specifically to growing his hair long, not to the abstention itself.
The Gemara asks Rabbi Elazar: but the nazirite is also called a sinner in the verse?
The Gemara answers that the term 'sinner' in the nazirite verse refers to one who became impure (by contact with a corpse), not to the abstention itself.
The Gemara challenges Rabbi Elazar's position by citing a contradictory statement from him.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar's own teaching that a person should always assess himself (whether he can fast), implying he does not view fasting as inherently sinful.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction about the fasting individual
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction about the fasting individual
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction regarding whether a fasting person is considered as if holiness dwells within him. It distinguishes between one who can endure the fast and one who cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one who can endure the fast (considered holy) and one who cannot (not considered holy).
Question: 'No difficulty: this one — who can pain himself, that one — who cannot pain himself.'

items.text: Reish Lakish and Rav Sheshet on the fasting scholar
items.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rav Sheshet on the fasting scholar
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that a fasting person is called a חסיד. Rav Sheshet adds a cynical remark about a student who fasts, saying a dog should eat his bread.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that a fasting person is called a חסיד (pious one), citing a verse.
Rav Sheshet cynically remarks that a student who fasts should have his bread eaten by a dog, implying the fast is detrimental to his Torah study.

items.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba and Reish Lakish on public fasts and Torah scholars
items.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba and Reish Lakish on public fasts and Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba states that the only public fast in Babylonia is Tisha B'Av. He also quotes Reish Lakish that a Torah scholar may not fast because it diminishes his Torah study.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba states that the only public fast in Babylonia is Tisha B'Av.

sub.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quotes Reish Lakish that a Torah scholar may not fast because it diminishes his Torah study.

items.text: Rav Huna on an individual who accepted a fast
items.text_en: Rav Huna on an individual who accepted a fast
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if an individual accepted a fast, even if he ate and drank all night, he recites תפילת תענית the next day. But if he spent the night fasting, he does not recite it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that an individual who accepted a fast recites תפילת תענית (the fast-day prayer) the next day if he ate and drank all night, but if he spent the night fasting, he does not recite it.

items.text: Rav Yosef's question about Rav Huna's reasoning
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's question about Rav Huna's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef questions whether Rav Huna holds that one does not fast for hours (אין מתענין לשעות) or that one does fast for hours but the one who fasts for hours does not recite תפילת תענית.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef questions whether Rav Huna holds that one does not fast for hours (אין מתענין לשעות) or that one does fast for hours but the one who fasts for hours does not recite תפילת תענית.

items.text: Abaye's answer explaining Rav Huna's position
items.text_en: Abaye's answer explaining Rav Huna's position
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that Rav Huna holds that one does fast for hours and recites תפילת תענית, but the case is different because the night hours were not included in the original acceptance.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that Rav Huna holds one does fast for hours (מתענין לשעות) and recites תפילת תענית, but here the night hours were not included in the original acceptance.

items.text: Mar Ukva's questions and the academy's answers
items.text_en: Mar Ukva's questions and the academy's answers
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva was asked three questions: about fasting for hours, about gentiles' vessels, and about what Moses wore during the seven days of consecration. He did not know, so he asked the academy, which ruled that one does fast for hours and recites תפילת תענית, that gentiles' vessels are permitted after twelve months, and that Moses served in a white shirt (or, according to Rav Kahana, a white shirt without a hem).

items.text: Abaye's clarification on a fast by hours
items.text_en: Abaye's clarification on a fast by hours
items.desc_en: Abaye questions the earlier statement that a fast by hours is valid only if one hasn't eaten until evening, arguing that this is a full fast. The Gemara explains that the case is where one reconsidered and decided to fast only part of the day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the earlier rule that a fast by hours is valid only if one hasn't eaten until evening.
Abaye objects that this is a full fast, not a partial one.
The Gemara clarifies that the case is where one reconsidered and decided to fast only part of the day.

items.text: Rav Chisda's principle and challenges
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's principle and challenges
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that a fast without sunset is not a valid fast. The Gemara brings challenges from the practice of the mishmar (priestly watch) who fast but do not complete, and from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony about Tisha b'Av, and from Rabbi Yochanan's statement about fasting until he returns home. Each is dismissed as merely self-affliction or a ruse to avoid the Nasi's meal.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that any fast without sunset is not considered a valid fast.
The Gemara objects from the practice of the mishmar (priestly watch) who fast but do not complete until sunset.
The Gemara dismisses the objection, explaining that the mishmar's fast is merely self-affliction, not a formal fast.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a second objection from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony that they fasted on a postponed Tisha b'Av but did not complete the fast.

sub.text: Gemara's answer dismissing the second objection
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer dismissing the second objection
sub.desc_en: The Gemara again dismisses the objection, explaining that this fast was also merely self-affliction.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Yochanan's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Yochanan's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a third objection from Rabbi Yochanan's statement that he would be in a fast until he returns home, without completing until sunset.

sub.text: Gemara's answer dismissing the third objection
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer dismissing the third objection
sub.desc_en: The Gemara dismisses the third objection, explaining that Rabbi Yochanan's statement was merely a ruse to avoid the Nasi's meal.

items.text: Shmuel's requirement for accepting the fast beforehand
items.text_en: Shmuel's requirement for accepting the fast beforehand
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that a fast not accepted before sunset is not a valid fast. Rabbah bar Sheilah compares such a fast to an empty wineskin filled with air.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that any fast not accepted before the day is not considered a fast.
The Gemara asks what if one sits and fasts without prior acceptance.
Rabbah bar Sheilah answers that it is like a bellows full of wind, i.e., meaningless.

items.text: When to accept the fast: Rav vs. Shmuel and the Megillat Taanit debate
items.text_en: When to accept the fast: Rav vs. Shmuel and the Megillat Taanit debate
items.desc_en: Rav says acceptance is at the Minchah prayer, Shmuel says during the Minchah prayer itself. Rav Yosef supports Shmuel from Megillat Taanit. The Gemara then debates the meaning of the word 'yesar' in Megillat Taanit, with a dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, and cites a baraita explaining how a vow can override or be overridden by the holidays listed in Megillat Taanit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks when one accepts the fast, and cites Rav's position that it is at the Minchah prayer.
Shmuel says the acceptance is during the Minchah prayer itself.
Rav Yosef supports Shmuel by citing Megillat Taanit, which uses the word 'yesar' (he shall be bound).
The Gemara asks whether 'yesar' means binding oneself in prayer, and answers that it means binding oneself (in a vow).

sub.text: Dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
sub.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi dispute the reading of the word: one says 'yesar' (active) and the other says 'ye'aser' (passive), and the Gemara asks what the latter means.
A baraita explains the passive reading: if a person's vow preceded the decree of Megillat Taanit, the vow overrides the decree; if the decree preceded the vow, the decree overrides the vow.

items.text: Until when may one eat before a fast?
items.text_en: Until when may one eat before a fast?
items.desc_en: The rabbis debate the deadline for eating before a fast: Rabbi says until dawn, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says until cockcrow. Abaye and Rava discuss exceptions for one who hasn't finished his meal or hasn't slept. Rav Ashi defines the state of being drowsy (mitnamnem).

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the debate: until when may one eat before a fast? Rabbi says until dawn.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon gives a second opinion: one may eat until cockcrow.
Abaye qualifies the debate: the dispute applies only if one has not finished his meal; if he finished, he may not eat.
Rava objects with a baraita: if one finished and stood up, he may still eat, contradicting Abaye's qualification.
The gemara resolves: the baraita refers to a case where one has not yet cleared the table.
An alternative version: Rava says the dispute applies only if one has not slept; if he slept, he may not eat.
Abaye objects with a baraita: if one slept and then stood up, he may still eat, contradicting Rava's qualification.
The gemara resolves: the baraita refers to one who is drowsy (mitnamnem), not fully asleep.
The gemara asks: what exactly is the definition of being drowsy (mitnamnem)?
Rav Ashi begins to define the state of being drowsy (the definition continues beyond the section).

items.text: Definition of a light sleeper
items.text_en: Definition of a light sleeper
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines the state of 'neither awake nor asleep' mentioned earlier, describing someone who responds when called but cannot reason and only remembers when reminded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defines the state of 'neither awake nor asleep' as one who responds when called but cannot reason and only remembers when reminded.

items.text: Individual fast and wearing shoes
items.text_en: Individual fast and wearing shoes
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Rav rules that an individual who accepts a fast is prohibited from wearing sandals, due to concern that he might have accepted a public fast. Rabbah bar Rav Sheila suggests a formula to specify an individual fast. The Gemara then discusses the practice of rabbis who wore shoes to the fast house, with Abaye and Rava, Marimar and Mar Zutra, and the rabbis of Rav Ashi's house each having different customs.

sub.text: Rav Kahana in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports in Rav's name that an individual who accepts a fast is prohibited from wearing sandals, due to concern that he might have accepted a public fast.
Rabbah bar Rav Sheila suggests a formula to specify an individual fast, saying 'Tomorrow I will be before you in an individual fast.'
The rabbis object to Rav Sheshet, noting that they see rabbis wearing shoes when coming to the fast house.
Rav Sheshet is angered and retorts that perhaps they also eat, implying that their practice is not reliable.

The Gemara reports different customs: Abaye and Rava put on shoes after washing, Marimar and Mar Zutra exchange shoes between feet, and the rabbis of Rav Ashi's house go out normally, following Shmuel's view that there is no public fast in Babylonia except Tisha B'Av.

items.text: Can one defer a fast?
items.text_en: Can one defer a fast?
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that a person may 'borrow' his fast and repay it later. Shmuel objects, arguing that a fast is not a vow but self-affliction; if one can afflict himself, he does, and if not, he does not. An alternative version has Shmuel saying it is obvious, comparing it to a vow which can be fulfilled later.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that a person may 'borrow' his fast and repay it later.
Shmuel objects, arguing that a fast is not a vow but self-affliction; if one can afflict himself, he does, and if not, he does not.
An alternative version has Shmuel saying it is obvious, comparing it to a vow which can be fulfilled later.

items.text: Fast for a dream
items.text_en: Fast for a dream
items.desc_en: Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi was offered food while fasting and was told he could defer his fast, but he refused because it was a fast for a dream. Rabbah bar Machseya in the name of Rav states that a fast is beneficial for a dream like fire for flax. Rav Chisda adds that it must be on the same day, and Rav Yosef says even on Shabbat. The remedy is to fast another day to atone for the fast.

sub.text: Narrative: Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi's visit
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi's visit
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi visits Rav Asi, who offers him a calf, but he refuses because he is fasting.
Rav Asi suggests that Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi defer his fast and repay it later, citing Rav Yehuda's ruling that one may borrow a fast.

sub.text: Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi explains that his fast is a fast for a dream, which cannot be deferred.

items.text: Mishnah: Additional communal fasts
items.text_en: Mishnah: Additional communal fasts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the sequence of communal fasts when rain does not come: after the first three fasts, the court decrees three more with additional restrictions (work, washing, anointing, wearing shoes, marital relations). If still unanswered, seven more fasts are decreed, totaling thirteen, with additional stringencies like blowing the shofar and closing shops. If still unanswered, the people reduce business and social activities, and individuals continue fasting until Nissan.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the first three fasts pass without answer, the court decrees three additional communal fasts with restrictions on work, washing, anointing, wearing shoes, and marital relations, and closes bathhouses.

The Mishnah continues that if still unanswered, the court decrees seven more fasts (totaling thirteen), with additional stringencies of blowing the shofar and closing shops, and on Monday shops open only at dusk, on Thursday they open freely for Shabbat honor.

The Mishnah concludes that if still unanswered, the people reduce business, building, planting, betrothals, marriages, and greetings, acting like people rebuked by God; individuals continue fasting until Nissan, and if rain falls after Nissan it is a curse, as the verse says 'Is it not the wheat harvest today?'

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of prohibition of work on a fast day
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of prohibition of work on a fast day
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why work is prohibited on a fast day, as it is a hardship. Rav Chisda in the name of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba derives from a verse that a fast is like a convocation (Atzeret), where work is forbidden. Rabbi Zeira explains that the verse 'gather the elders' indicates the fast is during the day, like the gathering of elders. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi supports Rav Huna that the gathering is from morning. Abaye describes the daily schedule: until midday they deal with city matters, then read Torah, then pray.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why work is prohibited on a fast day, since work is hardship, unlike other prohibitions which are pleasures.

sub.text: Rav Chisda in the name of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba derives from the verse 'קַדְּשׁוּ צוֹם קִרְאוּ עֲצָרָה' that a fast day is like a convocation (עֲצֶרֶת), where work is forbidden.
The Gemara objects that if the fast is like a convocation, it should begin at night like a festival.
Rabbi Zeira explains that the verse 'אִסְפוּ זְקֵנִים' indicates the fast is during the day, like the gathering of elders.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the fast begins only from midday.
Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi supports Rav Huna's view that the gathering is from morning.
Abaye describes the daily schedule: until midday they deal with city matters, then read Torah, then pray, citing the verse from Nehemiah.

items.text: Gemara's objection to the previous assumption
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to the previous assumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that one could reverse the ruling, citing a verse from Ezra where he arose from his fast before the evening offering, implying that bathing in cold water might be permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility of reversing the ruling, citing Ezra's verse where he arose from his fast before the evening offering, implying that bathing in cold water might be permitted.

items.text: Rav Chisda's distinction between mourning and pleasure
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction between mourning and pleasure
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that for mourning (e.g., Tisha b'Av and an actual mourner), both hot and cold water are forbidden; for public fasts (due to pleasure), only hot water is forbidden, but cold water is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda distinguishes between mourning (Tisha b'Av and an actual mourner), where both hot and cold water are forbidden, and public fasts (due to pleasure), where only hot water is forbidden but cold water is permitted.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah about closing bathhouses
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah about closing bathhouses
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin cites a Mishnah that closes bathhouses on fast days, implying only hot water is forbidden. Abaye objects that if cold water were also forbidden, rivers would need to be closed. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that the Mishnah's wording shows the prohibition is only for hot water.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin cites the Mishnah that closes bathhouses on fast days as supporting evidence for the distinction between hot and cold water.
Abaye objects that if cold water were also forbidden, the Mishnah would need to close rivers, not just bathhouses.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi resolves that the Mishnah's wording 'closing bathhouses' implies only hot water is forbidden, as cold water would not require closing a bathhouse.

items.text: Support from the law of obligatory immersions
items.text_en: Support from the law of obligatory immersions
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rav Chisda from a baraita that allows obligatory immersions on Tisha b'Av and Yom Kippur, presumably in cold water. Rav Chana bar Katina limits this to the hot springs of Tiberias. Rav Papa explains that Rabbi Chanina's statement about losing immersion refers to places where cold water is unavailable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to support Rav Chisda from a baraita that permits obligatory immersions on Tisha b'Av and Yom Kippur, implying cold water is allowed.
The Gemara questions whether the baraita refers to hot water, noting that hot water for immersion would be drawn water (שאובין), which is invalid for a mikveh.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita must refer to cold water, and that only those obligated in immersions may bathe, not others.
Rav Chana bar Katina rejects the support, explaining that the baraita refers only to the hot springs of Tiberias, which are naturally heated and not forbidden.
The Gemara objects: if cold water is permitted, why did Rabbi Chanina lament the loss of immersion in the Temple, since one could bathe in cold water?
Rav Papa resolves the objection by explaining that Rabbi Chanina's statement applies to a place where cold water is not available.

items.text: Proof from the laws of washing on fast days
items.text_en: Proof from the laws of washing on fast days
items.desc_en: A baraita states that on fast days, washing the whole body is forbidden, but face, hands, and feet are permitted. The Gemara assumes this refers to cold water, as Rav Sheshet forbids a mourner from even putting a finger in hot water. The Gemara deflects, saying the baraita deals with hot water and the comparison to a mourner applies only to the other restrictions.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that on fast days, washing the whole body is forbidden, but face, hands, and feet are permitted, and the same applies to a mourner.

The Gemara asks whether the baraita refers to all restrictions, and argues that if it dealt with hot water, even face, hands, and feet would be forbidden for a mourner, as Rav Sheshet forbids a mourner from even putting a finger in hot water; therefore it must refer to cold water.
The Gemara deflects, saying the baraita actually deals with hot water, and the comparison to a mourner applies only to the other restrictions (work and sandals), not to washing.

items.text: Rava's ruling and a challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and a challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a mourner may bathe in cold water during the entire seven days, citing a precedent of Rabbi Yosei who did so when overwhelmed by successive mournings. A baraita is brought to challenge Rava, but the Gemara does not resolve it here.

sub.text: Gemara's challenge (baraita via Rabbi Abba the Kohen)
sub.text_en: Gemara's challenge (baraita via Rabbi Abba the Kohen)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Chanina bathed in cold water during the entire seven days of mourning, challenging Rava's ruling.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by explaining that Rabbi Yosei was in a case of successive mournings (תכופים), where leniencies apply, citing a supporting baraita.
Rav Chisda clarifies the leniencies for successive mournings: shaving with a razor but not scissors, and laundering with water but not with natron or sand.
Rava rules that a mourner is permitted to bathe in cold water during the entire seven days, based on the precedent of Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara introduces a new baraita that challenges Rava's ruling, but does not resolve it here.

items.text: Initial inference from the Mishnah about a mourner and cold water
items.text_en: Initial inference from the Mishnah about a mourner and cold water
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a minor girl (na'arah) may disfigure herself during mourning, implying she may bathe in cold water. It rejects the possibility of hot water because Rav Chisda already prohibits a mourner from even inserting a finger into hot water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a minor girl (na'arah) is permitted to disfigure herself during mourning, implying she may bathe in cold water.
The Gemara asks whether the permission refers to bathing, and if so, in what type of water.
The Gemara rejects the possibility of hot water, citing Rav Chisda's ruling that a mourner is forbidden even to insert a finger into hot water.
The Gemara concludes that the permission must refer to cold water, but then rejects this as well, suggesting the Mishnah refers to eye makeup and face powder.

items.text: Supporting story and its rejection
items.text_en: Supporting story and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina who bathed in cold water during his mourning, which would support the inference. However, it rejects this proof by explaining that his mourning periods were consecutive (tekhafuhu avelav), and a baraita permits such a mourner to lighten his hair and launder his clothes in water.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina bathed in cold water for all seven days of mourning after his sons died, supporting the permissibility of cold water.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's case was exceptional because his mournings were consecutive, and a baraita permits such a person to lighten his hair with a razor and wash his garments in water.
Rav Chisda clarifies the baraita: the permission for consecutive mournings is limited to a razor (not scissors) and water (not soap or other cleansing agents).

items.text: Rava's prohibition of cold water and a second attempt at proof
items.text_en: Rava's prohibition of cold water and a second attempt at proof
items.desc_en: Rava states that a mourner is prohibited from cold water for all seven days, distinguishing it from meat and wine which are permitted to calm his fear. The Gemara then attempts to prove Rava's position from the Mishnah, but again deflects the proof to cosmetics (kikhul and pirkus).

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a mourner is prohibited from cold water for all seven days, and explains that meat and wine are permitted only to calm his fear.
The Gemara attempts to prove Rava's position from the Mishnah's distinction between a bogeret and a na'arah regarding beautification.
The Gemara deflects the proof, explaining that the Mishnah's distinction refers to cosmetics (kikhul and pirkus), not bathing.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling and the halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling and the halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda concludes that a mourner is prohibited from laundering (tikhboset) for seven days. The Gemara then states the halakha: a mourner may not bathe his entire body in either hot or cold water for seven days, but may wash his face, hands, and feet in cold water. Anointing is prohibited unless it is to remove filth.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a mourner is forbidden to launder clothes for all seven days.

The Stam concludes the halacha: a mourner is forbidden to bathe his entire body in either hot or cold water for seven days, but face, hands, and feet are permitted in cold water; anointing is forbidden unless to remove filth.

items.text: Dispute over where an individual inserts the fast-day prayer
items.text_en: Dispute over where an individual inserts the fast-day prayer
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah taught that an individual who accepts a fast recites the 'Aneinu' prayer between 'Go'el' and 'Rofe' in the Amidah. Rav Yitzchak objects that an individual cannot establish a blessing for himself, and instead says it in 'Shome'a Tefillah'. Rav Sheshet agrees with Rav Yitzchak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one inserts the prayer for a fast day (עננו) into the Amidah.
Rav Yehuda instructed his son Rav Yitzchak to teach that an individual who accepted a fast recites the fast-day prayer between 'Go'el' and 'Rofei' in the Amidah.
Rav Yitzchak objects that an individual cannot establish a new blessing for himself.
Rav Yitzchak and Rav Sheshet rule that the fast-day prayer is inserted into the 'Shomea Tefillah' blessing.
Rav Sheshet agrees with Rav Yitzchak that the individual says 'Aneinu' in 'Shome'a Tefillah'.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about the difference between individual and community
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about the difference between individual and community
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the only difference between an individual and a community is that one prays eighteen and the other nineteen blessings. The Gemara initially assumes this refers to an individual who accepted a fast versus a community fast, and concludes that an individual does establish a blessing for himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita that distinguishes between an individual and a community only by the number of blessings (18 vs. 19), but if the community's prayer leader recites 24 blessings, the baraita's numbers are inconsistent.

The Gemara reinterprets the baraita as comparing an individual who accepted a private fast to an individual who accepted a public fast, concluding that an individual can establish a blessing for himself.

items.text: Rejection and resolution of the challenge
items.text_en: Rejection and resolution of the challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by explaining that the baraita refers to the prayer leader (shliach tzibbur) on the first three fasts, where there are no twenty-four blessings. It then addresses further difficulties about the 'ein bein' formulation, concluding that the tanna only deals with prohibitions, not prayers, or that even on the middle fasts there are no twenty-four blessings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by explaining that the baraita refers to the prayer leader (שליח ציבור) on the first three fasts, where there are no twenty-four blessings.

The Gemara objects that the baraita uses the formulation 'אין בין' (there is no difference between), implying that the first three and middle three fasts are identical regarding the twenty-four blessings, contradicting the answer.

The Gemara first suggests that the tanna omitted (שייר) the difference in prayers, but rejects this because the 'אין בין' formulation implies completeness, then concludes that the tanna only deals with prohibitions, not prayers.
