The Gemara offers an alternative answer: even on the middle fasts, the prayer leader does not recite twenty-four blessings.
The Gemara objects by citing another baraita that uses 'אין בין' for the last seven fasts, implying completeness, and questions how the tanna could omit the difference in prayers.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by questioning whether the 'אין בין' formulation is meant to be exhaustive, implying that it is not.

items.text: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's omissions
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's omissions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah omitted the blessing of the Ark (תיבה) from the list of additional blessings. It argues that private matters are taught but public ones are not, and Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah's language that no omissions were made.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah omitted the blessing of the Ark (תיבה) from the list of additional blessings, and answers that private matters are taught but public ones are not.
Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah's language that no omissions were made, because the Mishnah says 'what are these additional' implying a complete list.
The Gemara resolves that the Ark blessing is not an omission because it is taught in another chapter, and similarly the twenty-four blessings are not an omission.

items.text: Where to insert the additional blessing
items.text_en: Where to insert the additional blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where in the Amidah the additional blessing for fast days is inserted. Rabbi Shmuel bar Sisratai and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi say between 'Go'el' and 'Rofe', while Rav Ashi says in 'Shome'a Tefillah'. The halakha follows Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where in the Amidah the additional blessings are inserted.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Sisratai and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Sisratai and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Sisratai, and similarly Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav, say the blessings are inserted between 'Go'el' and 'Rofe'.
Rav Ashi says in the name of Rabbi Yannai that the blessings are inserted in 'Shomea Tefillah'.
The Gemara rules that the halacha follows the opinion that the blessings are inserted in 'Shomea Tefillah'.

items.text: Contradictory baraitot on pregnant and nursing women fasting
items.text_en: Contradictory baraitot on pregnant and nursing women fasting
items.desc_en: Three baraitot contradict each other regarding whether pregnant and nursing women fast during the first or last set of fasts. Rav Ashi resolves them by taking the middle baraita as the baseline, which reconciles all three.

sub.desc_en: Three baraitot are cited with conflicting rulings about whether pregnant and nursing women fast in the first or last series of fasts.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradictions by holding the middle baraita as the baseline, reconciling all three.
The third baraita further contradicts the others, stating that they do not fast at all during either set.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradictions by taking the middle baraita as the baseline, which reconciles all three.

items.text: Debate on the meaning of 'התרעה'
items.text_en: Debate on the meaning of 'התרעה'
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether the term 'התרעה' in the Mishnah refers to shofar blasts or the 'עננו' prayer. Rav Yehuda says shofarot, while Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel bar Shilat says 'עננו'. A baraita about seven fasts with eighteen 'התרעות' seems to support shofarot, but the Gemara resolves that all agree shofarot are called 'התרעה', and they dispute only whether 'עננו' is also called 'התרעה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'התרעה' refers to in the Mishnah, and cites two opinions: Rav Yehuda says shofar blasts, and Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav says the 'עננו' prayer.

The Gemara initially assumes the two opinions are mutually exclusive, and raises a contradiction from a baraita that states seven fasts include eighteen 'התרעות', with the sign of Jericho (which used shofarot), challenging the view that 'התרעה' means 'עננו'.
The Gemara resolves that all agree shofar blasts are called 'התרעה', and the dispute is only whether 'עננו' is also called 'התרעה'.
The Gemara clarifies the logical hierarchy: one who says 'עננו' certainly includes shofarot, but one who says shofarot excludes 'עננו'.

items.text: Proof from a baraita and a Mishnah about Shabbat
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita and a Mishnah about Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita distinguishes between 'התרעה' with shofarot and 'צעקה' with speech, supporting the view that 'התרעה' is shofarot. A Mishnah about Shabbat shows that 'התרעה' can be done with 'עננו' on Shabbat, proving that 'עננו' is also called 'התרעה'. This indicates the dispute is between Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: A baraita distinguishes between 'התרעה' with shofarot and 'צעקה' with speech, supporting the view that 'התרעה' is shofarot.
The gemara introduces a Mishnah about Shabbat that shows a dispute between Tannaim regarding 'התרעה'.
The gemara concludes that the Mishnah must refer to 'עננו' (the prayer), proving that 'עננו' is also called 'התרעה', indicating the dispute is between Tannaim.

items.text: Transition to a story about Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah
items.text_en: Transition to a story about Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah
items.desc_en: The daf begins a narrative about a time of distress during the tenure of Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a narrative about a time of distress in the days of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia.

items.text: The dispute about extending fasts beyond thirteen
items.text_en: The dispute about extending fasts beyond thirteen
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami attempted to decree additional fasts beyond thirteen but was told not to burden the community. Rabbi Abba then cites Rabbi Yochanan that the limit applies only to rain, not to other calamities, and a baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabbi Ami decreed thirteen fasts without being answered, and when he sought to add more, he was told not to burden the community excessively.

Rabbi Abba explains that Rabbi Ami acted for himself, but Rabbi Yochanan rules that the limit of thirteen fasts applies only to rain, while for other calamities one may continue fasting until answered.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's distinction, stating that the three and seven fasts were only said for rain, but for other calamities one continues fasting until answered.

items.text: Defense of Rabbi Ami and a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Defense of Rabbi Ami and a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge against Rabbi Ami, but he defends himself by citing a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi says no more than thirteen fasts, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel attributes the limit to the end of the rainy season.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge against Rabbi Ami's position that one should not impose more than thirteen fasts.
Rabbi Ami defends himself by citing a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi holds that no more than thirteen fasts are decreed, because one does not burden the community excessively.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offers an alternative reason: the limit is not due to burdening the community, but because the rainy season has passed.

items.text: The case of Nineveh and the prayer for rain
items.text_en: The case of Nineveh and the prayer for rain
items.desc_en: The people of Nineveh ask Rabbi whether they should pray for rain as individuals or as a community. Rabbi rules they are like individuals and pray in 'Shomea Tefillah'. A challenge from Rabbi Yehuda's statement is deflected by noting Rabbi is a Tanna and disputes.

sub.text: People of Nineveh's question to Rabbi
sub.text_en: People of Nineveh's question to Rabbi
sub.desc_en: The people of Nineveh ask Rabbi whether they, who need rain even in summer, should pray as individuals (in 'Shomea Tefillah') or as a community (in 'Birkat HaShanim').
Rabbi rules that the people of Nineveh are like individuals and should pray in 'Shomea Tefillah'.

sub.text: Gemara's challenge from Rabbi Yehuda's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's challenge from Rabbi Yehuda's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that in the present era, prayer for rain depends on the years, places, and times, implying that Nineveh's situation might be different.
The Gemara deflects the objection by noting that Rabbi is a Tanna and can dispute the baraita attributed to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: The halakhic conclusion on the prayer placement
items.text_en: The halakhic conclusion on the prayer placement
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet dispute whether the prayer for rain is in 'Birkat HaShanim' or 'Shomea Tefillah'. The halakha is decided in favor of 'Shomea Tefillah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the halakhic conclusion regarding the placement of the prayer for rain.
Rav Nachman rules that the prayer for rain is placed in 'Birkat HaShanim' (the blessing of the years).
Rav Sheshet rules that the prayer for rain is placed in 'Shomea Tefillah' (the blessing that hears prayer).
The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Rav Sheshet, placing the prayer in 'Shomea Tefillah'.

items.text: The practice of opening the ark on fast days
items.text_en: The practice of opening the ark on fast days
items.desc_en: A question arises about the correct version of the Mishnah regarding opening the ark on Monday and Thursday. A baraita resolves it: on Monday they incline until evening, on Thursday they open all day due to Shabbat honor.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises a question about the correct version of the Mishnah: whether it says 'on Monday they incline until evening and on Thursday all day' or 'on Monday they incline and on Thursday they open all day'.

A baraita is cited to resolve the question: it explicitly states that on Monday they incline until evening and on Thursday they open all day due to Shabbat honor, and adds details about a person with two doors or a bench.

items.text: Restrictions on joyous activities and greetings
items.text_en: Restrictions on joyous activities and greetings
items.desc_en: If fasts are not answered, people reduce business, building, and planting. A Tanna specifies which building and planting are prohibited. Additionally, greetings are restricted: friends do not greet, and the ignorant are answered with difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the fasts pass without answer, people reduce business, building, and planting.
A Tanna specifies that the prohibited building is a joyous one (a wedding house for one's son) and the prohibited planting is a royal grove (אבווראנקי של מלכים).
The Mishnah adds that greetings are also restricted.
A baraita elaborates: friends do not greet each other; the ignorant who greet are answered with difficulty; and the people sit wrapped like mourners until Heaven has mercy.

items.text: Teachings of Rabbi Elazar on falling on one's face, sackcloth, and other practices
items.text_en: Teachings of Rabbi Elazar on falling on one's face, sackcloth, and other practices
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that only someone like Joshua may fall on his face, and only someone like Jehoram may wear sackcloth. He distinguishes between falling and tearing garments for different leaders. Rabbi Zeira objects regarding Joshua, and Rabbi Elazar further distinguishes between standing and bowing for kings and princes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that only someone answered like Joshua may fall on his face, citing the verse where God tells Joshua to rise.
Rabbi Elazar adds that only someone answered like Jehoram may wear sackcloth, citing the verse where Jehoram tears his garments and wears sackcloth.
Rabbi Elazar distinguishes between falling and tearing garments: Moses and Aaron fell on their faces, while Joshua and Caleb tore their garments.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that the verse says 'ויהושע' (and Joshua) with a vav, implying Joshua both fell and tore his garments, contradicting Rabbi Elazar's distinction.
Rabbi Elazar resolves by distinguishing between standing and bowing for kings and princes, citing a verse about God as Israel's redeemer.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous Gemara: the interpretation of 'שרים וישתחוו'
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous Gemara: the interpretation of 'שרים וישתחוו'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani) challenges the earlier interpretation of the verse, arguing that the phrasing 'שרים וישתחוו' implies both that the kings will see and rise, and that the princes will bow, not just one action.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects to the earlier interpretation of the verse, arguing that the phrasing 'שרים וישתחוו' (princes and they will bow) implies both that the kings will see and rise and that the princes will bow, not just one action.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement on light and joy
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement on light and joy
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that not all are destined for light and joy: the righteous receive light, and the upright receive joy, as supported by verses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak introduces his own statement, asserting that not all are destined for light and joy.
He states the principle that not everyone is destined for light and not everyone for joy.

He specifies that the righteous receive light and the upright receive joy, citing verses: 'אוֹר זָרֻעַ לַצַּדִּיק' (light is sown for the righteous) and 'וּלְיִשְׁרֵי לֵב שִׂמְחָה' (and for the upright of heart, joy).

items.text: Transition: 'הדרן עלך מאימתי'
items.text_en: Transition: 'הדרן עלך מאימתי'
items.desc_en: This segment marks the end of the previous chapter and the beginning of the new Mishnah on the order of fasts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter and transitions to the new Mishnah on the order of fasts.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The order of fast-day procedures
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The order of fast-day procedures
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the initial steps of a public fast: taking the ark out to the city square, placing ashes on the ark and on the heads of the Nasi and Av Beit Din, and the elder's admonition emphasizing repentance over fasting.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking how the order of fasts is conducted, then describes taking the ark out to the city square and placing ashes on the ark and on the heads of the Nasi and Av Beit Din.

The elder delivers words of admonition, citing the example of Nineveh to emphasize that God responds to repentance, not fasting, and quoting the verse 'קרעו לבבכם ואל בגדיכם' (rend your hearts, not your garments).

items.text: Mishnah: The prayer leader and the twenty-four blessings
items.text_en: Mishnah: The prayer leader and the twenty-four blessings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: when they stand for prayer, they appoint an elder with children and an empty home to lead, and he recites twenty-four blessings: the eighteen daily blessings plus six additional ones, including 'זכרונות' and 'שופרות' and specific psalms.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when they stand for prayer, they appoint an elder with children and an empty home to lead, so his heart is whole in prayer.
The Mishnah specifies that the prayer leader recites twenty-four blessings: the eighteen daily ones plus six additional ones, listing the specific psalms.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's alternative opinion on the additional blessings
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's alternative opinion on the additional blessings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that one need not recite 'זכרונות' and 'שופרות'; instead, one should substitute them with verses about famine and plague from the prophets.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that one need not recite the 'זכרונות' (Remembrances) and 'שופרות' (Shofarot) blessings; instead, one should substitute them with verses about famine and plague from the prophets.

items.text: Mishnah: The seven concluding blessings with historical responses
items.text_en: Mishnah: The seven concluding blessings with historical responses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details the seven concluding blessings, each invoking a biblical figure who was answered in time of need: Abraham at Mount Moriah, the ancestors at the Sea, Joshua at Gilgal, Samuel at Mizpah, Elijah on Mount Carmel, Jonah from the fish, and David and Solomon in Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the first concluding blessing, invoking Abraham at Mount Moriah, with the formula 'May He who answered Abraham answer you' and the closing blessing 'Go'el Yisrael'.
The Mishnah presents the second blessing, invoking the ancestors at the Sea of Reeds, with the closing blessing 'Zocher haNishkachot'.
The Mishnah presents the third blessing, invoking Joshua at Gilgal, with the closing blessing 'Shome'a Teru'ah'.
The Mishnah presents the fourth blessing, invoking Samuel at Mizpah, with the closing blessing 'Shome'a Tze'akah'.
The Mishnah presents the fifth blessing, invoking Elijah on Mount Carmel, with the closing blessing 'Shome'a Tefillah'.
The Mishnah presents the sixth blessing, invoking Jonah from the fish, with the closing blessing 'HaOneh b'Eit Tzarah'.
The Mishnah presents the seventh blessing, invoking David and Solomon in Jerusalem, with the closing blessing 'HaMerachem al ha'Aretz'.

items.text: Transition to a story: 'מעשה'
items.text_en: Transition to a story: 'מעשה'
items.desc_en: This segment introduces a story (מעשה) that will follow, serving as a narrative example.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story (מעשה) that will follow as a narrative example.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chalafta and Rabbi Chananya ben Tradyon
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chalafta and Rabbi Chananya ben Tradyon
items.desc_en: A story is told about a prayer leader who completed the entire blessing without the congregation responding 'Amen', leading the priests to blow trumpets and recite special prayers. When the matter came before the Sages, they said they did not practice this except at the Eastern Gate and on the Temple Mount.

sub.desc_en: A story is told about a prayer leader who completed the entire blessing without the congregation responding 'Amen', prompting the priests to blow trumpets and recite special prayers.
When the matter came before the Sages, they said they did not practice this except at the Eastern Gate and on the Temple Mount.

items.text: Mishnah: Rules for the priestly watches and patriarchal houses during fasts
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules for the priestly watches and patriarchal houses during fasts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details the fasting obligations for the priestly watches (משמר) and patriarchal houses (בית אב) during the three sets of fasts: the first three, the second three, and the last seven. Rabbi Yehoshua and the Sages dispute the specifics, and additional rules about drinking wine, haircutting, and laundering are given.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Yehoshua's position on the fasting obligations for the priestly watches and patriarchal houses during the three sets of fasts.
The Sages present a different set of fasting rules for the priestly watches and patriarchal houses across the three fast periods.
The Mishnah adds supplementary restrictions on drinking wine, haircutting, and laundering for the priestly watches and the ma'amad.

items.text: Mishnah: Rules of Megillat Taanit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules of Megillat Taanit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the rules for days listed in Megillat Taanit: for days on which eulogies are forbidden, the day before is prohibited and after is permitted according to the first Tanna, while Rabbi Yosei prohibits both before and after. For days on which fasting is forbidden, both before and after are permitted, but Rabbi Yosei prohibits the day before.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the rule for days in מגילת תענית (Megillat Taanit) on which eulogies are forbidden: the day before is prohibited, the day after is permitted.
רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei) disputes and rules that both the day before and the day after are prohibited for eulogies.
The Tanna Kamma states the rule for days on which fasting is forbidden: both the day before and the day after are permitted.
רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei) disputes and rules that the day before is prohibited, but the day after is permitted.

items.text: Mishnah: When to begin fasts and exceptions
items.text_en: Mishnah: When to begin fasts and exceptions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not decree a fast for the community starting on Thursday, to avoid disrupting market prices. The first three fasts are on Monday, Thursday, and Monday; the second three on Thursday, Monday, and Thursday. Rabbi Yosei argues that just as the first are not on Thursday, so too the second and last. Additionally, fasts are not decreed on New Moons, Chanukah, or Purim; if begun, they are not interrupted according to Rabban Gamliel, but Rabbi Meir says they do not complete the fast. The same applies to Tisha B'Av that falls on a Friday.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one does not begin a fast for the community on Thursday to avoid raising prices, and specifies the schedule for the first and second sets of three fasts.
רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei) argues that just as the first set of fasts does not begin on Thursday, so too the second and last sets should not begin on Thursday.
The Mishnah states that fasts are not decreed on New Moons, Chanukah, or Purim, and if begun, they are not interrupted according to רבן גמליאל (Rabban Gamliel).
רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) says that Rabban Gamliel concedes that on these days they do not complete the fast, and the same applies to Tisha B'Av that falls on a Friday.

items.text: Gemara: Question on the order of taking out the ark
items.text_en: Gemara: Question on the order of taking out the ark
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with the Mishnah's statement about taking out the ark and asks: even in the first fasts? It cites a contradiction from a baraita that says during the first three and second three fasts, they pray in the synagogue as usual, but only in the last seven do they take out the ark to the city square and put ashes on it. Rav Pappa clarifies that the Mishnah's rule applies only to the last seven fasts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's rule of taking out the ark applies even to the first three fasts, and raises a contradiction from a baraita.
The baraita states that during the first three and second three fasts, they pray in the synagogue as usual, but only in the last seven do they take out the ark and put ashes on it.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by clarifying that the Mishnah's rule applies only to the last seven fasts.

items.text: Gemara: Order of placing ashes on the Nasi and Av Beit Din
items.text_en: Gemara: Order of placing ashes on the Nasi and Av Beit Din
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's order: first it mentions the Nasi and Av Beit Din, then says each person puts ashes on his own head. This seems to contradict a baraita that in matters of greatness one begins with the greatest, but in matters of curse one begins with the smallest. The Gemara resolves that for the Nasi and Av Beit Din, it is an honor for them to be prayed for first, as they are important for seeking mercy for the community.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's order: first it mentions placing ashes on the Nasi and Av Beit Din, then says each person puts ashes on his own head, which seems to contradict the principle that in matters of curse one begins with the smallest.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi states that in matters of greatness one begins with the greatest, but in matters of curse one begins with the smallest, citing the curse of the serpent, Eve, and Adam as proof.
The Gemara resolves that placing ashes on the Nasi and Av Beit Din first is not a curse but an honor, as they are told: 'You are important to seek mercy for all of us.'

items.text: Gemara: Why does another person place ashes on the Nasi?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why does another person place ashes on the Nasi?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Nasi and Av Beit Din do not take ashes themselves and place them on their own heads, but rather another person does it. Rabbi Abba from Caesarea answers that one who is shamed by himself is not comparable to one who is shamed by others, implying that having another place the ashes increases the sense of shame and humility.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Nasi and Av Beit Din do not place ashes on their own heads, but rather another person does it for them.
Rabbi Abba from Caesarea answers that one who is shamed by himself is not comparable to one who is shamed by others, so having another place the ashes increases the sense of shame and humility.

items.text: Placement of ashes on the head
items.text_en: Placement of ashes on the head
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that ashes are placed where tefillin are worn, citing a verse from Isaiah about giving 'beauty for ashes'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the ashes are placed on the head.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that the ashes are placed where tefillin are worn, citing the verse from Isaiah about giving 'beauty for ashes'.

items.text: Why they go out to the street
items.text_en: Why they go out to the street
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba and Resh Lakish give reasons for going to the street: to publicize their distress after private prayers went unanswered, and to emphasize that exile itself atones. The difference between them is whether exile from one synagogue to another suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the community goes out to the street during a public fast.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba answers that they go out to say: we cried in private and were not answered, so we will humiliate ourselves in public.
Resh Lakish answers that going to the street declares: we have been exiled, and our exile atones for us.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations.
The Gemara resolves that the difference is whether exile from one synagogue to another suffices to atone.

items.text: Reasons for taking out the ark, sackcloth, and ashes
items.text_en: Reasons for taking out the ark, sackcloth, and ashes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that taking the ark to the street shows that a once-honored vessel is now disgraced. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says sackcloth makes us like animals. Rabbi Yehuda ben Pazzi and Resh Lakish explain that ashes on the ark symbolize God's presence with us in distress. Rabbi Zeira recounts his awe at seeing this practice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the ark is taken out to the city square.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that the ark is taken out to show that a once-honored vessel has been disgraced by our sins.
The Gemara asks why the community covers themselves in sackcloth.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba explains that sackcloth makes us like animals before God.
The Gemara asks why burnt ashes are placed on top of the ark.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Pazzi explains that the ashes symbolize God's presence with us in distress, citing the verse 'עִמּוֹ אָנֹכִי בְּצָרָה' (I am with him in distress).
Resh Lakish adds a supporting verse, 'בְּכׇל צָרָתָם לוֹ צָר' (In all their distress, He was distressed).
Rabbi Zeira recounts that when he saw the rabbis placing ashes on the ark, his entire body trembled.

items.text: Why ashes on each person's head
items.text_en: Why ashes on each person's head
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chama and Rabbi Chanina dispute the reason: one says it shows we are like ashes before God, the other says it recalls the ashes of Isaac. The difference is whether plain dust suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why ashes are placed on each person's head during the fast-day rituals.
One opinion (Rabbi Levi bar Chama) says the ashes symbolize that we are considered like ashes before God.
The other opinion (Rabbi Chanina) says the ashes are to recall the ashes of Isaac (the Akeidah).
The Gemara notes the practical difference between the two opinions: whether plain dust (עָפָר סְתָם) can substitute for ashes.

items.text: Why they go to the cemetery
items.text_en: Why they go to the cemetery
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chama and Rabbi Chanina dispute the reason: one says it shows we are like the dead, the other says the dead will plead for mercy. The difference is whether gentile graves are included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the community goes out to the cemetery during a fast.
Rabbi Levi bar Chama says one reason is to declare that we are considered like the dead before God.
Rabbi Chanina says the reason is so that the dead will plead for mercy on behalf of the living.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions.
The Gemara resolves that the difference is whether one goes to gentile graves, which would not be effective for the second reason since gentile dead do not plead for Israel.

items.text: Meaning of 'Har HaMoriah'
items.text_en: Meaning of 'Har HaMoriah'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chama and Rabbi Chanina dispute the meaning: one says it is the mountain from which instruction (hora'ah) went out to Israel, the other says it is the mountain from which fear (mora) went out to the nations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the meaning of the name 'Har HaMoriah' (the Temple Mount)?
One opinion (Rabbi Levi bar Chama) says it is the mountain from which instruction (הוראה, hora'ah) went out to Israel.
The other opinion (Rabbi Chanina) says it is the mountain from which fear (מורא, mora) went out to the nations of the world.

items.text: Who leads the words of rebuke
items.text_en: Who leads the words of rebuke
items.desc_en: A baraita states that an elder, a sage, or a distinguished person leads the rebuke. Abaye clarifies that the elder must also be a sage; otherwise, a sage or distinguished person leads.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the hierarchy for who leads the words of rebuke: an elder, a sage, or a distinguished person.
The gemara questions whether the baraita's 'elder' includes one who is not a sage.
Abaye clarifies that the baraita means the elder must also be a sage; otherwise, a sage or distinguished person leads.

items.text: The content of the rebuke: repentance and the example of Nineveh
items.text_en: The content of the rebuke: repentance and the example of Nineveh
items.desc_en: The elder's speech emphasizes that sack and fasting do not bring salvation, but repentance and good deeds do, as seen with the people of Nineveh. The Gemara elaborates on their actions: separating animals from young, crying out to God, and returning from violence, even uprooting entire buildings to restore stolen property.

sub.desc_en: The elder opens by declaring that sackcloth and fasting do not bring salvation, but repentance and good deeds do, citing the example of Nineveh where God saw their deeds, not their fasting.
The Gemara elaborates on the actions of the Ninevites: they separated animals from their young and cried out to God, saying if He does not have mercy on them, they will not have mercy on their young.
The Gemara continues: the Ninevites cried out to God in strength, asking whether the oppressed or the oppressor, the righteous or the wicked, is pushed aside before the other.
Shmuel explains that the Ninevites' repentance included returning stolen property even if it meant dismantling an entire building to restore a stolen beam to its owner.

items.text: The necessity of abandoning sin for repentance
items.text_en: The necessity of abandoning sin for repentance
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah compares one who confesses but does not abandon sin to someone holding a reptile; immersion is ineffective until the reptile is thrown away. This is supported by verses about confession and forsaking sin.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah compares a person who confesses a sin but does not abandon it to someone holding a reptile; immersion in all the waters of the world is ineffective until the reptile is thrown away.
Once the reptile is thrown away, immersion in a mikveh of forty se'ah immediately effects purification.

Two verses are cited: 'וּמוֹדֶה וְעֹזֵב יְרֻחָם' (one who confesses and forsakes will be shown mercy) and 'נִשָּׂא לְבָבֵנוּ אֶל כַּפָּיִם אֶל אֵל בַּשָּׁמָיִם' (we lift our hearts to our hands to God in heaven), supporting the necessity of both confession and abandonment of sin.

items.text: Qualifications of the prayer leader
items.text_en: Qualifications of the prayer leader
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the prayer leader must be a practiced person. Rabbi Yehuda adds specific qualities: one who is burdened but has no means, works in the field, has an empty house, is pleasant, humble, well-liked, has a sweet voice, and is expert in Torah, Prophets, Writings, midrash, halakhot, and aggadot. The rabbis had their eyes on Rav Yitzchak bar Ammi.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that when the community stands in prayer, they appoint a prayer leader who is a practiced person, not necessarily an elder or sage.

Rabbi Yehuda adds a detailed list of qualities the prayer leader must possess: burdened but poor, works in the field, empty house, pleasant, humble, well-liked, sweet voice, and expert in Torah, Prophets, Writings, midrash, halakhot, and aggadot.
The gemara notes that the rabbis had their eyes on Rav Yitzchak bar Ammi as the ideal candidate for prayer leader.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's descriptions
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's descriptions
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Abaye explain two phrases from the Mishnah: 'his house is empty' means empty of transgression, and 'his youth is beautiful' means he has no bad reputation from his youth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's phrase 'his house is empty' differs from 'burdened and without'.
Rav Chisda explains that 'his house is empty' means empty of transgression.
Abaye explains that 'his youth is beautiful' means he has no bad reputation from his youth.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse about the prayer leader
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse about the prayer leader
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Toviyah quoting Rav (or Rabbi Chama quoting Rabbi Elazar) explains that the verse 'My heritage became to me like a lion in the forest' refers to a prayer leader who is not fit to descend before the ark.

sub.text: Mar Zutra bar Toviyah quoting Rav (or Rabbi Chama quoting Rabbi Elazar)
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra bar Toviyah quoting Rav (or Rabbi Chama quoting Rabbi Elazar)
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Toviyah quoting Rav (or Rabbi Chama quoting Rabbi Elazar) interprets the verse 'My heritage became to me like a lion in the forest' as referring to a prayer leader who is not fit to descend before the ark.

items.text: Question on the number of additional blessings
items.text_en: Question on the number of additional blessings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says six additional blessings are added, but a baraita mentions a seventh blessing for the Sabbatical Year. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this by explaining that 'seventh' refers to the seventh of the long blessings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's count of six additional blessings, noting that a baraita mentions a seventh blessing for the Sabbatical Year.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by explaining that 'seventh' refers to the seventh of the long blessings, not an additional blessing.

items.text: Procedure for the blessings in the provinces
items.text_en: Procedure for the blessings in the provinces
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the order: the prayer leader prolongs the blessing 'Goel Yisrael', the congregation responds 'Amen', and the synagogue attendant instructs the priests to blow trumpets. This pattern repeats for each blessing, alternating between 'Tekiu' and 'Hariu'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita describes the procedure for the blessings in the provinces: the prayer leader prolongs the blessing 'Goel Yisrael', the congregation responds 'Amen', and the synagogue attendant instructs the priests to blow trumpets, alternating between 'Tekiu' and 'Hariu' for each blessing.

items.text: Distinction for the Temple: no 'Amen' response
items.text_en: Distinction for the Temple: no 'Amen' response
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that in the Temple, the practice differs because 'Amen' is not recited there. A verse from Nehemiah is cited to prove that each blessing is concluded with praise rather than 'Amen'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous practice applies only in the provinces (גבולין), but in the Temple the practice differs because 'Amen' is not recited there.
A verse from Nehemiah is cited to prove that in the Temple each blessing is concluded with praise (תהלה) rather than 'Amen'.

items.text: Temple procedure and its limitation
items.text_en: Temple procedure and its limitation
items.desc_en: In the Temple, the prayer leader says 'Baruch Hashem Elohei Yisrael... Baruch Goel Yisrael', and the congregation responds 'Baruch shem kevod malkhuto le'olam va'ed'. The synagogue attendant instructs the priests to blow trumpets. This practice was followed by Rabbi Chalafta and Rabbi Chananya, but the Sages said it was only done at the Eastern Gate and the Temple Mount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the prayer leader says in the Temple instead of saying 'Amen', and presents the Temple formula: 'ברוך ה' אלהי ישראל... ברוך גואל ישראל'.

The baraita details the Temple procedure: the congregation responds with 'ברוך שם כבוד מלכותו לעולם ועד', the synagogue attendant instructs the priests to blow trumpets, and this pattern repeats for each blessing.

Rabbi Chalafta in Tzippori and Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon in Sikhni followed this Temple procedure, but when the matter came before the Sages, they ruled that this practice was only done at the Eastern Gate and the Temple Mount.

items.text: Alternative version: placement of the six blessings
items.text_en: Alternative version: placement of the six blessings
items.desc_en: An alternative tradition states that the six additional blessings are recited between 'Goel' and 'Rofei Cholim', with the prayer leader prolonging the redemption blessing. In the Temple, they said 'Baruch Hashem... Baruch Goel Yisrael' without 'Amen', based on the same verse.

sub.desc_en: The alternative tradition states that the prayer leader recites twenty-four blessings (the standard eighteen plus six additional ones) between 'Goel' and 'Rofei Cholim', prolonging the redemption blessing, and the congregation responds 'Amen' after each blessing.

In the Temple, they said 'Baruch Hashem... Baruch Goel Yisrael' without 'Amen', citing the verse 'קוּמוּ בָּרְכוּ... וּמְרוֹמַם עַל כׇּל בְּרָכָה וּתְהִלָּה' to prove that in the Temple each blessing is answered with praise rather than 'Amen'.

items.text: Detailed baraita on Temple procedure with trumpet blasts
items.text_en: Detailed baraita on Temple procedure with trumpet blasts
items.desc_en: A baraita details the Temple practice: for the first blessing, the prayer leader says 'Baruch Hashem... Baruch Goel Yisrael', the congregation responds 'Baruch shem kevod...', and the attendant says 'Tekiu'. The priests blow tekiah, teruah, tekiah. For the second blessing, they say 'Baruch Zocher Hanishkachot', and the attendant says 'Hariu', with the priests blowing teruah, tekiah, teruah. This was practiced by Rabbi Chalafta and Rabbi Chananya, but the Sages limited it to the Eastern Gate and Temple Mount.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing the first blessing in the Temple: the prayer leader says 'Baruch Hashem... Baruch Goel Yisrael', the congregation responds 'Baruch shem kevod...', and the attendant says 'Tekiu'.
The baraita continues: for the first blessing, after the response, the priests blow tekiah, teruah, tekiah.
The baraita describes the second blessing: the prayer leader says 'Baruch Hashem... Baruch Zocher Hanishkachot', and the congregation responds 'Baruch shem kevod...'.
The baraita continues: for the second blessing, the attendant says 'Hariu', and the priests blow teruah, tekiah, teruah.
The baraita concludes: this pattern of alternating 'Tekiu' and 'Hariu' is repeated for each blessing until all are completed.

sub.text: Baraita — Rabbi Chalafta and Rabbi Chananya
sub.text_en: Baraita — Rabbi Chalafta and Rabbi Chananya
sub.desc_en: The baraita records that Rabbi Chalafta in Tzippori and Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon in Sikhni practiced this procedure.
The Sages limited this practice to the Eastern Gate and the Temple Mount.

items.text: טעם רבי יהודה שלא להזכיר זכרונות ושופרות
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on Zichronot and Shofarot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says that one does not need to recite the Zichronot (remembrance) blessings. Rabbi Adda from Yafo explains his reasoning: because they do not recite Zichronot and Shofarot (in this context).
items.desc: רבי אדא דמן יפו מסביר שרבי יהודה סובר שאין אומרים זכרונות ושופרות בתענית ציבור, אלא פסוקי צרה וזעקה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that one does not need to recite the Zichronot (remembrance) blessings during the additional blessings.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה פוטר את שליח הציבור מאמירת זכרונות ושופרות בתענית ציבור.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Adda from Yafo explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: because in this context they do not recite the Zichronot (remembrance) and Shofarot (shofar) blessings.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה פוטר את שליח הציבור מאמירת זכרונות ושופרות בתענית ציבור.

items.text: Prayer order on fast days and the exchange of cries and prayers
items.text_en: Prayer order on fast days and the exchange of cries and prayers
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the order of prayers for the seven fast day blessings, noting that on the first blessing one says 'He who answered Abraham...'. A baraita states that some exchange the cry for Elijah and the prayer for Samuel. The Gemara questions this because for Samuel both prayer and cry are written, but for Elijah only prayer is written; it resolves that 'Answer me, Lord, answer me' is a language of cry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that on the first blessing of the seven fast day blessings one says 'He who answered Abraham...'.
A baraita teaches that some exchange the cry for Elijah and the prayer for Samuel.
The Gemara questions the baraita: for Samuel both prayer and cry are written, but for Elijah only prayer is written, not cry.
The Gemara resolves that the phrase 'Answer me, Lord, answer me' is a language of cry, so Elijah's cry is implied.

items.text: Order of Yonah and David in the prayers
items.text_en: Order of Yonah and David in the prayers
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that on the sixth blessing one says 'He who answered Jonah...' and on the seventh 'He who answered David...', even though Jonah lived after David and Solomon. The reason given is that they wanted to conclude with 'Who has mercy on the land'. A baraita adds that due to Somkhos they said 'Blessed is He who humbles the haughty'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the order of the special blessings: on the sixth fast one says 'He who answered Jonah' and on the seventh 'He who answered David'.
The Gemara questions why Jonah, who lived after David and Solomon, is mentioned before them in the prayer order.
The Gemara answers that the order was chosen so that the series could conclude with the blessing 'Who has mercy on the land'.
A baraita adds that due to Somkhos they said 'Blessed is He who humbles the haughty' as the concluding blessing.

items.text: Priests' wine drinking restrictions during the watch
items.text_en: Priests' wine drinking restrictions during the watch
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why members of the watch (mishmar) may drink wine at night but not during the day, and why members of the father's house (beit av) may not drink at all. It then details the restrictions for a priest who knows his watch and father's house, only his watch, or neither, with Rabbi stating that ideally they should be forbidden forever but the remedy would be worse. Abaye concludes that today's priests who drink wine follow Rabbi's lenient view.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by explaining why members of the watch (mishmar) may drink wine at night but not during the day, due to concern that the daytime workload might become heavy and they would need to assist.
The baraita explains why members of the father's house (beit av) may not drink wine at any time, because they are constantly engaged in the Temple service.
The baraita rules that a priest who knows both his watch and his father's house is forbidden to drink wine for that entire day.
The baraita rules that a priest who knows his watch but not his father's house is forbidden to drink wine for that entire week.
The baraita rules that a priest who knows neither his watch nor his father's house is forbidden to drink wine for the entire year.
Rabbi states that ideally priests should be forbidden to drink wine forever, but the remedy (forcing them to abstain permanently) would be worse than the problem.
Abaye concludes that today's priests who drink wine follow Rabbi's lenient view, since the strict ideal would be impractical.

items.text: Prohibition on haircuts and laundry for the watch and ma'amad
items.text_en: Prohibition on haircuts and laundry for the watch and ma'amad
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that members of the watch and the ma'amad are forbidden to cut their hair or wash clothes, but on Thursday they are permitted due to Shabbat honor. Rabbi Yochanan explains the reason: so that they do not enter their watch when they are disheveled.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that members of the watch and the ma'amad are forbidden to cut their hair or wash clothes, but on Thursday they are permitted due to Shabbat honor.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this prohibition.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the prohibition is so that they do not enter their watch when they are disheveled.

items.text: Frequency of haircuts for king, high priest, and ordinary priest
items.text_en: Frequency of haircuts for king, high priest, and ordinary priest
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the king gets a haircut daily, the high priest every Friday, and the ordinary priest once every thirty days. The Gemara provides scriptural reasons: for the king from 'Your eyes shall see the king in his beauty', for the high priest because the watches are renewed, and for the ordinary priest from a gezerah shavah of 'pera' from a nazirite. The nazirite's thirty days are derived from the gematria of 'yihyeh'. Rav Pappa questions this, but Abaye explains the verse's structure. The Gemara then compares this to the prohibition of wine for priests, concluding that today's priests follow Rabbi's lenient view.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states the frequency of haircuts: the king daily, the high priest every Friday, and the ordinary priest once every thirty days.
Rabbi Abba bar Zavda provides the scriptural reason for the king's daily haircut: the verse 'Your eyes shall see the king in his beauty'.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak explains that the high priest's haircut is every Friday because the priestly watches are renewed then.
The Gemara derives the ordinary priest's thirty-day haircut interval via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'פֶּרַע' from a nazirite.
Rav Mattanah derives the nazirite's thirty-day period from the gematria of 'יִהְיֶה' (he shall be).
Rav Pappa objects that the verse might mean the priest should never let his hair grow long at all.
Abaye resolves that the verse's word order — 'וּפֶרַע לֹא יְשַׁלֵּחוּ' — implies the priest must grow his hair (פֶּרַע) but not let it grow excessively.
The Gemara objects that if the prohibition applies today, it would be perpetual, but it is limited by analogy to the wine prohibition which applies only during the Temple service.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi says priests are permanently forbidden wine but for a practical concern, and Abaye concludes that today's priests who drink wine follow Rabbi's lenient view.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Why is a priest with unkempt hair disqualified but a drunken priest not?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Why is a priest with unkempt hair disqualified but a drunken priest not?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier distinction between a priest with unkempt hair (פרועי ראש) and a drunken priest (שתויי יין). It suggests that just as a drunken priest can sleep off the effects, a priest with unkempt hair can cut his hair before entering. Rav Ashi answers that the Sages decreed only for drunkenness because it invalidates the service, but unkempt hair does not invalidate the service.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita: Both are punishable by death
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita: Both are punishable by death
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita that lists both drunken priests and priests with unkempt hair as liable to death. It derives this for unkempt hair from a juxtaposition (הקישא) with drunken priests in the verse. The Gemara then questions whether the juxtaposition also applies to invalidating the service, but concludes it only applies to the death penalty.

items.text: Ravina's question: Who said this before Ezekiel?
items.text_en: Ravina's question: Who said this before Ezekiel?
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: Before the prophet Ezekiel came, who taught that a priest with unkempt hair is liable to death? Rav Ashi responds that it was a tradition (גמירא) from Sinai, and Ezekiel merely provided a scriptural support. Similarly, the halakha that unkempt hair does not invalidate the service was also a tradition.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi who taught the death penalty for unkempt hair before the prophet Ezekiel.

Rav Ashi answers by analogy to Rav Chisda's statement about a law from the prophets, explaining that the death penalty for unkempt hair was received as a tradition (גמרא) and Ezekiel merely provided a scriptural support.
The Gemara concludes that the tradition was received only for the death penalty, not for disqualification of the service.

items.text: Introduction to Megillat Taanit: Days when eulogizing is prohibited
items.text_en: Introduction to Megillat Taanit: Days when eulogizing is prohibited
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any day written in Megillat Taanit as 'not to eulogize' is prohibited before it but permitted after it. A baraita lists specific days: from Rosh Chodesh Nisan until the eighth of Nisan (when the daily offering was established) and from the eighth until the end of the festival (when the festival of Shavuot was established) — all days on which eulogizing is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: any day listed in Megillat Taanit as 'not to eulogize' is forbidden before it and permitted after it.
The baraita lists specific days from Megillat Taanit, including from Rosh Chodesh Nisan to the eighth, and from the eighth to the end of the festival of Shavuot, as days when eulogizing is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why mention Rosh Chodesh?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why mention Rosh Chodesh?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita says 'from Rosh Chodesh Nisan' — since Rosh Chodesh itself is a holiday and already prohibited for eulogizing, it should say from the second of Nisan. Rav answers that the baraita includes the day before Rosh Chodesh to prohibit it as well. The Gemara then questions why the day before Rosh Chodesh needs a special prohibition, since Rosh Chodesh is Torah law and does not need reinforcement. A baraita explains that Torah laws do not need reinforcement, but rabbinic laws do.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why say 'until the end of the festival'?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why say 'until the end of the festival'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita says 'until the end of the festival' — it should say 'until the festival', since the festival itself is a holiday and already prohibited. Rav Pappa answers that the baraita includes the day after the festival to prohibit it as well, similar to Rav's earlier reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita says 'until the end of the festival' instead of 'until the festival', since the festival itself is a holiday and eulogizing is forbidden.
Rav Pappa begins to answer, citing Rav's principle that the mention is necessary to forbid the day before the festival.

items.text: Gemara's question on the 29th
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the 29th
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the 29th is singled out for prohibition, suggesting it could be because it is the day after the 28th, which was a festival. It cites Rabbi Yossi's view that both before and after are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the 29th is singled out for prohibition, suggesting it could be because it is the day after the 28th, which was a festival, and cites Rabbi Yossi's view that both before and after are forbidden.

items.text: Story of the 28th of Adar
items.text_en: Story of the 28th of Adar
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that on the 28th of Adar, good news came to the Jews that they would not be removed from Torah study. The story describes how Yehuda ben Shammu'a and his companions protested to a Roman matron, leading to the annulment of decrees, and that day was made a festival.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that on the 28th of Adar good news came that the Jews would not be removed from Torah, and recounts the evil decrees of the wicked kingdom.
The baraita describes how Yehuda ben Shammu'a and his companions sought advice from a Roman matron whose house was frequented by Roman nobles.
The matron instructs them to protest at night; they do so, their plea is accepted, the decrees are annulled, and that day is made a festival.

items.text: Abaye and Rav Ashi's explanations
items.text_en: Abaye and Rav Ashi's explanations
items.desc_en: Abaye says the ruling applies to a leap month. Rav Ashi argues that even in a regular month, the day after is forbidden for fasting but permitted for eulogies, but this day, being between two festivals, is treated like a festival itself, even forbidding eulogies.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the ruling about the 29th only applies to a leap month (חודש מעובר), where the 29th is the day after the 28th (the day the good news arrived) and thus forbidden for fasting and eulogies.

Rav Ashi argues that even in a regular month (חודש חסר), the day after the 28th is forbidden for fasting but permitted for eulogies; however, this particular day, falling between two festivals, is treated like a festival itself, forbidding even eulogies.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita says 'from the 8th' instead of 'from the 9th', and explains that the 8th itself is forbidden because if something happened to cancel the 7th, the 8th would be the first day of the festival. It then applies the same logic to the 29th.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita says 'from the 8th' instead of 'from the 9th', since the 8th itself is forbidden as the day the daily offering was restored.
The Gemara answers that the 8th itself is forbidden because if something happened to cancel the 7th, the 8th would become the first day of the festival.
The Gemara applies the same logic to the 29th: it is forbidden because if the 28th were cancelled, the 29th would be the day before the restored daily offering.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Asi reports that Rav ruled like Rabbi Yossi, while Shmuel ruled like Rabbi Meir. The Gemara notes a contradiction: Shmuel elsewhere ruled like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who permits before and after. It resolves that Shmuel initially followed Rabbi Meir, but later switched to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's more lenient view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Chiyya bar Asi said in the name of Rav that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yossi, while Shmuel said it follows Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara objects: Did Shmuel really say that? It cites a ברייתא (baraita) where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits before and after, and Shmuel ruled like him.

The Gemara resolves: Initially Shmuel thought no one was more lenient than Rabbi Meir, so he ruled like him; but when he heard Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was even more lenient, he switched to his view.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and clarification
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and clarification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan is cited as ruling like Rabbi Yossi, but Rabbi Chiyya explains that this applies only to not fasting, not to eulogies. The Gemara questions this because Rabbi Yochanan generally follows a stam Mishnah, and cites a Mishnah that says 'they advance and do not postpone'.

sub.text: Bali citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Bali citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Bali reports in the name of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba that Rabbi Yochanan ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba to Bali
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba to Bali
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba explains to Bali that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies only to not fasting, not to eulogies.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan actually said this, given his general principle.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's own principle that the halakha follows an unattributed mishnah.
The Gemara cites a mishnah that says 'they advance and do not postpone,' which seems to contradict Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.

items.text: Question about the timing of Purim and the permissibility of eulogies and fasts
items.text_en: Question about the timing of Purim and the permissibility of eulogies and fasts
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that certain days are permitted for eulogies and fasts, considering whether it refers to the 15th or 14th of Adar. It raises objections based on the Megillat Taanit and Rava's ruling, and considers alternative dates like the 13th (Nicanor) and 12th (Turianos), concluding that the Mishnah must refer to the 11th.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's permission for eulogies and fasts refers to the 15th or 14th of Adar, and objects that if it were the 15th, calling it the 14th would violate the prohibition of Megillat Taanit.
The Gemara cites Megillat Taanit, which forbids eulogies on the 14th and 15th, and Rava's explanation that the prohibition applies to each town's Purim day for the other town.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah refers to the 14th, calling it the 13th would conflict with Nicanor's day, and calling it the 12th would conflict with Turianos's day.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must refer to the 11th of Adar, which is permitted for eulogies and fasts.

items.text: Answer: The Mishnah refers to the 12th, and the day of Turianos was annulled
items.text_en: Answer: The Mishnah refers to the 12th, and the day of Turianos was annulled
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to those who read the Megillah on the 12th, and the day of Turianos itself was annulled because Shmaya and Achiyah were killed on that day. Rav Nachman's decree of a fast on the 12th is cited as a precedent, with the rabbis' objection and his response.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to those who read on the 14th but read on the 12th, and addresses the objection that the 12th is the day of Turianos.
The Gemara resolves that the day of Turianos itself was annulled because Shmaya and Achiyah his brothers were killed on that day.

The Gemara cites a precedent: Rav Nachman decreed a fast on the 12th, the rabbis objected that it was the day of Turianos, and he responded that the day itself was annulled because Shmaya and Achiyah his brother were killed on it.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the day before Nicanor
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the day before Nicanor
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the 12th is the day before Nicanor, which should still be prohibited. Rav Ashi resolves that since the day of Turianos itself was annulled, there is no concern for the day before Nicanor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the 12th is the day before Nicanor, which should still be prohibited.
Rav Ashi resolves that since the day of Turianos itself was annulled, there is no concern for the day before Nicanor.

items.text: Stories of Nicanor and Turianos
items.text_en: Stories of Nicanor and Turianos
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains who Nicanor and Turianos were. Nicanor was a Greek general who blasphemed and was killed by the Hasmoneans. Turianos sought to kill Lulianus and Pappus, who refused to be saved by a miracle, and were killed; subsequently, Roman officials avenged them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who Nicanor and Turianos were, introducing the need for background stories.
A baraita recounts Nicanor, a Greek governor who blasphemed against Judah and Jerusalem, and was killed and mutilated by the Hasmoneans.
The Gemara asks who Turianos was.
A baraita recounts Turianos seeking to kill Lulianus and Pappus, who refused to be saved by a miracle, explaining that they were deserving of punishment and that God would avenge them.
The baraita concludes that despite their words, Turianos killed them immediately, and Roman officials soon came and avenged them by crushing his skull with clubs.

items.text: Rules for decreeing fasts and the dispute about completing the fast
items.text_en: Rules for decreeing fasts and the dispute about completing the fast
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not decree a fast on the fifth day etc. The Gemara discusses how many fasts constitute a 'beginning' (Rav Acha says three, Rabbi Asi says one). Rav Yehuda cites Rav that this is Rabbi Meir's opinion, but the Sages say one may fast and complete. Mar Zutra rules in accordance with Rav Huna that the halakha is to fast and complete.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not decree a fast for the community on the fifth day (Thursday) or on New Moons.
The Gemara asks how many fasts constitute a 'beginning' (התחלה) that is prohibited on Thursday.
Rav Acha answers that the 'beginning' is three fasts.
Rabbi Asi answers that the 'beginning' is one fast.
Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav that the Mishnah's ruling is the opinion of Rabbi Meir citing Rabban Gamliel.
The Sages disagree and hold that one may fast and complete the fast even if it begins on Thursday.
Mar Zutra rules in the name of Rav Huna that the הלכה (binding law) is that one fasts and completes the fast.

items.text: Continuation of the order of fasts and special cases
items.text_en: Continuation of the order of fasts and special cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the order of fasts, noting that the previously mentioned fasts apply to the first drought, but for crops that have already been affected, one sounds the alarm immediately. Similarly, if rains stop between rains for forty days, or if rain falls only on certain areas, one sounds the alarm immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the previously discussed order of fasts, clarifying that these fasts apply only to the first drought.
The Gemara states that for crops that have already been affected, or if rains stop for forty days between rains, one sounds the alarm immediately because it is a plague of drought.
The Gemara adds that if rain falls only on certain areas or for specific vegetation, one sounds the alarm immediately, citing a verse from Amos about selective rainfall.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of alarm and fasting for afflicted cities and general calamities
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of alarm and fasting for afflicted cities and general calamities
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a city afflicted with plague or collapse fasts and sounds alarms, while surrounding cities fast but do not sound alarms; Rabbi Akiva says they sound alarms but do not fast. It defines plague as three deaths in three consecutive days in a city of 500 men. It lists calamities for which alarms are sounded everywhere, including blight, locusts, and sword. It recounts a story of elders decreeing a fast for blight in Ashkelon and for wolves eating children, with Rabbi Yosei arguing the alarm was for the sighting, not the eating. It then lists alarms on Shabbat for a besieged city or storm-tossed ship, with disputes between Rabbi Yosei and Shimon the Timni.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: an afflicted city fasts and sounds alarms, while surrounding cities fast but do not sound alarms.
Rabbi Akiva disputes: surrounding cities sound alarms but do not fast.
The Mishnah applies the same rule to a city with plague or collapse.
Rabbi Akiva again disputes: surrounding cities sound alarms but do not fast.
The Mishnah defines plague: three deaths in three consecutive days in a city of 500 men.
The Mishnah lists calamities for which alarms are sounded everywhere: blight, mildew, locusts, wild beasts, and sword.
The Mishnah recounts a story of elders decreeing a fast for blight in Ashkelon.
The Mishnah recounts another story of a fast for wolves eating children.
Rabbi Yosei argues the alarm was for the sighting of the wolves, not the eating.
The Mishnah lists alarms on Shabbat for a besieged city or storm-tossed ship.
Rabbi Yosei says the alarm on Shabbat is for help, not for crying out.
Shimon the Timni adds plague to the Shabbat alarms, but the Sages disagree.

items.text: Mishnah: The story of Honi the Circle-Drawer
items.text_en: Mishnah: The story of Honi the Circle-Drawer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah relates that for all communal troubles except excessive rain, alarms are sounded. It tells the story of Honi the Circle-Drawer, who was asked to pray for rain. He drew a circle, stood inside, and swore not to leave until God showed mercy. Rain fell, first in drops, then in torrents, then in blessing, until people had to flee to the Temple Mount. When asked to pray for the rain to stop, he sent them to check if the Stone of Claimants was erased. Shimon ben Shetach praised him but noted he would have decreed a ban if not for Honi's special relationship with God.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for all communal troubles except excessive rain, alarms are sounded.

sub.text: Mishnah's story of Honi the Circle-Drawer
sub.text_en: Mishnah's story of Honi the Circle-Drawer
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah recounts that people asked Honi the Circle-Drawer to pray for rain, and he told them to bring in Passover ovens so they would not melt, but his initial prayer was not answered.
Honi drew a circle, stood inside, swore not to leave until God showed mercy, and rain fell first in drops, then in torrents, then in blessing.
The rain fell so heavily that people fled to the Temple Mount, and when asked to pray for it to stop, Honi told them to check if the Stone of Claimants was erased.
Shimon ben Shetach sent word that he would have decreed a ban on Honi if not for his special relationship with God, citing the verse about a father rejoicing in his son.

items.text: Mishnah: When rain falls on a fast day
items.text_en: Mishnah: When rain falls on a fast day
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if rain falls before sunrise, the fast is not completed; after sunrise, it is completed. Rabbi Eliezer says the cutoff is noon. A story is told of a fast in Lod where rain fell before noon; Rabbi Tarfon told them to eat and drink and make a holiday, and they recited the Great Hallel in the evening.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: if rain falls before sunrise on a fast day, the fast is not completed; if after sunrise, it is completed.
Rabbi Eliezer offers an alternative cutoff: if rain falls before noon, the fast is not completed; after noon, it is completed.
A story is told of a fast in Lod where rain fell before noon; Rabbi Tarfon instructed them to eat and drink and make a holiday, and they recited the Great Hallel in the evening.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the order of fasts in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the order of fasts in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement about the order of fasts, noting a contradiction: the first and second rainfalls are for asking, the third for fasting. Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah refers to a case where the first, second, and third rainfalls have passed without rain; but if rain fell in the first rainfall and crops did not grow or changed, alarms are sounded immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah describes the order of fasts in the first rainfall, but a baraita states that the first and second rainfalls are for asking and only the third for fasting.

Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah's order applies when the first, second, and third rainfalls have passed without rain; but if rain fell in the first rainfall and crops did not grow or changed, alarms are sounded immediately.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the case of changed crops and the meaning of 'plague of scarcity'
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the case of changed crops and the meaning of 'plague of scarcity'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman specifies that the Mishnah's case of 'changed' crops refers to a change in form, not merely drying out, and that standing crops are included. The Gemara then asks about the meaning of 'plague of scarcity' in the Mishnah; Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains it is a plague that leads to scarcity. Rav Nachman adds a cryptic statement about rivers.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman specifies that the Mishnah's case of 'changed' crops refers only to a change in form, not mere drying out.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'changed', so Rav Nachman's clarification seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that Rav Nachman's statement is needed to exclude the case of standing crops that merely dried out, which might have been considered a change.
The Gemara asks about the meaning of the term 'plague of scarcity' in the Mishnah.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains that a 'plague of scarcity' is a plague that leads to scarcity.
Rav Nachman adds a cryptic statement about rivers, likely a tangential remark.

items.text: Defining famine and the role of prices
items.text_en: Defining famine and the role of prices
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines when a drought is considered a famine based on the availability and price of food. Rabbi Chanina distinguishes between a situation where a se'ah is sold for a sela and is available (scarcity) versus when it is not available (famine). Rabbi Yochanan adds that if money is cheap and produce expensive, they do not immediately declare a fast, but if money is expensive and produce cheap, they do, citing a personal memory of high prices and widespread hunger.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defines the terms: scarcity (בצורתא) is when a se'ah is sold for a sela and is available, while famine (כפנא) is when it is sold for four selas and is unavailable, as stated by Rabbi Chanina.

Rabbi Yochanan adds a distinction: the above rule applies only when money is cheap and produce expensive, but when money is expensive and produce cheap, they declare a fast immediately, citing a personal memory of high prices and widespread hunger in Tiberias.

items.text: Analyzing different types of rain damage
items.text_en: Analyzing different types of rain damage
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a baraita that distinguishes between rain that damages crops but not trees, and vice versa, explaining the meteorological conditions (gentle vs. torrential rain). It then questions a baraita that says rain damaged wells but not crops or trees, concluding that this occurs when rain falls in a flood (שפיכותא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita distinguishing rain that damages crops but not trees, and vice versa, and explains the meteorological conditions (gentle vs. torrential rain) for each case.
The Gemara questions a baraita that says rain damaged wells but not crops or trees, asking how such a scenario is possible.
The Gemara answers that this occurs when rain falls as a flood (שפיכותא), which fills wells without benefiting crops or trees.

items.text: Timing for declaring a fast on trees and wells
items.text_en: Timing for declaring a fast on trees and wells
items.desc_en: A baraita states that they declare a fast for trees during the period before Passover, and for wells during the period before Sukkot. If there is no drinking water, they declare a fast immediately, and the 'immediate' fast is on Monday, Thursday, and Monday. All such fasts are only declared in their own region.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that they declare a fast for trees during the period before Passover, for wells during the period before Sukkot, and if there is no drinking water, they declare a fast immediately.
The baraita specifies that the 'immediate' fast is on Monday, Thursday, and Monday, and that all such fasts are only declared in their own region.

items.text: Fasting for diphtheria and locusts
items.text_en: Fasting for diphtheria and locusts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that they declare a fast for diphtheria (אסכרה) when it is fatal, but not when it is not. They declare a fast for locusts (גובאי) even in small amounts. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that they also fast for the חָגָב (a type of locust).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that they sound the alarm for diphtheria (אסכרה) when it is fatal, but not when it is not fatal.
The Mishnah adds that they sound the alarm for locusts (גובאי) even in the smallest amount.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that they also sound the alarm for the חָגָב (a type of locust).

items.text: Fasting in Sabbatical years
items.text_en: Fasting in Sabbatical years
items.desc_en: Two baraitot discuss declaring a fast for trees in non-Sabbatical years and for wells even in the Sabbatical year. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that they also fast for trees in the Sabbatical year because they provide sustenance for the poor. The second baraita adds that they fast for aftergrowths (ספיחין) in the Sabbatical year for the same reason.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita states that they sound the alarm over trees in non-Sabbatical years, and over cisterns, ditches, and caves even in the Sabbatical Year.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that they also sound the alarm over trees in the Sabbatical Year because they provide sustenance for the poor.
A second baraita repeats the same ruling: they sound the alarm over trees in non-Sabbatical years and over cisterns, ditches, and caves even in the Sabbatical Year.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel again adds that they sound the alarm over trees in the Sabbatical Year.
The second baraita adds that they also sound the alarm over aftergrowths (ספיחין) in the Sabbatical Year because they serve as sustenance for the poor.

items.text: Parables on the nature of rainfall after the Temple's destruction
items.text_en: Parables on the nature of rainfall after the Temple's destruction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Parta states that since the Temple's destruction, rains have become 'shriveling' (צימוקין) for the world. The Gemara then presents a series of parables comparing years of timely vs. untimely rains, abundant vs. scarce rains, and the effect of abundant water on kneading clay.

sub.text: Baraita citation: Rabbi Elazar ben Parta
sub.text_en: Baraita citation: Rabbi Elazar ben Parta
sub.desc_en: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא (Rabbi Elazar ben Parta) states that since the Temple's destruction, rains have become 'צימוקין (shriveling)' for the world, and describes four types of years: abundant or scarce rains, and timely or untimely rains.

The Gemara presents a parable comparing a year with timely rains to a servant who receives his weekly portion on Sunday, allowing proper baking and eating, and a year with untimely rains to a servant who receives his portion on ערב שבת (Shabbat eve), resulting in improper preparation.

The Gemara presents a parable comparing a year with abundant rains to a servant who receives his entire portion at once, so that milling from a כור (kor) wastes the same amount as from a קב (kav), and dough from a kor diminishes like from a kav.

The Gemara presents a parable comparing a year with scarce rains to a servant who receives his portion little by little, so that the mill grinds from each kav the waste it would have ground from a kor, and dough diminishes from a kav as from a kor.

sub.text: Gemara's alternative parable (abundant rains and clay)
sub.text_en: Gemara's alternative parable (abundant rains and clay)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative parable: a year with abundant rains is like a person kneading clay with much water, where the water is not used up and the clay is well-kneaded, whereas with little water, the water runs out and the clay is not well-kneaded.

items.text: The story of Nakdimon ben Gurion
items.text_en: The story of Nakdimon ben Gurion
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story where Nakdimon ben Gurion borrowed twelve springs of water from a hegmon for the pilgrims, promising to return them or pay twelve silver talents. When the deadline arrived without rain, the hegmon demanded payment. Nakdimon delayed, confident that rain would come, and the hegmon mocked him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens the story: all Israel went up to Jerusalem for the festival without drinking water, so Nakdimon ben Gurion borrowed twelve springs from a hegmon (Roman official), promising to return them or pay twelve silver talents by a set deadline.
When the deadline arrived without rain, the hegmon sent a message in the morning demanding either the water or the money.
Nakdimon ben Gurion repeatedly delayed, replying that he still had time until the end of the day.
The hegmon mocked Nakdimon, noting that no rain had fallen all year, implying the debt would not be repaid.

items.text: Conclusion of Nakdimon's miracle and the sun's return
items.text_en: Conclusion of Nakdimon's miracle and the sun's return
items.desc_en: Nakdimon enters the Temple in distress and prays for rain, which comes. The hegemon then claims the rain fell under his authority since the sun had set. Nakdimon prays again, the clouds disperse, and the sun shines. The hegemon concedes, and the Gemara notes Nakdimon's name derives from the sun being 'pierced' for him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how rain could fall after the sun had set, and describes Nakdimon entering the Temple in distress to pray.
Nakdimon prays to God, declaring his intention was for the pilgrims' sake, and rain immediately falls, filling twelve springs.
The hegemon meets Nakdimon, demands payment, and claims the rain fell under his authority since the sun had already set.
Nakdimon re-enters the Temple, prays for God to demonstrate His love, and the clouds disperse with the sun shining.
The hegemon concedes that had the sun not returned, he would have had a claim against Nakdimon.
The Tanna explains that Nakdimon's real name was Buni, and he was called Nakdimon because the sun was pierced (נקדרה) for him.

items.text: Three for whom the sun shone early
