items.text_en: Three for whom the sun shone early
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the sun shone early for Moses, Joshua, and Nakdimon ben Gurion. It derives Joshua from Scripture, Nakdimon from tradition, and seeks a source for Moses. Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, and Rabbi Yochanan each offer a different derivation from verses.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that the sun shone early for three people—Moses, Joshua, and Nakdimon ben Gurion—and then asks for the scriptural source for Moses, since Nakdimon is known by tradition and Joshua is explicit in the verse.
Rabbi Elazar derives Moses' miracle from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'אָחֵל' (I will begin) appearing both in Moses' context and in Joshua's context.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani derives Moses' miracle from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'תֵּת' (giving) appearing both in Moses' verse and in the verse about the Amorites.
Rabbi Yochanan derives Moses' miracle directly from the verse itself, arguing that the fear of the nations described there occurred when the sun shone early for Moses.

items.text: Interpretation of a city without rain
items.text_en: Interpretation of a city without rain
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav interprets the Mishnah's statement about a city that did not receive rain as a curse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, describing a city that did not receive rain.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav interprets the Mishnah's statement as a curse, meaning both the city and its inhabitants are cursed.

items.text: Aggadic interpretations of Lamentations verses as blessings
items.text_en: Aggadic interpretations of Lamentations verses as blessings
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav interpret several verses from Lamentations as blessings: Jerusalem being like a menstruating woman implies a future remedy; being like a widow implies her husband will return; and being despised and lowly means Jews will not hold high office.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav interprets the verse 'Jerusalem became like a menstruating woman among them' as a blessing: just as a menstruating woman has a remedy (purification), so too Jerusalem has a future restoration.

Rav Yehuda interprets the verse 'She became like a widow' as a blessing: not a real widow, but like a woman whose husband has gone overseas and intends to return to her, implying God will return to Jerusalem.

Rav Yehuda interprets the verse 'I have made you despised and lowly' as a blessing: that Jews will not be appointed to high offices like river governors or judges, sparing them from corruption and sin.

items.text: Comparison of Ahijah's curse and Balaam's blessing
items.text_en: Comparison of Ahijah's curse and Balaam's blessing
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav says the curse of Ahijah the Shilonite is better than Balaam's blessing. Ahijah compared Israel to a reed, which bends but does not break, while Balaam compared them to a cedar, which is easily uprooted. The reed is also used for writing Torah scrolls.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav introduces the verse of Ahijah's curse and states that it is better than Balaam's blessing.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains that Ahijah compared Israel to a reed, which bends with the wind but does not break, symbolizing resilience.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani contrasts Balaam's blessing comparing Israel to a cedar, which is easily uprooted by a single wind, and notes the reed's merit of being used for writing Torah scrolls.

items.text: Lesson to be soft like a reed
items.text_en: Lesson to be soft like a reed
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with a teaching: one should always be soft like a reed, not hard like a cedar. It introduces a story about Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who was riding happily after learning much Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna teaches that a person should always be soft like a reed, not hard like a cedar.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story about Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who was riding happily after learning much Torah, illustrating the danger of pride.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's humility
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's humility
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon insults a man for his ugliness, but the man responds by telling him to complain to his Creator. Rabbi Elazar realizes his sin, begs forgiveness, and eventually forgives him. He then teaches that a person should be soft like a reed, not hard like a cedar.

sub.desc_en: The gemara narrates that Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon encountered an extremely ugly man, insulted him, and the man responded by telling him to complain to his Creator.
Rabbi Elazar realized his sin, begged forgiveness, and after the townspeople interceded, he forgave the man on condition that he not repeat such behavior.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's teaching
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's teaching
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar then taught that a person should always be soft like a reed (קנה) and not hard like a cedar (ארז), because the reed merited to provide the quill for writing a Torah scroll, tefillin, and mezuzot.

items.text: Definition of a collapsed building in a city
items.text_en: Definition of a collapsed building in a city
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's term 'collapsed building' (מפולת), explaining that it refers to buildings that are structurally sound (בריאות) and not shaky (רעועות), i.e., not expected to fall. It then questions the distinction between 'sound' and 'not expected to fall', and answers that it refers to buildings that fall due to their height or because they stand on a riverbank.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines 'collapsed building' (מפולת) as referring to structurally sound buildings (בריאות) that are not shaky (רעועות), i.e., not expected to fall.

The Gemara questions the redundancy in the baraita's phrasing, asking what the difference is between 'sound' (בריאות) and 'not expected to fall' (שאינן ראויות ליפול), and between 'shaky' (רעועות) and 'expected to fall' (ראויות ליפול).

The Gemara resolves the redundancy by explaining that the baraita refers to buildings that fall due to their height or because they stand on a riverbank, where they are structurally sound but still prone to collapse.

items.text: Story of the shaky wall in Neharde'a
items.text_en: Story of the shaky wall in Neharde'a
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that there was a shaky wall in Neharde'a that Rav and Shmuel would not pass under for thirteen years. One day, Rav Adda bar Ahava was with them, and Shmuel suggested they pass, relying on Rav Adda's merit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a shaky wall in Neharde'a that Rav and Shmuel avoided passing under for thirteen years.
Shmuel suggests to Rav that they can now pass under the wall, relying on the merit of Rav Adda bar Ahava who is with them.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's anger and the principle of not relying on miracles
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's anger and the principle of not relying on miracles
items.desc_en: Rav Huna had a donkey in a shaky house and asked Rav Adda bar Ahava to stay there while he moved it. After Rav Adda left, the house collapsed. Rav Adda became angry, and the Gemara explains that one should not stand in a dangerous place and rely on a miracle, as miracles deduct from one's merits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara narrates that Rav Huna had a donkey in a shaky house, used Rav Adda bar Ahava's presence to delay moving it, and after Rav Adda left, the house collapsed, causing Rav Adda to become angry.

The Gemara explains Rav Adda's anger by citing Rabbi Yannai's principle that one should not stand in danger and rely on a miracle, as miracles deduct from one's merits, and Rav Chanan supports this with a verse.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's virtuous deeds for longevity
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's virtuous deeds for longevity
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's students ask him how he merited long life. He lists several virtuous behaviors: never getting angry at home, not walking in front of someone greater, not meditating in filthy alleys, not walking four cubits without Torah and tefillin, not sleeping in the study hall, not rejoicing in a friend's downfall, and not calling someone by a derogatory nickname.

sub.text: Students of Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.text_en: Students of Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.desc_en: The students ask Rav Adda bar Ahava how he merited long life.

Rav Adda bar Ahava lists his virtuous behaviors: never getting angry at home, not walking in front of someone greater, not meditating in filthy alleys, not walking four cubits without Torah and tefillin, not sleeping in the study hall, not rejoicing in a friend's downfall, and not calling someone by a derogatory nickname.
An alternative version adds that he never called a friend by his nickname.

items.text: Rav Huna's virtuous deeds
items.text_en: Rav Huna's virtuous deeds
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rafram bar Pappa to recount Rav Huna's virtuous deeds. Rafram describes how Rav Huna would inspect the city, demolish shaky walls and rebuild them, buy leftover vegetables from gardeners and throw them into the river to prevent the poor from relying on them, hang a jug of medicine for anyone who needed it, and open his doors for the hungry. Rava comments that he can emulate all these except the last.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rafram bar Pappa to recount the virtuous deeds of Rav Huna.
Rafram bar Pappa says he does not recall Rav Huna's youth, but in his old age Rav Huna would inspect the city in a golden litter and demolish and rebuild shaky walls at his own expense.

Rafram bar Pappa describes how Rav Huna would buy leftover vegetables from gardeners and throw them into the river, explaining that giving them to the poor would cause reliance, and feeding them to animals is forbidden because human food may not be fed to animals.
Rafram bar Pappa explains that if Rav Huna did not buy the vegetables at all, he would cause the gardeners to stumble in the future by not having a buyer.
Rafram bar Pappa describes how Rav Huna would hang a jug of medicine for anyone who needed it, and an alternative version says he would place a jug of water for those needing to enter without danger.
Rafram bar Pappa describes how Rav Huna would open his doors when eating bread and invite anyone in need, and Rava comments that he can emulate all these deeds except the last one.

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion about Mahoza
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion about Mahoza
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the reason for the abundance of poor in Mahoza is because the city is large and has many wealthy people who support them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the abundance of poor in Mahoza is due to the many wealthy residents who support them.

items.text: Story of Ilfa and Rabbi Yochanan leaving Torah study
items.text_en: Story of Ilfa and Rabbi Yochanan leaving Torah study
items.desc_en: Ilfa and Rabbi Yochanan, distressed by poverty, decide to leave Torah study to engage in business. They sit under a crumbling wall, and two ministering angels discuss killing them for abandoning eternal life for temporal life. Rabbi Yochanan hears this and realizes he is destined for greatness, so he returns to study, while Ilfa does not return until Rabbi Yochanan becomes head of the academy.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Ilfa and Rabbi Yochanan, who were studying Torah but were greatly distressed by poverty, so they decided to leave and engage in business, and they sat under a crumbling wall while eating bread, and two ministering angels arrived.
Rabbi Yochanan heard one angel say to the other that they should drop the wall on Ilfa and Rabbi Yochanan because they are abandoning eternal life for temporal life.
The other angel replied to leave them alone because one of them is destined for greatness.
Rabbi Yochanan heard but Ilfa did not; Rabbi Yochanan asked Ilfa if he heard anything, and when Ilfa said no, Rabbi Yochanan inferred that he himself is the one destined for greatness.

Rabbi Yochanan said he would return to study, fulfilling the verse 'כִּי לֹא יֶחְדַּל אֶבְיוֹן מִקֶּרֶב הָאָרֶץ' (for the poor will never cease from the land), and he returned while Ilfa did not, until Rabbi Yochanan became head of the academy.

items.text: Ilfa's vow and the baraita about giving shekels on Shabbat
items.text_en: Ilfa's vow and the baraita about giving shekels on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Ilfa hangs himself on a ship's mast, vowing that if anyone asks him about a baraita of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Oshaya and he cannot answer, he will drown. An old man comes and teaches him a baraita about one who says 'give a shekel to my sons on Shabbat' and the ruling of Rabbi Meir that one must fulfill the words of the deceased. Ilfa identifies the baraita as Rabbi Meir's opinion.

sub.desc_en: Ilfa hangs himself on a ship's mast and vows that if anyone asks him about a baraita of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Oshaya and he cannot answer, he will drown.

An old man comes and teaches Ilfa a baraita about one who says 'give a shekel to my sons on Shabbat' and the ruling that if they are worthy of a sela they receive a sela, but if he said only a shekel they receive only a shekel.
Ilfa identifies the baraita as the opinion of Rabbi Meir, who holds that it is a מצוה (commandment) to fulfill the words of the deceased.

items.text: Story of Nachum Ish Gamzu's suffering and its cause
items.text_en: Story of Nachum Ish Gamzu's suffering and its cause
items.desc_en: Nachum Ish Gamzu was blind, armless, legless, and covered with boils. His students ask why such a righteous man suffers. He explains that he once delayed giving food to a poor man who died, and he cursed himself with these afflictions. He tells his students that it is good they see him in this state, for otherwise he would not have atonement.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Nachum Ish Gamzu's extreme physical afflictions and his precarious living situation.
The gemara recounts an incident where Nachum's students moved his bed and the house collapsed, demonstrating his prophetic confidence.
Nachum's students ask why such a completely righteous man suffers so terribly.
Nachum explains that he caused his own suffering by delaying to feed a poor man who then died.
Nachum recounts how he cursed himself with blindness, amputation, and boils for his lack of compassion.
The students lament seeing their rabbi in such a state, but Nachum insists it is good they see him, as otherwise he would lack atonement.

items.text: Nachum Ish Gamzu's mission to the king and the miracle of the dirt
items.text_en: Nachum Ish Gamzu's mission to the king and the miracle of the dirt
items.desc_en: Nachum is called 'Ish Gamzu' because he always says 'gam zu l'tovah' (this too is for the best). He is sent with a chest of precious stones to the Roman emperor, but innkeepers steal them and fill the chest with dirt. When the emperor sees dirt, he wants to kill the Jews, but Nachum says 'gam zu l'tovah'. Elijah appears and explains that this dirt is from Abraham, which turns into swords and arrows. The dirt helps conquer a city, and the emperor fills the chest with jewels and sends Nachum back with honor. The innkeepers are later killed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Nachum is called 'Ish Gamzu' and explains that he always said 'gam zu l'tovah' (this too is for the best).
The Gemara introduces a story: the Jews needed to send a gift to the Roman emperor and chose Nachum because he was experienced with miracles.
Nachum was sent with a chest of precious stones, but innkeepers stole them and filled the chest with dirt.

When Nachum arrived and the emperor saw dirt, he wanted to kill the Jews, but Nachum said 'gam zu l'tovah'; Elijah appeared and explained that this dirt was from Abraham, which turns into swords and arrows.
The dirt helped conquer a city, and the emperor filled the chest with jewels and sent Nachum back with honor.
The innkeepers tried to claim the dirt as theirs, but it was not found with them, and they were killed.

items.text: Definition of a plague (dever) in a city
items.text_en: Definition of a plague (dever) in a city
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita defining a plague: a city of 500 or 1000 foot soldiers that has nine deaths in three consecutive days is considered plagued. If the deaths occur in one day or over four days, it is not a plague. For a city of 500, three deaths in three days constitutes a plague.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines a plague (דבר) as a city of 500 or 1000 foot soldiers that has nine deaths in three consecutive days.
The baraita specifies that deaths in one day or over four days do not constitute a plague, and for a city of 500, three deaths in three days constitute a plague.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's decree and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's support
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's decree and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's support
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the case of a city that normally has 500 soldiers and has three deaths in one day, which is considered a plague. Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda decreed a fast, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports this by citing Rabbi Meir's principle of a fortiori reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the case: a city called Drokeret that normally sends 500 soldiers had three deaths in one day.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's decree
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's decree
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda decreed a fast in response to the three deaths.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports the decree by citing Rabbi Meir's a fortiori reasoning: if a goring ox that kept its distance is liable, one that came close is certainly liable.

items.text: The exchange about honor and visiting
items.text_en: The exchange about honor and visiting
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda asks Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak to come to him, but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak declines, citing Rabbi Yosei's principle that a person honors his place, not the other way around, with examples from Sinai and the Tabernacle. Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda then offers to go to him, but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it is better for a lesser person to visit a greater one.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's invitation
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's invitation
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda asks Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak to come to him.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's refusal with principle
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's refusal with principle
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak declines, citing Rabbi Yosei's principle that a person honors his place, not vice versa, with examples from Sinai and the Tabernacle.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's offer and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's response
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's offer and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's response
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda offers to go to him, but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it is better for a lesser person to visit a greater one.

items.text: Stories of Rav and Rav Huna's merit protecting their neighborhoods
items.text_en: Stories of Rav and Rav Huna's merit protecting their neighborhoods
items.desc_en: In Sura there was a plague, but not in Rav's neighborhood. They thought it was due to Rav's great merit, but a dream revealed it was due to a man who lent shovels and picks for burial. Similarly, in Drokert there was a fire, but not in Rav Huna's neighborhood, due to a woman who heated her oven and lent it to her neighbors.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's fasts for locusts and swine plague
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's fasts for locusts and swine plague
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda decreed a fast for locusts, but was told they do not cause damage; he responded that they carry provisions. He also decreed a fast for a plague among swine, and the Gemara explains that this is because swine intestines resemble those of humans, so a plague affecting them is a concern for humans.

sub.desc_en: People inform Rav Yehuda that locusts have arrived, and he decrees a fast.
People object that the locusts do not cause damage.
Rav Yehuda responds that the locusts carry provisions (provisions for the journey), implying they will cause damage later.
People inform Rav Yehuda of a plague among swine, and he decrees a fast.
The Gemara questions whether Rav Yehuda holds that a plague sent upon one species is sent upon all species.
The Gemara answers that swine are different because their intestines resemble those of humans, so a plague among them is a concern for humans.

items.text: Shmuel and Rav Nachman's fasts for distant plagues
items.text_en: Shmuel and Rav Nachman's fasts for distant plagues
items.desc_en: Shmuel decreed a fast for a plague in Bei Choza'i despite its distance, because there was a crossing that connected them. Rav Nachman decreed a fast for a plague in Eretz Yisrael, reasoning that if the mistress is stricken, the maidservant is certainly affected. The Gemara questions this, noting that Shmuel's case involved a plague in a different place, but answers that there were caravans traveling between them.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel is told of a plague in Bei Choza'i and decrees a fast.
They object that the plague is far away, implying a fast is inappropriate.
Shmuel answers that there is a crossing (מעברא) that connects them, making the plague relevant.
Rav Nachman is told of a plague in Eretz Yisrael and decrees a fast.
Rav Nachman explains his fast by analogy: if the mistress (Eretz Yisrael) is stricken, the maidservant (Babylonia) is certainly affected.
The Gemara questions: Rav Nachman's reasoning applies only to a mistress-maidservant relationship, not to two maidservants (two distant places), yet Shmuel decreed a fast for a distant plague.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel's case is different because there were caravans (שיירתא) traveling between the places, creating a connection.

items.text: The story of Abba the blood-letter and his merits
items.text_en: The story of Abba the blood-letter and his merits
items.desc_en: Abba the blood-letter received daily greetings from the heavenly academy, while Abaye received them only on Shabbat eve and Rava on Yom Kippur eve. Abaye was distressed, but was told he could not emulate Abba's deeds. The Gemara details Abba's practices: he separated men and women, had a garment with a slit for modesty, provided a private place for payments, did not charge Torah scholars, and gave them money for food. Abaye sent scholars to test him, and Abba hosted them generously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Abba the blood-letter received daily greetings from the heavenly academy, while Abaye received them only on Shabbat eve and Rava on Yom Kippur eve.
Abaye was distressed that Abba received more frequent greetings, but was told he could not emulate Abba's deeds.
The Gemara asks what Abba's deeds were that merited such honor.
The Gemara details Abba's practices: he separated men and women, had a garment with a slit for modesty, and provided a private place for payments so the poor would not be embarrassed.

sub.text: Stam (narrative of Abba's generosity to scholars)
sub.text_en: Stam (narrative of Abba's generosity to scholars)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that Abba did not charge Torah scholars, gave them money for food, and when Abaye sent scholars to test him, Abba hosted them generously.

items.text: Rava's distress and the resolution of the money matter
items.text_en: Rava's distress and the resolution of the money matter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the story of Rava and the Sages who borrowed money from him. They return the money and explain they needed it for redeeming captives. Rava is distressed because of Abaye, and the Sages tell him he has shamed the entire city.

sub.text: Narrative: the Sages return the money
sub.text_en: Narrative: the Sages return the money
sub.desc_en: The Sages bring the garments to the market, have Rava appraise them, and then return them to him, stating that the money was his all along.
The Sages ask Rava what he suspected about them when they borrowed the money.
Rava explains that he suspected they needed the money for redeeming captives and were too embarrassed to tell him, and that he has since mentally allocated the money to charity.

sub.text: Narrative: Rava's distress and the Sages' rebuke
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rava's distress and the Sages' rebuke
sub.desc_en: Rava is distressed because of Abaye, and the Sages tell him that he has shamed the entire city.

items.text: Rabbi Beroka and Elijah identify the righteous men of the marketplace
items.text_en: Rabbi Beroka and Elijah identify the righteous men of the marketplace
items.desc_en: Rabbi Beroka, who frequented the market of Bei Laphat, was told by Elijah that a certain man wearing black shoes and no tekhelet is a share in the World to Come. The man explains his work as a jailer who separates men and women and saves Jewish women from gentiles. Two brothers are also identified as having a share in the World to Come because they cheer the sad and make peace between quarreling parties.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Beroka, who frequented the market of Bei Laphat, was told by Elijah that a certain man wearing black shoes and no tekhelet has a share in the World to Come.
The man explains that he is a jailer who separates men and women, and once saved a betrothed Jewish girl from gentiles by pretending she had a discharge.
The jailer explains that he dresses like a gentile to avoid suspicion and to inform the rabbis of decrees, and that he delayed answering Rabbi Beroka because he was busy hearing a decree.
Elijah points out two brothers who also have a share in the World to Come because they cheer the sad and make peace between quarreling parties.

items.text: Baraita on sounding the alarm for blight, locusts, and wild beasts
items.text_en: Baraita on sounding the alarm for blight, locusts, and wild beasts
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited listing the calamities for which one sounds the alarm everywhere: blight, mildew, locusts, and a wild beast. Rabbi Akiva adds that for blight and mildew even a small amount suffices, and for locusts even if only one wing is seen in Eretz Yisrael.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing the calamities for which one sounds the alarm everywhere: blight, mildew, locusts, and a wild beast.
Rabbi Akiva adds that for blight and mildew even a small amount suffices, and for locusts even if only one wing is seen in Eretz Yisrael.

items.text: Criteria for a 'sent' wild beast
items.text_en: Criteria for a 'sent' wild beast
items.desc_en: A baraita defines when a wild beast is considered 'sent' (requiring alarm) versus not sent. Signs include appearing in the city (sent) vs. the field (not sent), by day (sent) vs. night (not sent), chasing two people (sent) vs. hiding from them (not sent), and killing one of two (sent) vs. both (not sent).

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that a 'sent' wild beast triggers alarm, and defines it by location (city vs. field) and time (day vs. night).
The baraita continues with additional signs: chasing two people, killing one of two, and taking a child from a crib all indicate a 'sent' beast.

items.text: Gemara resolves contradiction between city/day and night criteria
items.text_en: Gemara resolves contradiction between city/day and night criteria
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction: the baraita first says 'seen in the city' is sent regardless of day or night, but then says 'by day' is sent and 'by night' is not. The resolution: 'seen in the city by day' is sent; 'in the city by night' is not sent; and in the field even by day is not sent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: it first says 'seen in the city' is sent regardless of day or night, but then says 'by day' is sent and 'by night' is not.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the baraita means 'seen in the city by day' is sent; 'in the city by night' is not sent; and in the field even by day is not sent.

items.text: Gemara resolves contradiction between chasing and hiding criteria
items.text_en: Gemara resolves contradiction between chasing and hiding criteria
items.desc_en: Another contradiction: the baraita says if it chased two people it is sent (implying if it stands still it is not), but then says if it hid from them it is not sent (implying if it stands still it is sent). The resolution: the first case is in a field near a marsh (where standing still is suspicious), the second in a field not near a marsh.

sub.desc_en: The gemara points out a contradiction: the baraita first implies that standing still means the animal is not sent, but then implies that standing still means it is sent.
The gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a field near a marsh (where standing still is suspicious) and a field not near a marsh (where standing still is not suspicious).

items.text: Rav Pappa resolves contradictions regarding killing two people and taking a child from a cradle
items.text_en: Rav Pappa resolves contradictions regarding killing two people and taking a child from a cradle
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves a contradiction: the baraita says if it killed one of two it is sent, but if it killed both it is not sent, yet earlier it said even if it chased them it is sent. Rav Pappa explains that the case of killing both is in a marsh (where it is normal). Similarly, the case of taking a child from a roof is obvious, but Rav Pappa explains it refers to a hunter's trap (where it is unusual).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: the baraita says if the beast killed two people and ate one it is sent, but if it ate both it is not sent, yet earlier it said even if it chased them it is sent.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case of killing both is in a marsh (אגמא), where such behavior is normal and therefore not a sign of being sent.
The Gemara asks why the baraita needs to state the obvious case of a beast going up to a roof and taking a child from a cradle.
Rav Pappa explains that the case refers to a hunter's trap (כוכי דציידי), where the beast's action is unusual and therefore a sign of being sent.

items.text: Baraita on the sword of peace and the example of Pharaoh Necho
items.text_en: Baraita on the sword of peace and the example of Pharaoh Necho
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the 'sword' mentioned in the Mishnah includes even a sword of peace, as there is no greater sword of peace than that of Pharaoh Necho, yet King Josiah was still struck down by it, as the verse states.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the 'sword' in the Mishnah includes even a sword of peace, citing Pharaoh Necho as the ultimate example of a sword of peace, yet King Josiah was struck down by it.

items.text: Josiah's reliance on idolatry
items.text_en: Josiah's reliance on idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse about Josiah's battle, interpreting 'Elohim who is with me' as idolatry, which led to his downfall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse where Necho sends messengers to Josiah, warning him not to interfere with 'Elohim who is with me'.
The Gemara asks what 'Elohim who is with me' refers to.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that 'Elohim who is with me' refers to idolatry, and Necho concluded that since Josiah relied on idolatry, he could defeat him.

items.text: Josiah's body riddled like a sieve
items.text_en: Josiah's body riddled like a sieve
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that Josiah's body was pierced like a sieve by the arrows.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the verse 'and the archers shot King Josiah' teaches that his entire body was made like a sieve.

items.text: Why Josiah was punished
items.text_en: Why Josiah was punished
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan says Josiah was punished for not consulting Jeremiah, misinterpreting a verse about a sword of peace.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan states that Josiah was punished because he should have consulted Jeremiah but did not.
The Gemara asks what verse Josiah misinterpreted, citing the verse 'and a sword shall not pass through your land'.
The Gemara questions what type of sword is meant, rejecting the possibility of a non-peaceful sword because the verse promises peace.
The Gemara concludes that the verse refers even to a sword of peace, but Josiah did not realize that his generation was not worthy of such a blessing.

items.text: Jeremiah's comfort at Josiah's death
items.text_en: Jeremiah's comfort at Josiah's death
items.desc_en: At Josiah's death, Jeremiah heard him justifying the decree and applied the verse 'The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the Lord'.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes that at the moment of Josiah's death, Jeremiah saw his lips moving and suspected he might have said something improper in his pain.
Jeremiah leaned in and heard Josiah justifying the divine decree upon himself, reciting the verse 'Righteous is the Lord, for I have rebelled against His mouth'.
Jeremiah then applied to him the verse 'The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the Lord', expressing comfort.

items.text: Uncertainty about the measure of the oven
items.text_en: Uncertainty about the measure of the oven
items.desc_en: A question arises whether the measure of the oven refers to grain or bread, and whether it is the covering or the loaf; left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises a question: does the measure of the oven refer to grain or bread?
The gemara cites a baraita that says 'the full mouth of the oven' to resolve the question.
The gemara raises a second question: does the measure refer to the covering of the oven or the loaf that surrounds its mouth?
The gemara leaves the question unresolved with 'תיקו' (let it stand).

items.text: Wolves swallowing children
items.text_en: Wolves swallowing children
items.desc_en: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak relates an incident where wolves swallowed children and the sages ruled the flesh pure and the bones impure.

sub.text: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.text_en: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.desc_en: Ulla reports an incident where wolves swallowed children and the sages ruled the flesh pure and the bones impure.

items.text: Sounding alarms on Shabbat
items.text_en: Sounding alarms on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita lists cases where alarms are sounded on Shabbat, and Rabbi Yosei argues an individual may not fast excessively lest he become dependent on others.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists cases where alarms are sounded on Shabbat (a besieged city, a river, a storm-tossed ship, an individual pursued by enemies, bandits, or an evil spirit) and states that an individual may fast voluntarily.
Rabbi Yosei objects that an individual may not fast excessively, lest he become dependent on others and they not have mercy on him.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav provides a scriptural basis for Rabbi Yosei's position: the verse 'וַיְהִי הָאָדָם לְנֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה' teaches that one must preserve the soul God gave him.

items.text: Dispute about sounding alarms for plague
items.text_en: Dispute about sounding alarms for plague
items.desc_en: A question whether the sages agreed with Shimon HaTimni about plague on weekdays; resolved by a baraita with Rabbi Chanan ben Pitom in the name of Rabbi Akiva who says not at all.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises a question: did the sages disagree with Shimon HaTimni only regarding Shabbat, but agree regarding weekdays, or did they disagree entirely?
The gemara cites a baraita that rules one sounds alarms for plague on Shabbat, and certainly on weekdays, supporting the view that the sages agreed with Shimon HaTimni on weekdays.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanan ben Pitom in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanan ben Pitom in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan ben Pitom cites Rabbi Akiva who rules that one does not sound alarms for plague at all, contradicting the first baraita and resolving the question in favor of the sages' complete disagreement.

items.text: No alarm for abundant rain
items.text_en: No alarm for abundant rain
items.desc_en: A baraita states alarms are sounded for all troubles except abundant rain; Rabbi Yochanan explains one does not pray for an excess of good, citing a verse about tithes.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that alarms are sounded for every trouble that may come upon the community, except for an abundance of rain.
The gemara asks for the reason why abundant rain is excluded.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that one does not pray for an excess of good.
Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse about tithes to prove that one does not pray for an excess of good.
The gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'עַד בְּלִי דָּי' (until there is no more need).
Rami bar Rav Yod explains that the phrase means until your lips wear out from saying 'enough'.

items.text: Alarm for abundant rain in the diaspora
items.text_en: Alarm for abundant rain in the diaspora
items.desc_en: Rami bar Rav Yod says in the diaspora they do sound alarms for abundant rain, as it causes houses to become graves.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Rav Yod states that in the diaspora they sound alarms for abundant rain, because it causes houses to become graves.

items.text: How much rain is too much
items.text_en: How much rain is too much
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer is asked how much rain is enough to pray for it to stop; he says when one can splash his feet in water at Kerem Afel; Rabba bar bar Chana describes the place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rabbi Eliezer: to what point may rain fall such that people pray for it to stop?
Rabbi Eliezer answers: until a person can stand at Kerem Afel and splash his feet in water.
The Gemara objects: a baraita says 'his hands' (not feet) — implying the measure is different.
The Gemara resolves: we say 'his feet' are like 'his hands' — the same measure applies.
Rabba bar bar Chana testifies that he personally saw Kerem Afel, describing its height with a vivid image of a rider and spear.

items.text: Ideal rain is moderate
items.text_en: Ideal rain is moderate
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that the verse 'I will give your rains in their time' means rain that is neither excessive nor insufficient but moderate, as too much rain damages the land.

sub.desc_en: The baraita interprets the verse 'I will give your rains in their time' as referring to moderate rain, neither excessive nor insufficient, because excessive rain damages the land and prevents it from producing fruit.

items.text: Rains in the days of Shimon ben Shetach and Herod
items.text_en: Rains in the days of Shimon ben Shetach and Herod
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'in their time' as referring to rains on Wednesday and Shabbat nights, citing the days of Shimon ben Shetach when rains fell only on those nights, causing extraordinary growth, and the days of Herod when rains fell at night to allow work on the Temple by day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'in their time' as rains falling on Wednesday and Shabbat nights, citing the days of Shimon ben Shetach when this occurred with extraordinary growth, and the days of Herod when rains fell at night to allow Temple construction by day.

items.text: The story of Honi HaMe'agel's prayer for rain
items.text_en: The story of Honi HaMe'agel's prayer for rain
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that when most of Adar passed without rain, the Sages sent for Honi HaMe'agel. He drew a circle, stood inside, and swore not to leave until God showed mercy. Rain fell in stages: first a drizzle, then a storm, and finally a blessing. He then prayed for the rain to stop, offering a thanksgiving offering, and the rain ceased.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing that when most of Adar passed without rain, the Sages sent for Honi HaMe'agel to pray, and when his initial prayer failed, he drew a circle and stood inside it like Habakkuk.
Honi prays to God, declaring himself as a household member and swearing by God's great name not to move until He shows mercy on His children.
Rain begins to drip, and Honi's students remark that it seems only enough to release his oath, not to truly water the land.
Honi rejects the first rain, specifying he asked for cistern- and cave-filling rain, and the rain then falls furiously with each drop measured at a log.
The students object that the violent rain seems intended to destroy the world, not to bless it.
Honi rejects the stormy rain, asking for rain of favor, blessing, and generosity, and the rain then falls properly until everyone goes up to the Temple Mount due to the abundance.
The people ask Honi to pray for the rain to stop, just as he prayed for it to fall.
Honi responds that he has a tradition that one does not pray for an excess of good to cease.
Despite the tradition, Honi brings a thanksgiving offering, prays for the rain to stop, and the rain ceases, allowing people to go to the field and gather mushrooms.

Shimon ben Shetach sends a message to Honi, saying that were he not Honi, he would decree a נידוי (ban) for causing God's name to be profaned, but he cannot because Honi is like a son who cajoles his father and gets his way, and the verse 'יִשְׂמַח אָבִיךָ וְאִמֶּךָ' applies to him.

items.text: The message from the Chamber of Hewn Stone
items.text_en: The message from the Chamber of Hewn Stone
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse sent by the members of the Chamber of Hewn Stone to Honi HaMe'agel, interpreting each phrase as referring to his power of prayer: he decreed below and God fulfilled above, he illuminated a dark generation, raised the lowly, and saved the innocent.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the verse sent by the Chamber of Hewn Stone to Honi HaMe'agel.
The baraita interprets the first phrase: Honi decreed below and God fulfilled above.
The baraita interprets the second phrase: Honi illuminated a dark generation through his prayer.
The baraita interprets the third phrase: Honi raised the lowly generation through his prayer.
The baraita interprets the fourth phrase: Honi saved the innocent generation through his prayer.
The baraita interprets the fifth phrase: Honi delivered the impure generation through his prayer.
The baraita interprets the sixth phrase: Honi saved the generation through the pure works of his hands.

items.text: Honi's seventy-year sleep and death
items.text_en: Honi's seventy-year sleep and death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan relates that Honi was troubled by the verse 'we were like dreamers'. One day he saw a man planting a carob tree, slept for seventy years, and upon waking found the tree bearing fruit. He went to the study hall but was not recognized, and his feelings were hurt; he prayed for mercy and died.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports that Honi was troubled by the verse 'we were like dreamers' and wondered if anyone could sleep for seventy years in a dream.
Honi sees a man planting a carob tree, learns it takes seventy years to bear fruit, and the man explains he plants for his descendants as his ancestors planted for him.
Honi falls asleep for seventy years, wakes to find the tree bearing fruit and the man is the planter's grandson, confirming the seventy-year sleep.
Honi goes home and to the study hall, is not recognized or honored, prays for mercy and dies, and Rava comments that people say either companionship or death.

items.text: Abba Hilkia's power to bring rain
items.text_en: Abba Hilkia's power to bring rain
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Abba Hilkia, Honi's grandson, who also had the power to bring rain through prayer. When the world needed rain, the Sages sent a pair of rabbis to him, but they found him plowing in the field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Abba Hilkia, Honi's grandson, who also had the power to bring rain through prayer.
The Gemara recounts a specific incident when the world needed rain, and the Sages sent a pair of rabbis to Abba Hilkia, finding him plowing in the field.

items.text: Abba Hilkia's unusual conduct described
items.text_en: Abba Hilkia's unusual conduct described
items.desc_en: The Gemara details Abba Hilkia's peculiar actions: carrying wood and cloak on one shoulder, not wearing shoes until reaching water, lifting his garment at thorns, his wife greeting him adorned, entering his house after her, and distributing bread to children.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes Abba Hilkia's unusual conduct: carrying wood and cloak on one shoulder, not wearing shoes until reaching water, lifting his garment at thorns, his wife greeting him adorned, entering his house after her, and distributing bread to children.

items.text: Abba Hilkia prays for rain in secret
items.text_en: Abba Hilkia prays for rain in secret
items.desc_en: Abba Hilkia tells his wife that the rabbis came for rain, so they go to the roof to pray separately. Clouds gather first from his wife's corner. After descending, he tells the rabbis that God did not need them to come to him.

sub.desc_en: Abba Hilkia tells his wife that the rabbis came for rain, they go up to the roof to pray, clouds come from his wife's corner, and he blesses God for not needing them.
They go up to the roof and pray in separate corners; clouds gather first from his wife's corner.
After descending, Abba Hilkia asks why the rabbis came and declares that God did not need them to come to him.

items.text: First two questions: greeting and carrying wood
items.text_en: First two questions: greeting and carrying wood
items.desc_en: The rabbis ask why Abba Hilkia did not return their greeting and why he carried wood and cloak on one shoulder. He explains he was a day laborer and did not want to be idle, and the cloak was borrowed.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask why Abba Hilkia did not return their greeting, and he explains he was a day laborer and did not want to waste time.
The rabbis ask why he carried wood and cloak on one shoulder, and he explains the cloak was borrowed, so he carried it separately.

items.text: Questions about shoes and thorns
items.text_en: Questions about shoes and thorns
items.desc_en: The rabbis ask why he only wore shoes near water and why he lifted his garment at thorns. He answers that he could see the road but not the water, and that some thorns heal while others do not.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask why he did not wear shoes on the road but put them on at water, and why he lifted his garment at thorns; he explains he could see the road but not water, and thorns that heal and those that do not.
Abba Hilkia explains that he could see the road clearly but could not see the water, so he wore shoes only near water to avoid injury.
The rabbis ask Abba Hilkia why he lifted his garment when passing through thorns and briars.
Abba Hilkia explains that some thorns cause wounds that heal while others do not, so he lifts his garment to avoid the harmful ones.

items.text: Questions about wife's greeting and entry order
items.text_en: Questions about wife's greeting and entry order
items.desc_en: The rabbis ask why his wife greeted him adorned and why she entered first. He explains he did not want to look at other women, and that they did not check him for lice.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask why his wife greeted him adorned and why she entered first; he explains the first was to avoid looking at other women, and the second because they did not trust him.
Abba Hilkia explains that his wife adorned herself to prevent him from looking at other women, and she entered first because the rabbis did not check him for lice.

items.text: Questions about bread distribution
items.text_en: Questions about bread distribution
items.desc_en: The rabbis ask why he did not invite them to eat and why he gave one loaf to an older child and two to a younger. He explains there was not enough bread, and the older child was at home while the younger was in the study hall.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask why he did not invite them to eat and why he gave one bread to the older child and two to the younger; he explains the bread was scarce and the older child was at home while the younger was at the synagogue.
Abba Hilkia explains that there was not enough bread, and the older child was at home while the younger was in the study hall.

items.text: Why clouds came from wife's corner
items.text_en: Why clouds came from wife's corner
items.desc_en: The rabbis ask why clouds gathered first from his wife's corner. He explains she gives bread to the poor directly, while he gives money indirectly, or alternatively, she prayed for the wicked neighbors to repent while he prayed for them to die.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask why clouds came from his wife's corner; he explains she gives bread to the poor directly while he gives money, or alternatively, he prayed for the death of local thugs while she prayed for their repentance.
Abba Hilkia answers that his wife is more present at home and gives bread directly to the poor, bringing them immediate benefit, whereas he gives money indirectly.
Alternatively, Abba Hilkia explains that he prayed for the wicked neighbors to die, while his wife prayed for them to repent, and they indeed repented.

items.text: Hanan ha-Nehba's prayer for rain
items.text_en: Hanan ha-Nehba's prayer for rain
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Hanan ha-Nehba, grandson of Honi ha-Me'agel, who would be grabbed by schoolchildren who asked him for rain. He prayed that God would provide rain for the innocent children who do not distinguish between a father who gives rain and one who does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Hanan the Hidden, grandson of Honi the Circle-Drawer, who would be grabbed by schoolchildren to pray for rain, and explains why he was called 'the Hidden'.

items.text: Comparison of Babylonian and Land of Israel righteous
items.text_en: Comparison of Babylonian and Land of Israel righteous
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika contrasts the Babylonian sages Rav Huna and Rav Hisda, who gather to pray for rain, with the Land of Israel sages like Rabbi Yonah, who pretends to buy grain but secretly prays in a low place, covered in sackcloth.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika invites Rav Safra to observe the contrast between the powerful righteous of the Land of Israel and the pious of Babylonia.
The Babylonian sages Rav Huna and Rav Hisda gather together and pray for rain openly.

sub.text: Description of Land of Israel sages
sub.text_en: Description of Land of Israel sages
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonah pretends to go buy grain but secretly prays in a low place covered in sackcloth, then claims the rain made the market cheap.

items.text: Rabbi Mani's prayer at his father's grave
items.text_en: Rabbi Mani's prayer at his father's grave
items.desc_en: Rabbi Mani, son of Rabbi Yonah, was troubled by the house of the Nasi. He prostrated on his father's grave and cried out. The horses of the Nasi's entourage became stuck until they agreed to stop troubling him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Mani, son of Rabbi Yona, was troubled by the house of the Nasi, prostrated on his father's grave, and the horses' legs stuck until they agreed not to trouble him.

items.text: Rabbi Mani's requests from Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elyashiv
items.text_en: Rabbi Mani's requests from Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elyashiv
items.desc_en: Rabbi Mani complains to Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elyashiv about his wealthy in-laws, his crowded conditions, and his wife Hannah. Rabbi Yitzchak decrees that they become poor, then rich, that Hannah become beautiful, and finally that she return to her original state when she becomes haughty.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Mani complains to Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elyashiv about his wealthy in-laws and crowded conditions, and Rabbi Yitzchak decrees that they become poor and then rich.
Rabbi Mani complains about his wife Hannah's haughtiness, and Rabbi Yitzchak decrees that she become beautiful and then return to her original state.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's response to students seeking wisdom
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's response to students seeking wisdom
items.desc_en: Two students ask Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elyashiv to pray for them to become very wise. He responds that wisdom was with him but he sent it away.

sub.desc_en: Two students asked Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elyashiv to pray for them to become very wise, and he replied that wisdom was with him and he sent it away.
Rabbi Yitzchak responds that wisdom was with him but he sent it away.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin leaves Rabbi Yosei of Yokeret
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin leaves Rabbi Yosei of Yokeret
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin, who was studying before Rabbi Yosei of Yokeret, left him and came before Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin left Rabbi Yosei of Yokeret and came before Rav Ashi.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling and the identity of the sage
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling and the identity of the sage
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that one who catches a fish on Shabbat is liable once a sela-sized scale dries on it. The Gemara questions whether this ruling was said by Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Avin, and the sage confirms he is that Rabbi Yosei. He explains why he left Rabbi Yosei of Yokeret, citing the latter's lack of compassion for his own children.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens with Shmuel stating that one who catches a fish on Shabbat is liable once a sela-sized scale dries on it.
The Gemara asks why the sage did not mention the fins as a sign of fish.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Avin's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Avin's answer
sub.desc_en: The sage responds that the ruling was said by Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Avin, and he confirms that he is that Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara asks whether the sage was not frequently before Rabbi Yosei of Yokeret, and he confirms.
The Gemara asks why the sage left Rabbi Yosei of Yokeret and came here.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Avin's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Avin's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Avin explains that he left because Rabbi Yosei of Yokeret lacked compassion for his own children, so he would certainly not have compassion for him.

items.text: The son's miracle with the fig tree
items.text_en: The son's miracle with the fig tree
items.desc_en: The son hired workers who became hungry, and he commanded a fig tree to produce fruit out of season, which it did. When the father arrived, he explained his delay was due to a mitzvah. The workers told him about the miracle, and the father cursed the son to die young for troubling God to act unnaturally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the son's miracle and recounts how he commanded a fig tree to produce fruit out of season for hungry workers.
The father arrives, learns of the miracle, and curses the son to die young for troubling God to act unnaturally.

items.text: The daughter's beauty and the father's curse
items.text_en: The daughter's beauty and the father's curse
items.desc_en: The daughter was so beautiful that a man digging a drain stared at her. The father told her to return to dust so that people would not stumble because of her, implying she died young.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what happened with the daughter of the sage.
The narrative describes the daughter's beauty and the father's curse that she return to dust to prevent people from stumbling because of her.

items.text: The miraculous donkey
items.text_en: The miraculous donkey
items.desc_en: The family had a donkey that would return home with its exact hire fee each evening. One day, someone placed a pair of sandals on it, and it refused to move until they were removed, demonstrating its honesty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara narrates that the family had a donkey which would return home each evening with its exact hire fee, and once refused to move until a pair of sandals placed on it was removed.

items.text: Elazar Ish Birta's charity and the miracle of the wheat
items.text_en: Elazar Ish Birta's charity and the miracle of the wheat
items.desc_en: Elazar would give all his money to charity collectors, who hid from him. Once, he gave away his daughter's dowry money to orphans. His wife found the house filled with wheat through a miracle, but Elazar declared it consecrated, leaving his daughter with only a poor person's share.

sub.desc_en: Introduces Elazar Ish Birta, who gave all his money to charity collectors, causing them to hide from him, and describes his trip to buy a dowry for his daughter.
Elazar runs after the charity collectors, asks what they are doing, and upon hearing they are collecting for orphans, declares the orphans take precedence over his daughter.
Elazar gives all his money to the collectors, leaving only one zuz, with which he buys wheat and stores it in a granary.
Elazar's wife asks his daughter what he brought, and upon opening the granary, finds it miraculously filled with wheat overflowing through the door.
Elazar's daughter tells him of the miracle, but he declares the wheat consecrated (הקדש), leaving her only the share of a poor person.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's prayer and the generation's decline
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's prayer and the generation's decline
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decreed a fast but rain did not come. He lamented the distance from Shmuel HaRamati to Yehuda ben Gamliel, and his distress brought rain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decreed a fast and prayed for rain, but rain did not come.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia laments the distance from Shmuel HaRamati to Yehuda ben Gamliel and the decline of the generation.
His distress caused rain to come.

items.text: The Nasi's fast without informing Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: The Nasi's fast without informing Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The house of the Nasi decreed a fast without informing Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish until morning. Reish Lakish objected that they had not accepted it from the previous night, but Rabbi Yochanan said they follow the majority.

sub.desc_en: The house of the Nasi decreed a fast without informing Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish until morning.
Reish Lakish objects that they had not accepted the fast from the previous night.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that they follow the majority, so the fast is valid even without their prior acceptance.

items.text: Oshaya's parable of the bride and the Nasi's distress
items.text_en: Oshaya's parable of the bride and the Nasi's distress
items.desc_en: The house of the Nasi decreed a fast without rain. Oshaya Z'eira taught a verse about communal sin, comparing it to a bride whose eyes determine if her body needs inspection. The Nasi's servants tormented him, but the townspeople defended him, noting his actions are for Heaven's sake.

sub.desc_en: The house of the Nasi decreed a fast but no rain came.
Oshaya Z'eira taught a verse about communal sin, implying the Nasi's generation was at fault.
He gave a parable of a bride whose eyes determine if her whole body needs inspection, comparing the Nasi's generation to a bride with defective eyes.
The Nasi's servants came and tormented him by placing a scarf around his neck.
The townspeople defended the Nasi, saying since all his actions are for Heaven's sake, the servants should also leave him alone.

items.text: Ilfa's merit for providing wine for Kiddush and Havdalah
items.text_en: Ilfa's merit for providing wine for Kiddush and Havdalah
items.desc_en: Rabbi decreed a fast without rain. Ilfa led the prayers, and when he said 'Mashiv HaRuach' a wind blew, and 'Morid HaGeshem' brought rain. He explained his merit: he lived in a cramped place without wine for Kiddush and Havdalah, and he would trouble himself to bring wine for the community.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: Rabbi decreed a fast, and when Ilfa led the prayers, his recitation of 'Mashiv HaRuach' and 'Morid HaGeshem' brought wind and rain.
Rabbi asks Ilfa what merit caused his prayers to be answered.
Ilfa explains his merit: he lived in a cramped place without wine for קידוש (Kiddush) and הבדלה (Havdalah), yet he would trouble himself to bring wine for the community to fulfill their obligation.

items.text: The teacher of children who brought rain
items.text_en: The teacher of children who brought rain
items.desc_en: Rav visited a place and decreed a fast without rain. The prayer leader said 'Mashiv HaRuach' and a wind blew, then 'Morid HaGeshem' and rain came. He explained he teaches poor and rich children equally, takes no fee from those who cannot pay, and uses fish glue to coax negligent students to read.

sub.desc_en: Rav visits a place, decrees a fast, and the prayer leader brings rain by reciting 'Mashiv HaRuach' and 'Morid HaGeshem'.
Rav asks the prayer leader what his merit is.
The prayer leader explains that he teaches poor and rich children equally, takes no fee from those who cannot pay, and uses fish glue to coax negligent students to read.

items.text: Rav Nachman's self-deprecation brings rain
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's self-deprecation brings rain
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman decreed a fast but rain did not come. He said to throw him from the roof to the ground. His distress brought rain.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman decreed a fast, prayed for rain without success, then ordered himself thrown from the roof, and his distress brought rain.

items.text: Rabba's comparison to Rav Yehuda's generation
items.text_en: Rabba's comparison to Rav Yehuda's generation
items.desc_en: Rabba decreed a fast without rain. People noted that Rav Yehuda's fasts always brought rain. Rabba responded that he cannot help it; in Rav Yehuda's generation, all study was Torah, whereas now they are superior in study.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabba decreed a fast and prayed for rain, but no rain came.
The people point out that when Rav Yehuda decreed a fast, rain always came, implicitly criticizing Rabba's lack of efficacy.
Rabba responds that he cannot help it, explaining that in Rav Yehuda's generation all study was Torah (תנ

items.text: Rav Yehuda's merit vs. the generation's unworthiness
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's merit vs. the generation's unworthiness
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts Rav Yehuda's mastery of all six orders of Mishnah and his ability to bring rain by removing a shoe, with the current generation's inability to be answered despite fasting all day. It questions whether the lack of rain is due to deeds, but notes that great people cannot change the generation's fate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts Rav Yehuda's mastery of all six orders of Mishnah with the current generation's lesser expertise.
The Gemara questions why Rav Yehuda could bring rain by removing one shoe, while the current generation's fasting goes unanswered.
The Gemara resolves that the lack of rain is not due to deeds, but because the generation is unworthy compared to Rav Yehuda's time.

items.text: Rav Yehuda brings rain by removing one shoe
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda brings rain by removing one shoe
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda sees people breaking bread and infers plenty, but then causes a famine by staring. The rabbis ask Rav Kahana to have Rav Yehuda go to the market to see the famine. Rav Yehuda sees a crowd buying cheap dates, infers famine, and has his attendant remove one shoe, bringing rain. Elijah then warns that removing the second shoe would destroy the world.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda sees people breaking bread, infers plenty, but then stares at them and causes a famine.
The rabbis ask Rav Kahana to have Rav Yehuda go to the market to see the famine.
Rav Yehuda goes to the market, sees cheap dates, infers famine, removes one shoe, and rain falls; Elijah warns that removing the second shoe would destroy the world.

items.text: Rav Mari's vision of angels bringing flour
items.text_en: Rav Mari's vision of angels bringing flour
items.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel recounts seeing angels disguised as sailors bringing fine flour in boats. He tells the people not to buy it because it is a miracle, and that tomorrow boats of wheat from Parzina will arrive.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel's account
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel's account
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari recounts seeing angels disguised as sailors bringing fine flour in boats, and tells the people not to buy it because it is a miracle.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel's prediction
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel's prediction
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari predicts that tomorrow boats of wheat from Parzina will arrive, resolving the shortage.

items.text: Rava's fast in Hagronya and Rabbi Elazar's dream
items.text_en: Rava's fast in Hagronya and Rabbi Elazar's dream
items.desc_en: Rava decrees a fast in Hagronya but no rain comes. He tells everyone to sleep in their fast, and the next day asks for a dream interpretation. Rabbi Elazar from Hagronya reports a dream blessing, and Rava infers it is a time of favor, prays, and rain comes.

sub.desc_en: Rava arrives in Hagronya, decrees a fast, but no rain comes.
Rava tells everyone to sleep in their fast, implying a request for dream revelation.
The next day, Rava asks if anyone had a dream to share.
Rabbi Elazar from Hagronya reports his dream blessing: 'Great peace to the great rabbi from the great Master, who from His goodness bestows good upon His people.'
Rava infers it is a time of favor, prays for rain, and rain comes.

items.text: Rava's trial with Ifra Hormiz and King Shapur
items.text_en: Rava's trial with Ifra Hormiz and King Shapur
items.desc_en: A man is executed by Rava for marrying a non-Jew, and King Shapur seeks to harm Rava. His mother Ifra Hormiz warns him not to engage with Jews because God answers them. She tests Rava by asking him to pray for rain in Tammuz. Rava prays but no rain comes until he laments that the generation does not see God's deeds as their ancestors did. Rain then floods the city, and his father appears in a dream rebuking him for troubling Heaven, and Rava changes his place, finding his bed slashed.

sub.desc_en: A man is executed by Rava for marrying a non-Jew, and King Shapur seeks to harm Rava.
Ifra Hormiz warns her son not to engage with Jews because God answers their prayers.
King Shapur questions his mother's claim, noting that rain comes in its season.
King Shapur challenges Rava to pray for rain during the dry season of Tammuz.
Ifra Hormiz sends word to Rava to pray for rain, but no rain comes.
Rava laments that the current generation does not see God's deeds as their ancestors did.
Rain falls so heavily that the drainage channels of Mahoza flow into the Tigris.
Rava's father appears in a dream rebuking him for troubling Heaven, and Rava changes his place, finding his bed slashed.

items.text: Rav Pappa's fast and Rav Nachman bar Ushpazti's advice
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's fast and Rav Nachman bar Ushpazti's advice
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa decrees a fast but no rain comes. He burns his cooking pot in distress and prays, but still no rain. Rav Nachman bar Ushpazti suggests that if he burns another pot, rain will come. Rav Pappa is embarrassed, his mind weakens, and rain comes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa decrees a fast but no rain comes.
Rav Pappa's mind weakens, he burns his cooking pot and prays, but still no rain comes.
Rav Nachman bar Ushpazti suggests that if Rav Pappa burns another pot, rain will come.
Rav Pappa is embarrassed, his mind weakens, and rain comes.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's prayer for rain
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's prayer for rain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa is caught in rain while traveling. He prays that the world be at ease while he suffers, and the rain stops. When he reaches home, he prays that the world suffer while he is at ease, and the rain returns.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, caught in rain while traveling, prays that the world be at ease while he suffers, and the rain stops.
When he reaches home, he prays that the world suffer while he is at ease, and the rain returns.

items.text: The High Priest's prayer and Rabbi Chanina's merit
items.text_en: The High Priest's prayer and Rabbi Chanina's merit
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef questions the efficacy of the High Priest's prayer compared to Rabbi Chanina's. The Mishnah describes the High Priest's short prayer in the outer chamber. Ravin and Rava bar Adda quote Rav Yehuda that the prayer is for a rainy and 'shchuna' year. The Gemara clarifies 'shchuna' means moderate, not hot. The prayer also asks that travelers' prayers not enter before God. Rav Acha bar Rava adds a prayer for the continuation of the Davidic dynasty and that Israel not need each other's gifts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef questions what benefit the High Priest's prayer has compared to Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's merit.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that the High Priest recited a short prayer in the outer chamber.

sub.text: Ravin and Rava bar Adda quoting Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Ravin and Rava bar Adda quoting Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Ravin and Rava bar Adda quote Rav Yehuda that the prayer was for a rainy and 'shchuna' year.
The Gemara objects that 'shchuna' (hot) is a bad thing, not a blessing.
The Gemara resolves that the prayer means: if the year is hot, let it be rainy and cloudy.
The prayer also asks that travelers' prayers not enter before God.
Rav Acha bar Rava adds that the prayer included requests for the continuation of the Davidic dynasty and that Israel not need gifts from each other or from other nations.

items.text: The Bat Kol about Rabbi Chanina's sustenance
items.text_en: The Bat Kol about Rabbi Chanina's sustenance
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav says that a heavenly voice declares daily that the entire world is sustained for the sake of Chanina My son, yet Chanina My son is satisfied with a kab of carobs from one Shabbat eve to the next. His wife would heat the oven every Shabbat eve and throw in smoke-producing material to avoid shame.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav reports that a heavenly voice (בת קול) declares daily that the entire world is sustained for the sake of Chanina My son, yet Chanina My son is satisfied with a kab of carobs from one Shabbat eve to the next.

The gemara adds a narrative detail: his wife would habitually heat the oven every Shabbat eve and throw in smoke-producing material to avoid shame from neighbors who would see no actual food being cooked.

items.text: The miracle of the neighbor's oven
items.text_en: The miracle of the neighbor's oven
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's wife, embarrassed by their poverty, hides when a neighbor knocks. A miracle occurs: the oven is filled with bread and the trough with dough, and the neighbor, thinking the bread is burning, calls out to her.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the story: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's wife, embarrassed by their poverty, hides when a neighbor knocks.
A miracle occurs: the oven is filled with bread and the trough with dough, and the neighbor, thinking the bread is burning, calls out to her.

items.text: The golden table leg
items.text_en: The golden table leg
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina's wife complains about their constant suffering. He prays and receives a golden table leg from heaven. However, a dream reveals that in the future, the righteous will eat at a three-legged golden table, while they will have only two legs. He prays again to have it taken away, and the second miracle is considered greater.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina's wife asks him how long they will suffer, and he suggests she pray for something to be given to them.
Rabbi Chanina prays and receives a golden table leg from heaven, but a dream reveals that the righteous will eat at a three-legged golden table while he will have only two legs.
Rabbi Chanina asks his wife if she is content that everyone else will eat at a complete table while they eat at a deficient one, and she suggests he pray to have the leg taken away.
Rabbi Chanina prays again and the leg is taken away, and the gemara comments that the second miracle was greater because it is easier to give than to take back.

items.text: The vinegar that burned like oil
items.text_en: The vinegar that burned like oil
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina's daughter mistakenly uses vinegar instead of oil for Shabbat lights. He comforts her, saying that the One who commanded oil to burn can command vinegar to burn. The vinegar burned the entire day, even providing light for Havdalah.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna recounts that Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa saw his daughter distressed because she mistakenly used vinegar instead of oil for Shabbat lights.
Rabbi Chanina comforts his daughter, asserting that the One who commanded oil to burn can command vinegar to burn.
A baraita testifies that the vinegar burned the entire day, even providing light for Havdalah.

items.text: The goats and the wolves
items.text_en: The goats and the wolves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's goats were accused of causing damage. He declared that if they were damaging, wolves would eat them; if not, each would bring a wolf home on its horns. That night, each goat brought a wolf on its horns.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces that Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa had goats, and people complained they were causing damage.
Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa declares that if the goats are truly damaging, wolves will eat them; if not, each goat will bring a wolf home on its horns.
The narrator reports that that night, each goat indeed brought a wolf on its horns, confirming their innocence.

items.text: The house that was too short
items.text_en: The house that was too short
items.desc_en: A woman named Eichu built a house but the beams did not reach the walls. Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa prayed, and the walls miraculously extended to meet the beams. The Tanna and others testify to seeing the house with beams extending beyond the walls.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces a neighbor woman who was building a house but the beams did not reach the walls.
The woman comes before Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and states her problem: she built a house but the beams do not reach the walls.
Rabbi Chanina asks the woman's name, and when she says 'Eichu', he prays that her beams should reach the walls.
A Tanna reports that the beams extended until they protruded a cubit on each side.
Some say that they made supports (סניפין) for the beams rather than the beams extending.
Polemo testifies that he saw the house with beams protruding a cubit on each side, and was told that this is the house Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa roofed with his prayer.

items.text: The source of the goats
items.text_en: The source of the goats
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Chanina had goats, given his poverty and the prohibition against raising small cattle in Eretz Yisrael. Rav Pinchas explains that someone left chickens at his door, his wife raised them, and they sold them to buy goats. The original owner later identified them and took them back.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa had goats, given his poverty and the rabbinic prohibition against raising small cattle in Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Pinchas begins a story: a man passed by Rabbi Chanina's house and left chickens there, which his wife found.
The man told her not to eat the eggs; the chickens multiplied, were sold, and with the proceeds they bought goats.
The original owner later identified the chickens by a סימן (distinguishing mark) and took back the goats, which were the very goats that bears later carried off by their horns.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat's vision
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat's vision
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was extremely poor. He fell asleep and had a vision where he spoke with the Holy One, blessed be He. He complained about his suffering, and God offered to restart the world so he might be born at a time of sustenance. Rabbi Elazar declined, and God promised him thirteen rivers of pure balsam oil in the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: The gemara describes Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat's extreme poverty, his eating a garlic clove, fainting, and the sages seeing him cry and laugh with a flame from his nose.
Upon awakening, the sages ask Rabbi Elazar why he cried and laughed, and he recounts that the Holy One, blessed be He, offered to restart the world so he might be born in a time of sustenance.
Rabbi Elazar questions whether such suffering is possible, and after God confirms his suffering is greater, he declines the offer to restart the world.
God promises Rabbi Elazar thirteen rivers of pure balsam oil in the World to Come as a reward for his refusal, and when Rabbi Elazar asks for more, God rebukes him with a slap.

items.text: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's prayer for rain
items.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's prayer for rain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina decreed a fast but no rain came. The people compared him to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who succeeded. He humbly said he was not like the son of Levi. They tried to focus their hearts, but still no rain. He then commanded the sky to cover its face, and after a moment of resistance, rain came.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Chama bar Chanina decreed a fast but no rain came.
The people object that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi succeeded in bringing rain through his fast.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's humble response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's humble response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina humbly says he is not comparable to the son of Levi (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi).
The people suggest that they try to focus their hearts together, hoping the community's repentance will bring rain.
They prayed but still no rain came.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina asks the people if they are willing for rain to come on their account, and they answer yes.
He commands the sky to cover its face; after initial resistance, the sky complies and rain comes.

items.text: Levi's harsh prayer and its consequence
items.text_en: Levi's harsh prayer and its consequence
items.desc_en: Levi decreed a fast but no rain came. He complained to God, saying He sits in heaven and does not have mercy. Rain came, but Levi became lame. Rabbi Elazar comments that one should never speak harshly to heaven, as a great man did so and became lame. The Gemara notes that Levi also became lame from bowing before Rabbi, so both caused his lameness.

sub.desc_en: Levi decreed a fast but no rain came, and he complained harshly to God.
Rain came, but Levi became lame as a consequence.
Rabbi Elazar teaches that one should never speak harshly to heaven, citing Levi as an example.
The Gemara objects that Levi's lameness might have been caused by bowing before Rabbi, not by his harsh prayer.
The Gemara resolves that both causes — the harsh prayer and the bowing — contributed to his lameness.

items.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Lulyani diverts the clouds
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Lulyani diverts the clouds
