items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Lulyani heard clouds discussing bringing rain to Ammon and Moab. He protested to God that when the Torah was given, those nations rejected it, so why should they receive rain? He commanded the clouds to pour rain here instead, and they did.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Lulyani overhears clouds discussing bringing rain to Ammon and Moab.
Rabbi Chiya protests to God that since the nations rejected the Torah, they should not receive rain.
Rabbi Chiya commands the clouds to pour rain here instead, and they comply.

items.text: Derasha on the righteous as a palm and cedar
items.text_en: Derasha on the righteous as a palm and cedar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Lulyani begins a derasha on the verse 'The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree; he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.' He explains that if only the palm were mentioned, one might think the righteous have no replacement, so the cedar is mentioned.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Lulyani opens a derasha on the verse 'The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree; he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon,' questioning why both similes are needed and suggesting that if only the palm were mentioned, one might think the righteous have no replacement.

items.text: Clarification of the cedar metaphor
items.text_en: Clarification of the cedar metaphor
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a cedar tree regenerates from its stump, citing a baraita that says it does not. It resolves that the verse refers to other types of cedars, as taught by Rabbah bar Huna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse's metaphor: a cedar without renewal would imply the righteous have no renewal, and a palm without fruit would imply the righteous bear no fruit.
The Gemara objects: does a cedar regenerate from its stump? A baraita states that for cedars and palms one must dig below and uproot, because they do not regenerate.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rabbah bar Huna
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rabbah bar Huna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the verse refers to other types of cedars, as taught by Rabbah bar Huna that there are ten species of cedar.

items.text: Stories of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva's prayers for rain
items.text_en: Stories of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva's prayers for rain
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Eliezer decreed thirteen fasts without rain, and when the people began to leave, he rebuked them, causing rain. Another story tells that Rabbi Eliezer prayed twenty-four blessings without success, but Rabbi Akiva's prayer was answered, and a heavenly voice explained that Rabbi Akiva was more forgiving.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a story of Rabbi Eliezer decreeing thirteen fasts without rain, and when the people began to leave, he rebuked them, causing rain to fall.

A second story recounts that Rabbi Eliezer prayed twenty-four blessings without success, but Rabbi Akiva's prayer was answered, and a heavenly voice (בת קול) explained that Rabbi Akiva was more forgiving.

items.text: How much rain is enough to break the fast
items.text_en: How much rain is enough to break the fast
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute about how much rain must fall for the community to stop fasting: Rabbi Meir says enough to fill a plow's knee, while the Sages give different measures for different soil types. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that for every handbreadth above ground, the deep brings up three handbreadths, and the Gemara resolves a contradiction about two handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking how much rain must fall for the community to cease fasting, and records Rabbi Meir's view: enough to fill the knee of a plow.
The Sages give different measures for three soil types: a handbreadth for dry soil, two for medium, and three for tilled soil.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that for every handbreadth of rain above ground, the deep brings up three handbreadths.
The Gemara objects: a baraita elsewhere says only two handbreadths, contradicting Rabbi Shimon's three.
The Gemara resolves: the two-handbreadth baraita refers to tilled soil, while Rabbi Shimon's three-handbreadth measure applies to untilled soil.

items.text: The deeps call to each other during the water libation
items.text_en: The deeps call to each other during the water libation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that during the water libation on Sukkot, the upper and lower deeps call to each other. Rabbah adds that he saw a creature between the deeps that commands them to release their waters.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that during the water libation (ניסוך המים) on Sukkot, the upper deep calls to the lower deep to release its waters, citing the verse 'תְּהוֹם אֶל תְּהוֹם קוֹרֵא' (deep calls to deep).

Rabbah testifies that he personally saw a creature (רידיא) standing between the upper and lower deeps, which commands each deep to release its waters, citing the verse 'הַנִּצָּנִים נִרְאוּ בָּאָרֶץ' (the blossoms appear in the land).

items.text: When to complete a fast if rain falls
items.text_en: When to complete a fast if rain falls
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute about when rain must fall to exempt from completing the fast: before sunrise (Rabbi Meir), before noon (Rabbi Judah), before the ninth hour (Rabbi Yose). Stories follow about Rabbi Judah the Prince and Samuel the Small applying these rules, with Samuel explaining that early rain is like a servant receiving a favor quietly, while late rain is like one who suffers first.

sub.desc_en: A baraita (תנו רבנן) opens the section with the dispute: if rain falls before sunrise or before noon, according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah, the fast is not completed or is completed, respectively.
Rabbi Yose adds his opinion that the critical time is the ninth hour, and he cites the precedent of King Ahab who fasted from the ninth hour onward as a proof-text.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Judah the Prince
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Judah the Prince
sub.desc_en: A story about Rabbi Judah the Prince who decreed a fast and rain fell after sunrise; he thought to complete the fast, but Rabbi Ammi corrected him: we learn the rule from 'before noon' or 'after noon', not from sunrise.

A story about Samuel the Small: he decreed a fast, rain fell before sunrise, and the people attributed it to the community's merit. Samuel explained the parable of a servant who receives a favor before troubling his master.

sub.text: Second story about Samuel the Small
sub.text_en: Second story about Samuel the Small
sub.desc_en: Another story: rain fell after sunset, and again the people praised the community; Samuel explained this time a parable of a servant who must suffer first before receiving.
The gemara clarifies what would constitute 'the community's merit' for Samuel the Small: if his prayer for wind is instantly answered and rain immediately follows.

items.text: Samuel the Small's power and the Hallel question
items.text_en: Samuel the Small's power and the Hallel question
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Samuel the Small's merit was that when he said 'Mashiv HaRuach' the wind blew, and when he said 'Morid HaGeshem' rain came. The final segment begins a story about a fast in Lod and asks why Hallel was not recited initially, with Abaye and Rava answering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What was the nature of Samuel the Small's merit that the community attributed to him?
The Gemara explains: When Samuel the Small said 'Mashiv HaRuach' (He causes the wind to blow), the wind blew; when he said 'Morid HaGeshem' (He brings down the rain), rain came.
The Gemara asks: In the story of the fast in Lod, why did they not recite Hallel (the praise psalms) from the outset?
Abaye and Rava both answer: Because Hallel is not recited on a communal fast day.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous sugya: fasting on a full stomach
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous sugya: fasting on a full stomach
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction about fasting on a full stomach by distinguishing the people of Machoza, who are accustomed to drunkenness, thus allowing them to eat after rain falls.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the ruling that one may not fast on a full stomach, citing Rav Pappa's practice of allowing eating after rain fell.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the people of Machoza, who are accustomed to drunkenness, thus allowing them to eat after rain falls.

items.text: Transition: Hadran on the chapter
items.text_en: Transition: Hadran on the chapter
items.desc_en: A brief formulaic conclusion to the previous chapter, marking the end of the discussion on the order of fasts.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the previous chapter with the standard formulaic 'Hadran' statement.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Priestly blessing four times a day
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Priestly blessing four times a day
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in three periods of the year—fasts, ma'amadot, and Yom Kippur—the priests bless the people four times daily: at Shacharit, Musaf, Minchah, and Ne'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that in three periods of the year—fasts, ma'amadot, and Yom Kippur—the priests perform the priestly blessing (נשיאת כפים) four times daily: at Shacharit, Musaf, Minchah, and Ne'ilah.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of ma'amadot and their institution
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of ma'amadot and their institution
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the rationale for ma'amadot: since a person's offering is brought while he is not present, the early prophets instituted 24 watches, each with a ma'amad of priests, Levites, and Israelites in Jerusalem. The Israelites in the watch would gather in their towns and read from Genesis, fasting four days a week, except on Shabbat eve and Sunday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the ma'amadot and asks how a person's offering can be brought when he is not present.
The early prophets instituted 24 watches, each with a ma'amad of priests, Levites, and Israelites in Jerusalem.
When the watch's time arrives, priests and Levites go up to Jerusalem, while Israelites gather in their towns, read from Genesis, and fast four days a week, except on Shabbat eve and Sunday.

items.text: Mishnah: Torah reading schedule for ma'amadot
items.text_en: Mishnah: Torah reading schedule for ma'amadot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details the specific portions of Genesis read each day of the week, and the procedure for reading: a large portion is read by two, a small one by one, at Shacharit and Musaf; at Minchah they read by heart like the Shema; on Shabbat eve at Minchah they do not enter due to Shabbat honor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the Torah portions from Genesis read each day of the week for the ma'amadot.

The Mishnah details the reading procedure: a large portion is read by two, a small one by one, at Shacharit and Musaf; at Minchah they read by heart like the Shema; on Shabbat eve at Minchah they do not enter due to Shabbat honor.

items.text: Mishnah and dispute: Exceptions for Hallel and additional offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah and dispute: Exceptions for Hallel and additional offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on a day with Hallel there is no ma'amad at Shacharit, with a Musaf offering no Ne'ilah, with a wood-offering no Minchah. Ben Azzai reports that Rabbi Yehoshua taught the opposite: Musaf offering cancels Minchah, wood-offering cancels Ne'ilah. Rabbi Akiva then retracted to agree with Ben Azzai.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: a day with Hallel cancels the ma'amad at Shacharit, a Musaf offering cancels Ne'ilah, and a wood-offering cancels Minchah, attributed to Rabbi Akiva.
Ben Azzai reports that Rabbi Yehoshua taught the opposite pairing: Musaf offering cancels Minchah, wood-offering cancels Ne'ilah.
Rabbi Akiva retracted his original position and adopted the version of Ben Azzai.

items.text: Mishnah: Times for wood-offerings and their impact on ma'amad
items.text_en: Mishnah: Times for wood-offerings and their impact on ma'amad
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists nine times for the wood-offering of priests and people, including specific dates and families. On the first of Tevet, there is no ma'amad because it includes Hallel, a Musaf offering, and a wood-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the nine times for the wood-offering of priests and people, beginning with the first of Nisan and the family of Arach ben Yehuda, and including priests, Levites, and those who erred in their tribe.
The Mishnah continues listing the remaining dates, culminating with the first of Tevet, on which there is no ma'amad because it includes Hallel, a Musaf offering, and a wood-offering.

items.text: Transition to the next Mishnah: Five events on 17 Tammuz and 9 Av
items.text_en: Transition to the next Mishnah: Five events on 17 Tammuz and 9 Av
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing the five calamities that occurred to our ancestors on the 17th of Tammuz and five on the 9th of Av, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that five calamities befell our ancestors on the 17th of Tammuz and five on the 9th of Av.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Five calamities on the Seventeenth of Tammuz and the Ninth of Av
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Five calamities on the Seventeenth of Tammuz and the Ninth of Av
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the five events that occurred on the Seventeenth of Tammuz (breaking of the tablets, cessation of the daily offering, breaching of the city, Apostomos burning the Torah, and placing an idol in the Temple) and the five on the Ninth of Av (decree against the generation of the wilderness, destruction of both Temples, capture of Betar, and plowing of the city).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the five calamities on the Seventeenth of Tammuz and the five on the Ninth of Av.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of the period leading to Tisha B'Av and the joy of the fifteenth of Av
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of the period leading to Tisha B'Av and the joy of the fifteenth of Av
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when Av begins, joy is diminished; on the Shabbat that includes Tisha B'Av, one may not cut hair or wash clothes; on Thursday it is permitted for the honor of Shabbat. On the eve of Tisha B'Av, one may not eat two cooked dishes, meat, or drink wine. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says one should change one's routine; Rabbi Yehuda requires overturning the bed, but the Sages did not agree.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that when Av begins, joy is diminished, and on the Shabbat containing Tisha B'Av, haircutting and laundering are forbidden, but on Thursday they are permitted for Shabbat honor.
The Mishnah rules that on the eve of Tisha B'Av, one may not eat two cooked dishes, meat, or drink wine.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says one should change one's routine on the eve of Tisha B'Av.
Rabbi Yehuda requires overturning the bed, but the Sages did not agree with him.

items.text: Mishnah: The fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur as joyous days
items.text_en: Mishnah: The fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur as joyous days
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel declares that there were no better days for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur, when the daughters of Jerusalem would go out in borrowed white garments to avoid shaming those without, and dance in the vineyards, saying: 'Young man, lift your eyes and see what you choose for yourself; do not look at beauty but at family.' The Gemara adds a verse about the giving of the Torah and the building of the Temple.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel declares that there were no better days for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur, when the daughters of Jerusalem would go out in borrowed white garments to avoid shaming those without, and all garments require immersion.

The Mishnah describes how the daughters of Jerusalem would dance in the vineyards, saying to the young men to choose based on family rather than beauty, and cites verses about the fear of God and praise of a virtuous woman.

The Gemara adds a verse about the giving of the Torah and the building of the Temple, interpreting 'the day of his wedding' as the giving of the Torah and 'the day of the joy of his heart' as the building of the Temple.

items.text: Gemara: Textual difficulty and resolution regarding the Mishnah's list
items.text_en: Gemara: Textual difficulty and resolution regarding the Mishnah's list
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that priests raise their hands at three times of the year: fasts, ma'amadot, and Yom Kippur. It notes that fasts and ma'amadot do not have a Musaf prayer, so the Mishnah must be missing text. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah actually means: at three times priests raise their hands whenever they pray, and there are four times a day (Shacharit, Musaf, Minchah, and Ne'ilah), and these are the three times: fasts, ma'amadot, and Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's list, noting that fasts and ma'amadot have no Musaf prayer, so the Mishnah's mention of them in a context of four prayer times is problematic.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is missing text and actually means: at three times priests raise their hands whenever they pray, and there are four times a day (Shacharit, Musaf, Minchah, and Ne'ilah), and these are the three times: fasts, ma'amadot, and Yom Kippur.

items.text: Debate: Which prayers include priestly blessing?
items.text_en: Debate: Which prayers include priestly blessing?
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada bar Avuha cites Rabbi Meir that all four prayers include the blessing, but the Sages (identified as Rabbi Yehuda) say only Shacharit and Musaf include it, while Minchah and Ne'ilah do not. Rabbi Yosei says Ne'ilah includes it but Minchah does not. The Gemara explains their reasoning: Rabbi Meir holds that the usual reason for not raising hands at Minchah (drunkenness) does not apply on fast days; Rabbi Yehuda holds that the rabbis decreed only where drunkenness is common; Rabbi Yosei holds that Minchah, which occurs daily, was decreed upon, but Ne'ilah, which is rare, was not.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada bar Avuha citing Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada bar Avuha citing Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada bar Avuha attributes the Mishnah's view to Rabbi Meir, while the Sages (identified as Rabbi Yehuda) limit the priestly blessing to Shacharit and Musaf only.
The Gemara identifies the Sages as Rabbi Yehuda and cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei each state their positions on which prayers include the priestly blessing.
The Gemara asks what is the basis of their dispute.
Rabbi Meir holds that the usual reason for not raising hands at Minchah — drunkenness — does not apply on fast days.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that the rabbis decreed against the priestly blessing only where drunkenness is common — at Minchah and Ne'ilah — but not at Shacharit and Musaf.
Rabbi Yosei holds that the rabbis decreed only on Minchah, which occurs daily, but not on Ne'ilah, which is rare.

items.text: Halachic rulings and the practice regarding Minchah on fast days
items.text_en: Halachic rulings and the practice regarding Minchah on fast days
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that the halacha follows Rabbi Meir; Rabbi Yochanan said the people practice like Rabbi Meir; Rava said it is a custom like Rabbi Meir. The Gemara explains the differences: 'halacha' means we teach it in public; 'custom' means we instruct but do not teach; 'people practice' means we do not instruct but if one does it, we do not object. Rav Nachman rules that the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei, and the Gemara explains that today priests raise their hands at Minchah on fast days because it is close to sunset and resembles Ne'ilah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Meir regarding priestly blessing at Minchah on fast days.
Rabbi Yochanan states that the people practice (נָהֲגוּ) according to Rabbi Meir's opinion.
Rava declares that the custom (מִנְהָג) follows Rabbi Meir.

The Gemara explains the practical difference between the three formulations: 'הלכה' means we teach it publicly in the study hall; 'מנהג' means we instruct but do not teach publicly; 'נהגו' means we do not instruct but do not object if one performs it.
Rav Nachman rules that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yosei, who permits priestly blessing at Ne'ilah but not at Minchah.
The Gemara explains that today priests raise their hands at Minchah on fast days because it is close to sunset and thus resembles the Ne'ilah prayer, which is permitted even according to Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Prohibition of a drunk priest from raising his hands
items.text_en: Prohibition of a drunk priest from raising his hands
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that a drunk priest is forbidden from raising his hands. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara derives this from the juxtaposition of the priestly blessing section to the nazirite section: just as a nazirite is forbidden wine, so a priest is forbidden wine. An objection is raised that a nazirite is also forbidden grape seeds, but Rabbi Yitzchak answers that the verse 'to serve and to bless in His name' teaches that just as a server (priest in the Temple) is permitted grape seeds, so a priest blessing is permitted grape seeds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that all agree a drunk priest is forbidden from raising his hands (נשיאת כפים).
The Gemara asks: what is the source for this prohibition?

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara answers: the section of the priestly blessing is juxtaposed to the nazirite section, teaching that just as a nazirite is forbidden wine, so a priest blessing is forbidden wine.

sub.text: Avuha deRabbi Zeira (or Oshaya bar Zavda)
sub.text_en: Avuha deRabbi Zeira (or Oshaya bar Zavda)
sub.desc_en: Avuha deRabbi Zeira (or Oshaya bar Zavda) objects: if the analogy is exact, just as a nazirite is forbidden grape seeds (חרצן), so a priest blessing should be forbidden grape seeds.

Rabbi Yitzchak resolves the objection: the verse 'לשרתו ולברך בשמו' (to serve and to bless in His name) teaches that just as a server (priest in the Temple) is permitted grape seeds, so a priest blessing is permitted grape seeds.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the priestly blessing
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the priestly blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if a blemished priest cannot serve, he also cannot bless, but this is refuted by linking the blessing to the nazirite rather than to service. The Gemara then notes that the derivation is a rabbinic support and is treated leniently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if a blemished priest cannot serve, he also cannot bless, but notes that the blessing is linked to the nazirite rather than to service.
The Gemara resolves that the derivation is a rabbinic support (אסמכתא) and is treated leniently.

items.text: Introduction to the ma'amadot
items.text_en: Introduction to the ma'amadot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah explains that ma'amadot were instituted because the Torah says 'Command the children of Israel... My offering, My bread,' and since a person's sacrifice is offered without him being present, the early prophets instituted twenty-four watches, each with a ma'amad in Jerusalem of priests, Levites, and Israelites.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the ma'amadot and cites the verse 'Command the children of Israel... My offering, My bread' as the scriptural basis.

The Mishnah explains that since a person's sacrifice is offered without him present, the early prophets instituted twenty-four watches, each with a ma'amad in Jerusalem of priests, Levites, and Israelites.

items.text: Baraita on the distribution of watches
items.text_en: Baraita on the distribution of watches
items.desc_en: A baraita states that there were twenty-four watches in Eretz Yisrael and twelve in Jericho, but the Gemara corrects that twelve of them were in Jericho. Half the watch would go up from Eretz Yisrael and half from Jericho to provide water and food for their brethren in Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that there were twenty-four watches in Eretz Yisrael and twelve in Jericho.
The Gemara objects that twelve watches in Jericho alone would be far too many.
The Gemara corrects that twelve of the total watches were in Jericho, with half the watch going up from Eretz Yisrael and half from Jericho to provide water and food for their brethren in Jerusalem.

items.text: Dispute about what is essential for the sacrifice
items.text_en: Dispute about what is essential for the sacrifice
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says that priests, Levites, and Israelites are essential for the sacrifice. In a baraita, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says that priests, Levites, and musical instruments are essential. The Gemara explains that they disagree about whether the essence of song is vocal or instrumental.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that priests, Levites, and Israelites are essential for the sacrifice.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: A baraita taught by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that priests, Levites, and musical instruments are essential for the sacrifice.
The Gemara explains that the dispute is about whether the essence of song is vocal (requiring Israelites) or instrumental (requiring instruments).

items.text: Rav's tradition on the development of the watches
items.text_en: Rav's tradition on the development of the watches
items.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya in the name of Rav says that Moses instituted eight watches for Israel, four from Elazar and four from Itamar. Samuel later established them as sixteen, and David established them as twenty-four, as per the verse.

sub.text: Rav Chama bar Gurya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya reports Rav's tradition that Moses instituted eight priestly watches, Samuel expanded them to sixteen, and David to twenty-four, citing a verse.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says Moses instituted eight watches, and David and Samuel established them as twenty-four. Rav Chama bar Gurya explains that the baraita means that from the foundation of David and Samuel they were established as twenty-four.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states David and Samuel together established the twenty-four watches, contradicting Rav's claim that Samuel only set sixteen.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita means the twenty-four watches were established from the foundation laid by David and Samuel, not that Samuel personally set sixteen.

items.text: Another baraita and resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Another baraita and resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that Moses instituted sixteen watches, eight from Elazar and eight from Itamar, and when the sons of Elazar increased, they divided them into twenty-four. The Gemara explains the verse and concludes that this refutes Rav Chama bar Gurya, who responds that it is a dispute among Tannaim and he follows the one who says eight.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Moses instituted sixteen watches, eight from Elazar and eight from Itamar, and when the sons of Elazar increased, they divided them into twenty-four, citing a verse.

The Gemara asks why the baraita adds a second verse, and explains that it preempts a possible claim that the sons of Itamar also increased, then cites the verse as proof that the original count was four for Itamar.
The Gemara declares that this baraita refutes Rav Chama bar Gurya's position that Moses instituted only eight watches.
Rav Chama bar Gurya responds that the dispute is among Tannaim, and he follows the Tanna who says eight watches.

items.text: Baraita on the watches that returned from the exile
items.text_en: Baraita on the watches that returned from the exile
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the four watches that came up from the exile: Yedaiah, Charim, Pashchur, and Immer. The prophets among them established additional watches.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the four priestly watches that returned from the Babylonian exile, and notes that the prophets among them expanded the system.

items.text: Arrangement of the priestly watches
items.text_en: Arrangement of the priestly watches
items.desc_en: The mishnah describes how the twenty-four priestly watches were divided and placed in a lottery, with Yedayah taking six shares, and the prophets stipulating that even if Yehoiarib returns, Yedayah remains primary.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah describes the lottery dividing the twenty-four priestly watches, with Yedayah taking six shares and others following similarly.
The prophets stipulated that even if Yehoiarib returns, Yedayah remains primary and Yehoiarib is secondary.

items.text: Scriptural basis for the ma'amadot
items.text_en: Scriptural basis for the ma'amadot
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the ma'amadot are essential for the world's existence, citing a dialogue between Abraham and God where God promises that reading the order of sacrifices substitutes for actual offerings when the Temple is not standing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the practice of the ma'amadot and asks for its source, citing Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha quoting Rav Asi that without ma'amadot heaven and earth would not endure, and citing the verse where Abraham asks God for assurance.
Abraham asks God whether Israel will be destroyed if they sin, and requests to know by what merit they will inherit the land.
God responds that when the Temple stands, sacrifices atone; when it does not, reading the order of sacrifices is credited as if they were offered, and God forgives their sins.

items.text: Fasts of the ma'amad
items.text_en: Fasts of the ma'amad
items.desc_en: A baraisa details that the men of the ma'amad fast four days a week: Monday for seafarers, Tuesday for desert travelers, Wednesday for children's croup, and Thursday for pregnant and nursing women, but not on Friday or Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa opens by stating that the men of the ma'amad (מעמד) would pray for their brothers' sacrifice to be accepted and would gather for four fasts on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday, with Monday's fast for seafarers and Tuesday's for desert travelers.

The baraisa continues with Wednesday's fast for croup (אסכרא) not to fall on children, Thursday's fast for pregnant and nursing women, and explains that they did not fast on Friday due to Shabbat honor, and certainly not on Shabbat itself.

items.text: Reason for not fasting on Sunday
items.text_en: Reason for not fasting on Sunday
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why they do not fast on Sunday, and three answers are given: Rabbi Yochanan says because of the Christians, Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says because it is the third day after creation, and Resh Lakish says because of the extra soul given on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the ma'amad does not fast on Sunday (the first day of the week).
Rabbi Yochanan answers that Sunday is avoided because of the Christians (נוצרים), who might misinterpret the fast as honoring their day of worship.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani answers that Sunday is the third day after creation, and fasting on it would be inappropriate because it is associated with the creation of the world.

Resh Lakish answers that Sunday is avoided because of the extra soul (נשמה יתירה) given on Shabbat, which departs at the end of Shabbat, and fasting on Sunday would be inappropriate as the soul is still weakened.

items.text: Reading of the Torah on the first day
items.text_en: Reading of the Torah on the first day
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that on the first day they read 'Bereishit' and 'Yehi Rakia', with a baraisa stating that 'Bereishit' is read by two and 'Yehi Rakia' by one, raising the question of how to handle the five verses of 'Bereishit' when the minimum is three.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the Torah reading for the first day: 'Bereishit' and 'Yehi Rakia', with 'Bereishit' read by two and 'Yehi Rakia' by one.
The Gemara notes that 'Yehi Rakia' has three verses, so one reader is fine.
The Gemara asks why 'Bereishit' requires two readers, since it has five verses.
The Gemara cites a baraita that a Torah reader must read no fewer than three verses, explaining why five verses cannot be split as 2 and 3.

items.text: Debate: skipping versus breaking verses
items.text_en: Debate: skipping versus breaking verses
items.desc_en: Rav says one may skip verses, while Shmuel says one may break a verse. The Gemara explains their reasoning: Rav holds that we cannot break a verse that Moses did not break, while Shmuel argues that it is necessary to avoid confusion for those entering and leaving.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that one may skip verses, while Shmuel states that one may break a verse.
The Gemara asks why Rav does not adopt Shmuel's position of breaking a verse.
The Gemara explains that Rav holds we cannot break a verse that Moses did not break.
The Gemara objects to Shmuel by citing Rabbi Chanina's statement that breaking a verse was only permitted for schoolchildren.
The Gemara defends Shmuel by arguing that just as breaking a verse was necessary for children, here too it is necessary to avoid confusion.
The Gemara asks why Shmuel does not adopt Rav's position of skipping verses.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel rejects skipping because it would cause confusion for those entering and leaving the synagogue.

items.text: Challenge from a baraisa
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraisa
items.desc_en: A baraisa is brought that discusses how to read a parashah of six or five verses, and the Gemara challenges both Rav and Shmuel: why not skip or break? The Gemara answers that the case there is different.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa is cited that prescribes how to read a parashah of six or five verses, with an alternative opinion about the minimum number of verses to begin a parashah.
The Gemara objects: according to the one who says skip (דולג) or the one who says break (פוסק), why not apply that method here?
The Gemara resolves that the case there is different, implying the baraisa's scenario does not apply to the ma'amadot reading.

items.text: Reading the Torah portion on fast days
items.text_en: Reading the Torah portion on fast days
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the Mishnah's statement regarding the reading of the large portion on fast days: whether it is read from a scroll in the morning and musaf, and by heart in the afternoon, or only in the morning from a scroll, and in musaf and afternoon by heart. A baraita is brought to resolve this, with Rabbi Yosei objecting to an individual reading Torah by heart in public, concluding that all read it by heart like the Shema.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the second reader has space to read from the ensuing paragraph.

The Gemara raises a dilemma about the Mishnah's statement: whether the large portion is read from a scroll in the morning and musaf, and by heart in the afternoon, or only in the morning from a scroll, and in musaf and afternoon by heart.
A baraita is brought to resolve the dilemma, stating that in the morning and musaf they read from a scroll, but in the afternoon an individual reads by heart.
Rabbi Yosei objects to the baraita, questioning whether an individual can read Torah by heart in public.
Rabbi Yosei concludes that all enter and read the portion by heart together, like the recitation of Shema.

items.text: Distinction between Hallel and Ma'amad
items.text_en: Distinction between Hallel and Ma'amad
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any day with Hallel has no Ma'amad. The Gemara explains the difference: these are words of Torah, and those are words of the Scribes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any day with Hallel has no Ma'amad.
The Gemara asks what is the difference between these two categories.
The Gemara explains that the days with Hallel are words of Torah, while those with Ma'amad are words of the Scribes.

items.text: Reason for the wood-offering times
items.text_en: Reason for the wood-offering times
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the times for the wood-offering of priests and people were instituted: when the exiles returned, they found no wood in the chamber and donated their own. The prophets stipulated that even if the chamber is full, these families should donate, as per the verse in Nehemiah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the times for the wood-offering of priests and people were instituted, and answers that when the exiles returned they found no wood in the chamber and these families donated their own.
The baraita adds that the prophets stipulated that even if the chamber is full, these families should donate, as per the verse in Nehemiah.

items.text: Stories of the families Gonvei Eli and Kotzei Ketzi'ot
items.text_en: Stories of the families Gonvei Eli and Kotzei Ketzi'ot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who were the families Gonvei Eli and Kotzei Ketzi'ot. It relates how during a wicked kingdom's decree against bringing wood and first fruits, the righteous disguised first fruits in baskets covered with dried figs, and wood as ladders for doves, to smuggle them to Jerusalem. The verse praises them as righteous, while Jeroboam and his associates are cursed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who were the families Gonvei Eli and Kotzei Ketzi'ot.
The Sages relate how the righteous smuggled first fruits to Jerusalem by covering them with dried figs and carrying them on a עֱלִי (yoke).
A baraita tells a parallel story of the family Salmai HaNetofati, who smuggled wood to Jerusalem by disguising it as ladders for doves.

The Gemara concludes that the verse praises these righteous families with 'זֵכֶר צַדִּיק לִבְרָכָה' (the memory of the righteous is a blessing) and curses Jeroboam and his associates with 'וְשֵׁם רְשָׁעִים יִרְקָב' (the name of the wicked shall rot).

items.text: Identity of Benei Pachat Moav ben Yehuda
items.text_en: Identity of Benei Pachat Moav ben Yehuda
items.desc_en: A baraita identifies Benei Pachat Moav ben Yehuda as Benei David ben Yehuda according to Rabbi Meir, while Rabbi Yosei says they are Benei Yoav ben Tzeruya.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on the twentieth of the month, the family of Benei Pachat Moav ben Yehuda brought wood.
A baraita identifies Benei Pachat Moav ben Yehuda as Benei David ben Yehuda according to Rabbi Meir, while Rabbi Yosei says they are Benei Yoav ben Tzeruya.

items.text: Identity of Benei Adin ben Yehuda
items.text_en: Identity of Benei Adin ben Yehuda
items.desc_en: A baraita identifies Benei Adin ben Yehuda as Benei David ben Yehuda according to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Yosei says they are Benei Yoav ben Tzeruya.

sub.desc_en: A baraita identifies Benei Adin ben Yehuda as Benei David ben Yehuda according to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Yosei says they are Benei Yoav ben Tzeruya.

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with the opinions
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with the opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whose opinion the Mishnah follows regarding Benei Parosh on the first of Tevet, as it does not match Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, or Rabbi Yosei. It concludes that it is always Rabbi Yosei, and there are two tannaim who support his view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishnah follows regarding Benei Parosh on the first of Tevet, noting it does not match Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, or Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah followed Rabbi Meir, it would have said 'Benei David ben Yehuda' instead of 'Benei Parosh'.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah followed Rabbi Yehuda, it would also have said 'Benei David ben Yehuda'.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah followed Rabbi Yosei, it would have said 'Benei Yoav ben Tzeruya'.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah always follows Rabbi Yosei, and there are two tannaim who support his view, explaining the discrepancy in the name.

items.text: Question about the first of Tevet
items.text_en: Question about the first of Tevet
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on the first of Tevet there was no Ma'amad. Mar Kashisha, son of Rav Chisda, asks Rav Ashi a question about this.

sub.text: Mar Kashisha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Kashisha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha, son of Rav Chisda, asks Rav Ashi about the Mishnah's statement that on the first of Tevet there was no Ma'amad.

items.text: Gemara's question about Hallel and Musaf on Rosh Chodesh
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Hallel and Musaf on Rosh Chodesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Hallel, which is not a biblical obligation, overrides the Ma'amad, while Musaf, which is biblical, does not. Rav Ashi responds that if even the non-biblical Hallel overrides, certainly the biblical Musaf should not. The Gemara then cites Rabbi Yosei's opinion that any day with Musaf has a Ma'amad, implying that Hallel overrides the Ma'amad for Ne'ilah, not Musaf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Hallel, which is not a biblical obligation, overrides the Ma'amad, while Musaf, which is biblical, does not.
Rav Ashi responds that if even the non-biblical Hallel overrides, certainly the biblical Musaf should not.
The interlocutor clarifies that his point is that only the non-biblical Hallel should override, not the biblical Musaf.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's citation of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's citation of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites Rabbi Yosei's baraita that any day with Musaf has a Ma'amad, and then questions whether the Ma'amad of Musaf itself is overridden.
The Gemara concludes that the Ma'amad in question is for Ne'ilah, proving that Hallel overrides its own Ma'amad but not others.

items.text: Rava's deduction that Hallel on Rosh Chodesh is not biblical
items.text_en: Rava's deduction that Hallel on Rosh Chodesh is not biblical
items.desc_en: Rava argues that if Hallel on Rosh Chodesh were biblical, the Mishnah would have listed it as a reason for no Ma'amad on the first of Nisan, alongside Musaf and the wood-offering. Since it does not, this proves Hallel on Rosh Chodesh is not a Torah obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not also list Hallel as a reason for no Ma'amad on the first of Nisan, alongside Musaf and the wood-offering.
Rava answers that the omission proves that Hallel on Rosh Chodesh is not a Torah obligation (דאורייתא), only a rabbinic custom.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's list of days for full Hallel
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's list of days for full Hallel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak, lists the eighteen days in the Land of Israel and twenty-one in the diaspora when an individual recites the full Hallel. Rosh Chodesh is not included, supporting Rava's claim that Hallel on Rosh Chodesh is not biblical.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak, lists the eighteen days in the Land of Israel and twenty-one in the diaspora when an individual recites the full Hallel, excluding Rosh Chodesh.

items.text: Rav's observation of Hallel recitation in Babylonia
items.text_en: Rav's observation of Hallel recitation in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Rav visited Babylonia and saw people reciting Hallel on Rosh Chodesh. He initially wanted to stop them, but when he saw they were skipping verses, he concluded it is a custom of their ancestors. The Gemara adds that an individual should not begin Hallel on Rosh Chodesh, but if he began, he finishes.

sub.desc_en: Rav visited Babylonia and saw people reciting Hallel on Rosh Chodesh.
Rav initially wanted to stop them from reciting Hallel.
When Rav saw they were skipping verses, he concluded it is a custom of their ancestors.
The Gemara adds a baraita that an individual should not begin Hallel on Rosh Chodesh, but if he began, he finishes.

items.text: Source for the breaking of the tablets on the 17th of Tammuz
items.text_en: Source for the breaking of the tablets on the 17th of Tammuz
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the source for the breaking of the tablets on the 17th of Tammuz. It cites a dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the first Tanna about whether the Ten Commandments were given on the 6th or 7th of Sivan. According to the view that they were given on the 7th, Moses ascended on the 7th and descended on the 17th of Tammuz, breaking the tablets.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that the tablets were broken on the 17th of Tammuz?
A baraita is cited: the Ten Commandments were given on the 6th of Sivan (first Tanna) or the 7th (Rabbi Yosei); according to the first Tanna, Moses ascended on the 7th.
The Gemara explains: according to the view that the Torah was given on the 7th, Moses ascended on the 7th and, after 40 days (24 of Sivan + 16 of Tammuz), descended on the 17th of Tammuz.
The Gemara concludes: on the 17th of Tammuz Moses descended and broke the tablets, as the verse states.

items.text: Source for the cessation of the daily offering
items.text_en: Source for the cessation of the daily offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the source for the cessation of the daily offering on the 17th of Tammuz is a tradition (Gemara).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the source for the cessation of the daily offering on the 17th of Tammuz is a tradition (גמרא).

items.text: Reconciliation of the date of the breaching of Jerusalem's walls
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the date of the breaching of Jerusalem's walls
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says the city was breached on the 17th of Tammuz, when the verse in Jeremiah says it was on the 9th. Rava resolves this by explaining that the first breach was on the 9th (in the First Temple period), but the second breach (in the Second Temple period) was on the 17th.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's date of the 17th of Tammuz for the breaching of Jerusalem, citing the verse in Jeremiah that places it on the 9th.
Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the First Temple period, when the city was breached on the 9th, and the Second Temple period, when it was breached on the 17th.

items.text: Sources for the burning of the Torah and the placement of an idol in the Temple
items.text_en: Sources for the burning of the Torah and the placement of an idol in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the source for Apostomos burning the Torah is a tradition. For the placement of an idol in the Temple, it cites Daniel. It then questions whether there was only one idol, citing another verse that implies multiple idols. Rava explains there were two idols, and one broke the other's hand, revealing an inscription.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the source for Apostomos burning the Torah is a tradition (גמרא).
The Gemara cites a verse from Daniel to prove the placement of an idol in the Temple.
The Gemara questions whether there was only one idol, citing another verse that implies multiple idols.
Rava explains there were two idols, and one broke the other's hand, revealing an inscription.

items.text: Opening statement: the five calamities of Tisha B'Av
items.text_en: Opening statement: the five calamities of Tisha B'Av
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five events that happened on the Ninth of Av: the decree against the wilderness generation, the destruction of both Temples, the fall of Beitar, and the plowing of the city.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a poetic statement attributing the destruction to divine will, then lists the five calamities of Tisha B'Av.

items.text: Derivation of the decree against the wilderness generation
items.text_en: Derivation of the decree against the wilderness generation
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that the spies were sent on the 29th of Sivan, and their return with the bad report led to the people weeping on the night of the Ninth of Av, establishing that date as a time of weeping for generations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that on the Ninth of Av it was decreed that our ancestors would not enter the Land?
Mar establishes the timeline: in the first year Moses built the Tabernacle, in the second he erected it and sent the spies.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains that on that day the people strayed from God, and the verses show that the events culminated on the 22nd of Sivan.
The Gemara calculates that Miriam's seven-day isolation ended on the 29th of Sivan, and then the verse commands sending the spies.
A baraita confirms that the spies were sent on the 29th of Sivan, but the Gemara notes a discrepancy: the forty days of spying would end one day short of the Ninth of Av.
Abaye resolves the discrepancy by explaining that the month of Tammuz that year was made full (29 days), so the spies returned on the 8th of Av.

sub.text: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah citing Rabbi Yochanan states that the night of weeping was the night of the Ninth of Av, and God declared that since they wept for nothing, He would establish that night as a time of weeping for generations.

items.text: The destruction of the First Temple
items.text_en: The destruction of the First Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between verses stating the Temple was burned on the seventh and on the tenth of Av, explaining that the enemies entered on the seventh, desecrated it, and set fire on the ninth. Rabbi Yochanan would have fixed the fast on the tenth, but the Rabbis prioritize the beginning of the calamity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one verse says the First Temple was burned on the seventh of Av, another on the tenth.
A baraita resolves the contradiction: the enemies entered on the seventh, desecrated the Temple on the seventh and eighth, and set fire on the ninth.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the fire was set on the ninth near nightfall and continued burning, so he would have fixed the fast on the tenth, when most of the Temple burned.
The Rabbis reject Rabbi Yochanan's view, ruling that the beginning of the calamity (the ninth) takes precedence for the fast.

items.text: The destruction of the Second Temple
items.text_en: The destruction of the Second Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition that the Second Temple was also destroyed on the Ninth of Av, which was the end of Shabbat, the end of a Sabbatical year, and the week of the priestly watch of Yehoyariv. The Levites were singing a psalm when the enemies came.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the Second Temple was also destroyed on the Ninth of Av, citing a baraita that merit is assigned to a meritorious day and guilt to a guilty day.

The baraita recounts that the First Temple was destroyed on the Ninth of Av, at the end of Shabbat, at the end of a Sabbatical year, during the watch of Yehoyariv, and the Levites were singing a psalm when the enemies came, and the same happened with the Second Temple.

items.text: The fall of Beitar
items.text_en: The fall of Beitar
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly notes that Beitar was captured on the Ninth of Av, citing a tradition (gemara) that this event occurred on that date.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition that Beitar was captured on the Ninth of Av.

items.text: The plowing of the city and the story of the hegemon
items.text_en: The plowing of the city and the story of the hegemon
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that when Turnusrufus plowed the Temple, a decree was issued against Rabban Gamliel. A hegemon helped him escape by jumping off a roof, and a bat kol declared that hegemon merited the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that when Turnusrufus plowed the Temple, a decree was issued to execute Rabban Gamliel.
A hegemon came to the study hall and cryptically announced that the 'man with the nose' was sought, prompting Rabban Gamliel to hide.

sub.text: Dialogue between hegemon and Rabban Gamliel
sub.text_en: Dialogue between hegemon and Rabban Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The hegemon privately asked Rabban Gamliel if he would bring him to the World to Come in exchange for saving him, and Rabban Gamliel swore to do so.
The hegemon climbed to the roof, jumped, and died, because it was known that when a decree is issued and one of the leaders dies, the decree is annulled.
A bat kol (heavenly voice) declared that the hegemon is destined for the World to Come.

items.text: The young priests and the keys of the Temple
items.text_en: The young priests and the keys of the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that after the First Temple's destruction, young priests threw the keys to heaven, a hand received them, and they jumped into the fire. Isaiah lamented over them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that after the First Temple's destruction, young priests gathered on the roof, declared the keys entrusted to God, and threw them upward, where a hand-like form received them.
The baraita continues that the priests then jumped into the fire, and Isaiah lamented over them with a verse describing the city's cries.
The Gemara adds that a verse about God is also applied to this event, describing Him as breaking down the wall and crying out to the mountain.

items.text: The halakha: decreasing joy from Av and increasing from Adar
items.text_en: The halakha: decreasing joy from Av and increasing from Adar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when Av begins, joy is diminished. Rav Yehudah adds that just as joy decreases in Av, it increases when Adar begins.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that when the month of Av begins, one diminishes joy.
Rav Yehudah adds in the name of Rav that just as joy is diminished when Av begins, so too joy is increased when Adar begins.

items.text: Rav Pappa's advice on litigation with a gentile
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's advice on litigation with a gentile
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa advises that a Jew who has a lawsuit with a gentile should avoid him in Av, when the Jew's fortune is weak, and pursue him in Adar, when his fortune is strong.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that a Jew with a lawsuit against a gentile should avoid him in Av (when fortune is weak) and pursue him in Adar (when fortune is strong).

items.text: Interpretation of verses by Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Interpretation of verses by Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav interprets two verses: 'לָתֵת לָכֶם אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה' refers to dates and linen garments, and 'רְאֵה רֵיחַ בְּנִי' refers to the scent of an apple orchard.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav interprets the verse 'לָתֵת לָכֶם אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה' as referring to dates and linen garments.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav interprets the verse 'רְאֵה רֵיחַ בְּנִי' as referring to the scent of an apple orchard.

items.text: Dispute on laundering during the week of Tisha B'Av
items.text_en: Dispute on laundering during the week of Tisha B'Av
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman permits laundering if one does not intend to wear the garment immediately, while Rav Sheshet prohibits even laundering for later use, citing the practice of the house of Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic prohibition: during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, one may not cut hair or launder clothes.
Rav Nachman limits the prohibition: laundering is forbidden only if one intends to wear the garment immediately, but laundering for later use is permitted.
Rav Sheshet objects and prohibits even laundering for later use.
Rav Sheshet supports his position by citing the practice of the house of Rav, where the launderers ceased work entirely during that week.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding laundering on Thursday
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding laundering on Thursday
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges the leniency from a baraita that permits laundering on Thursday for the honor of Shabbat. The Gemara initially assumes this refers to laundering for later use, but resolves that it refers to laundering for immediate wear when one has only one garment, citing Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges the leniency by citing a baraita that permits laundering on Thursday for the honor of Shabbat, questioning whether this refers to laundering for immediate wear.
The Gemara initially assumes the baraita refers to laundering for later use, concluding that only Thursday is permitted but the entire week is forbidden.

sub.text: Gemara's final resolution with support from Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Gemara's final resolution with support from Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to laundering for immediate wear when one has only one garment, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about laundering on חול המועד (intermediate festival days) and Rabbi Elazar's similar distinction.

items.text: Conclusive refutation of Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: Conclusive refutation of Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly prohibits laundering even for later use before Tisha B'Av, and states that our ironing is like their laundering, but linen garments are exempt from ironing. This is a conclusive refutation of Rav Sheshet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that explicitly prohibits laundering even for later use before Tisha B'Av.
The baraita adds that our ironing is like their laundering, but linen garments are exempt from ironing.
The Gemara declares this a conclusive refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of Rav Sheshet's position.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on linen garments
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on linen garments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that although linen garments are exempt from ironing, they are still prohibited to wear during the week of Tisha B'Av.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Giyorei in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Giyorei in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that although linen garments are exempt from ironing, they are still prohibited to wear during the week of Tisha B'Av.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the scope of the prohibition
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the scope of the prohibition
items.desc_en: Rav permits laundering after Tisha B'Av, while Shmuel prohibits it. A baraita is brought that seems to support Rav, detailing the rules based on which day Tisha B'Av falls, and Abaye or Rav Acha bar Yaakov curses the one who permits laundering after Tisha B'Av.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the prohibition of laundering and haircutting applies only before Tisha B'Av, but after it is permitted.
Shmuel objects and rules that even after Tisha B'Av the prohibition continues.
The Gemara cites a baraita that details the rules of laundering based on which day Tisha B'Av falls, which seems to support Rav's position.

The baraita specifies that when Tisha B'Av falls on Sunday through Thursday, laundering is prohibited before but permitted after, and when it falls on Friday, laundering is permitted on Thursday or Friday afternoon.

sub.text: Abaye or Rav Acha bar Yaakov's curse
sub.text_en: Abaye or Rav Acha bar Yaakov's curse
sub.desc_en: Abaye or Rav Acha bar Yaakov curses the one who permits laundering after Tisha B'Av, indicating opposition to Rav's lenient ruling.

items.text: Refutation of Shmuel from the reading of the Torah
items.text_en: Refutation of Shmuel from the reading of the Torah
items.desc_en: A baraita states that when Tisha B'Av falls on Monday or Thursday, three read from the Torah and one is the maftir; on Tuesday or Wednesday, one reads and one is the maftir. Rabbi Yosei says always three read. This refutes Shmuel's position.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the reading rules for Tisha B'Av on different weekdays, with Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei disagreeing.
The gemara declares that this baraita refutes Shmuel's position.

items.text: Shmuel's defense and the tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Shmuel's defense and the tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Shmuel deflects the refutation by claiming it is a dispute among Tannaim. He cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir prohibits from Rosh Chodesh until the fast, Rabbi Yehuda prohibits the entire month, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel prohibits only that week. Rabbi Yochanan explains that all three derive their positions from the same verse.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel deflects the refutation by claiming the prohibition is a dispute among Tannaim.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Meir prohibits from Rosh Chodesh until the fast, Rabbi Yehuda prohibits the entire month, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel prohibits only that week.
A second baraita is cited with the same three positions regarding mourning practices.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that all three Tannaim derive their positions from the same verse, 'וְהִשְׁבַּתִּי כָּל מְשׂוֹשָׂהּ חַגָּהּ חָדְשָׁהּ וְשַׁבַּתָּהּ' (I will cause all her joy to cease, her festival, her new moon, and her Sabbath).

items.text: Rava's ruling on the dispute about the prohibition from the New Moon
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on the dispute about the prohibition from the New Moon
items.desc_en: Rava rules in accordance with both Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Meir, each lenient in different respects, and explains why both rulings are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the scriptural derivations for the two positions regarding the prohibition from the New Moon or the entire week.
Rava rules in accordance with both Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Meir, each lenient in different respects, and explains why both rulings are necessary.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's leniencies regarding the eve of Tisha B'Av
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's leniencies regarding the eve of Tisha B'Av
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda limits the prohibition of eating two cooked dishes to after the sixth hour and to the final meal before the fast, and the Gemara explains why both leniencies are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition of eating two cooked dishes on the eve of Tisha B'Av.
Rav Yehuda limits the prohibition to after the sixth hour, permitting it before then.
Rav Yehuda further limits the prohibition to the final meal before the fast, permitting it in other meals.
The Gemara explains that both leniencies are necessary, as each alone might have been misinterpreted to permit even more.

items.text: Baraitot on the eve of Tisha B'Av restrictions
items.text_en: Baraitot on the eve of Tisha B'Av restrictions
items.desc_en: Three baraitot are cited: one permits meat and wine if one intends to eat another meal, another records the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion, and a third discusses reducing one's usual consumption.

sub.desc_en: A baraita permits meat and wine on the eve of Tisha B'Av only if one intends to eat another meal.

A baraita records the dispute between Rabbi Meir (who forbids two dishes) and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (who requires change), with Rabbi Yehuda's explanation of the change, all limited to after the sixth hour.

A third baraita presents Rabbi Meir's absolute prohibition, the Sages' requirement to reduce meat and wine, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's leniency for those accustomed to radish or salted fish after the meal.

items.text: Baraita on the distinction between Tisha B'Av and other fasts
items.text_en: Baraita on the distinction between Tisha B'Av and other fasts
items.desc_en: A baraita distinguishes between restrictions that are specifically due to Tisha B'Av (meat, wine, bathing) and those that are not, with Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosei adding that bathing is permitted when meat is permitted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that on Tisha B'Av itself, meat, wine, and bathing are forbidden, while on other fasts only bathing is forbidden.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosei citing his father
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosei citing his father
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosei adds in his father's name that whenever meat is permitted, bathing is also permitted.

items.text: Mourning practices on Tisha B'Av and the dispute about Torah study
items.text_en: Mourning practices on Tisha B'Av and the dispute about Torah study
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the mourning practices of Tisha B'Av, including the prohibition of Torah study, with a dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Yehuda about whether one may read in unfamiliar places.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that all mourning practices apply on Tisha B'Av, including prohibitions on eating, drinking, anointing, wearing shoes, marital relations, and Torah study.

The baraita continues with a leniency: one may read in unfamiliar places, read Lamentations, Job, and the harsh passages of Jeremiah, and schoolchildren are dismissed because the precepts of the Lord rejoice the heart.
Rabbi Yehuda disputes the leniency: one may not read even in unfamiliar places, but may read Job, Lamentations, and the harsh passages of Jeremiah, and schoolchildren are dismissed.

items.text: Definitions of salted meat and new wine
items.text_en: Definitions of salted meat and new wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the definitions of salted meat (as long as it is like a peace-offering) and new wine (as long as it is fermenting, which is three days), citing a baraita about wine not being susceptible to exposure during fermentation.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that on the eve of the Ninth of Av, one may eat heavily salted meat and drink wine from the press.
The Gemara asks: For how long must meat be salted to be considered salted meat and thus permitted?

sub.text: Rav Hinana bar Kahana in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Hinana bar Kahana in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Hinana bar Kahana in the name of Shmuel answers: As long as it is like a peace-offering, which may be eaten for two days and one night.
The Gemara asks: For how long is wine considered from the press and thus permitted?
The Gemara answers: As long as it is fermenting.
A Tanna teaches that fermenting wine is not susceptible to exposure, and its fermentation period is three days.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's custom on the eve of Tisha B'Av
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's custom on the eve of Tisha B'Av
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav describes Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's custom of eating dry bread with salt on the eve of Tisha B'Av, sitting between the oven and the stove.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav that Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's custom on the eve of Tisha B'Av was to eat dry bread with salt while sitting between the oven and the stove.

items.text: Opening description of a mourner's behavior
items.text_en: Opening description of a mourner's behavior
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes a person who eats and drinks between the oven and the stove, resembling one whose deceased lies before him, establishing the context of mourning practices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes a mourner who eats and drinks between the oven and stove, resembling one whose deceased lies before him, establishing the context of mourning practices.

items.text: Mishnah on work on Tisha b'Av and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
items.text_en: Mishnah on work on Tisha b'Av and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about varying customs of work on Tisha b'Av, where Torah scholars refrain, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says everyone should act like a Torah scholar. A supporting baraita is brought.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that on Tisha b'Av, work is done where customary, and Torah scholars always refrain.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that everyone should act like a Torah scholar and refrain from work, and a supporting baraita is cited.

items.text: Baraitot on eating, drinking, and working on Tisha b'Av
items.text_en: Baraitot on eating, drinking, and working on Tisha b'Av
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel compares eating and drinking on Tisha b'Av to Yom Kippur. Rabbi Akiva says one who works will never see a blessing. The Sages link mourning for Jerusalem to seeing its joy, citing a verse. Another baraita states that eating meat and drinking wine incurs a curse.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel comparing eating and drinking on Tisha b'Av to Yom Kippur.
Rabbi Akiva states that one who works on Tisha b'Av will never see a sign of blessing.
The Sages link working on Tisha b'Av to not mourning for Jerusalem, citing a verse that one who mourns will see its joy.
Another baraita states that eating meat and drinking wine on Tisha b'Av incurs a curse, as the verse says 'their iniquities shall be upon their bones'.

items.text: Dispute about overturning beds on Tisha b'Av
items.text_en: Dispute about overturning beds on Tisha b'Av
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda requires overturning beds, but the Sages disagree. A baraita clarifies the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda concedes for those unable, and the Sages concede for those able. The difference is about other beds. Rava rules like our Tanna that the Sages did not agree at all.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Yehuda requires overturning beds on Tisha b'Av, but the Sages did not agree with him.
A baraita records the Sages' objection to Rabbi Yehuda: what about pregnant and nursing women who cannot overturn their beds?
Rabbi Yehuda responds that he only required overturning beds for those who are physically able.
Another baraita confirms that Rabbi Yehuda concedes to the Sages for those unable, and the Sages concede to Rabbi Yehuda for those able.
The Gemara asks: what is the practical difference between the two positions if they both concede?
The Gemara answers: the difference lies in other beds (beyond the one the person sleeps on).
A baraita clarifies that when they said to overturn the bed, one overturns all beds in the house, not just his own.
Rava rules like our Tanna (of the Mishnah) that the Sages did not agree with Rabbi Yehuda at all.

items.text: Introduction of the fifteenth of Av as a festival
items.text_en: Introduction of the fifteenth of Av as a festival
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states there were no better festivals for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur. The Gemara explains Yom Kippur's significance: forgiveness and the giving of the second tablets.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel declares that there were no better festivals for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur, and the Gemara explains Yom Kippur's significance as a day of forgiveness and the giving of the second tablets.

items.text: Reasons for the fifteenth of Av's significance
items.text_en: Reasons for the fifteenth of Av's significance
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents multiple reasons: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says it was when tribes were permitted to intermarry; Rav Yosef citing Rav Nachman says it was when the tribe of Benjamin was allowed to enter the congregation; Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan says it was when the generation of the wilderness died; Ulla says it was when Hoshea ben Elah removed the guards set up by Jeroboam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason for the fifteenth of Av being a festival.
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says it was the day when the tribes were permitted to intermarry, based on a דרש (exegesis) of the verse about the daughters of Zelophehad.
Rav Yosef citing Rav Nachman says it was the day when the tribe of Benjamin was allowed to enter the congregation, based on a דרש (exegesis) of the oath at Mitzpah.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan says it was the day when the generation of the wilderness finished dying, after which divine speech resumed with Moses.
Ulla says it was the day when Hoshea ben Elah removed the guards that Jeroboam ben Nevat had stationed on the roads to prevent Israel from making the pilgrimage.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The days of rejoicing
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The days of rejoicing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on the 15th of Av and on Yom Kippur, the daughters of Jerusalem would go out and dance in the vineyards, and whoever did not have a wife would go there.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on the 15th of Av and Yom Kippur, the daughters of Jerusalem go out and dance in the vineyards, and whoever does not have a wife goes there.

items.text: Rav Mattana's reason: The burial of the slain of Beitar
items.text_en: Rav Mattana's reason: The burial of the slain of Beitar
items.desc_en: Rav Mattana explains that the 15th of Av is the day when the slain of Beitar were finally allowed to be buried, and on that day the Sages instituted the blessing of 'Hatov Vehametiv' in Yavneh.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana explains that the 15th of Av is the day the slain of Beitar were given burial, and the blessing 'הטוב והמטיב' (Who is good and does good) was instituted in Yavneh.

Rav Mattana adds that on that day the Sages instituted the blessing of 'הטוב והמטיב' (Who is good and does good) in Yavneh, explaining that 'הטוב' (the good) refers to the fact that the bodies did not decompose, and 'והמטיב' (who does good) refers to their being granted burial.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's reason: The cessation of wood chopping
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's reason: The cessation of wood chopping
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef state that the 15th of Av is the day when they stopped cutting wood for the altar, as from that day the sun's strength wanes and the wood no longer dries properly. Rav Menashya adds that this day is called 'the day of the breaking of the sickle', and from then on, one who adds study gains, and one who does not will be punished.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef state that the 15th of Av is the day they stopped cutting wood for the altar, citing a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol that from that day the sun's strength wanes and wood no longer dries properly.
Rav Menashya adds that this day is called 'the day of the breaking of the sickle', and from then on, one who adds Torah study gains, and one who does not will be 'gathered'.
Rav Yosef explains the ambiguous term 'יֵאָסֵף' (will be gathered) as a euphemism for death: 'may his mother bury him'.

items.text: The daughters of Jerusalem borrow garments
items.text_en: The daughters of Jerusalem borrow garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the Mishnah's statement that the daughters of Jerusalem would borrow garments from each other, even a princess from a commoner, to avoid embarrassing those who had none.

sub.desc_en: A baraita describes the borrowing of garments among women of different social ranks to avoid shaming those without.

items.text: All garments require immersion
items.text_en: All garments require immersion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that even garments that are folded and placed in a box require immersion before being worn.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar adds that even garments folded and stored in a box require immersion.
Rabbi Elazar adds that even garments folded and stored in a box require immersion.

items.text: The daughters of Israel go out and dance
items.text_en: The daughters of Israel go out and dance
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that whoever does not have a wife should go to the vineyards where the daughters of Israel dance.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one without a wife goes to the vineyards where the daughters dance.

items.text: What the different groups of daughters said
items.text_en: What the different groups of daughters said
items.desc_en: The Gemara records what the beautiful, the well-born, and the ugly daughters would say to the young men: the beautiful focused on beauty, the well-born on family, and the ugly on a heavenly reward.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records the sayings of the beautiful, well-born, and ugly daughters: the beautiful direct attention to beauty, the well-born to family, and the ugly to a marriage for Heaven's sake.
The baraita records what the well-born daughters would say: focus on family, for a woman is only for children.
The baraita records what the ugly daughters would say: take your acquisition for the sake of Heaven, provided you adorn us with gold.

items.text: The future dance of the righteous
items.text_en: The future dance of the righteous
items.desc_en: Ulla Bira'ah quotes Rabbi Elazar that in the future, God will make a dance for the righteous in the Garden of Eden, and each one will point to God, as it is said: 'Behold, this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He will save us.'

sub.desc_en: Ulla Bira'ah in the name of Rabbi Elazar says that in the future, God will make a dance for the righteous in the Garden of Eden, and they will point to Him with the verse from Isaiah.
